#3511. The Role of the “Queen Mother” in Monarchies Around the World: Queen Sofía, Sonia of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands

Queen Sofía celebrated her 88th birthday on November 2 and remains a pillar of the Spanish royal family, with a demanding schedule that includes at least one official engagement per week. Queen Sofía has never set aside her institutional role, unlike some other European “queen mothers” (this official title is used only in the United Kingdom but is commonly used to refer to the mothers of kings), who, to a greater or lesser extent, continue to work for the monarchy in their respective countries.

This week, Queen Sofía will be in San Fernando, Cádiz, where she will serve as patroness of the ceremony to present the National Ensign to the Marine Corps, a special unit within the Navy and the world’s oldest marine corps, created in 1537 by Emperor Charles I. Far from retiring from public life, the Queen Emerita continues to play an important role within the Crown; she retains her office at Zarzuela and receives an official stipend.

She also remains closely involved in the day-to-day activities of the Queen Sofía Foundation and regularly visits the provincial offices of the Spanish Federation of Food Banks to learn about its charitable work, among other projects. Always discreet, Felipe VI’s mother has weathered the controversies surrounding Juan Carlos and maintained a professional image dedicated to serving the Spanish people—one that her family circumstances have not tarnished.

Queen Sonja, a great source of support today for her son, King Haakon.

Following the death of her husband, King Harald, in late August, and with the newly crowned Queen Mette-Marit on medical leave, Queen Sonja of Norway has become a pillar of support for her son, Haakon VIII. Sonia of Norway is 89 years old and in recent months has had minor health scares that led to her being hospitalized for a few days in the hospital. But despite everything, she continues her duties as a member of the Norwegian royal family. Just a few days ago, Queen Sonja traveled to Málaga to attend the opening of an exhibition on Picasso and Munch at the Picasso Museum in the Andalusian city, and was all smiles during a visit to a Norwegian school in Benalmádena.

On November 3, Queen Sonja accompanied her son Haakon to an official dinner to welcome the provincial governors at the Royal Palace—an important event at which the king will have his mother’s support in the absence of his wife and his daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, who is currently focused on her university studies in Oslo. Two days later, Queen Sonja will visit the Furniture Maker School in Askim, attend the opening of a furniture exhibition at the Center for Democracy at Fort Høytorp, and meet with members of the Indre Østfold Women’s Group and young people at the Re:læx youth center in Askim.

After more than three decades as queen, Sonia of Norway has stayed by her son’s side, at a time when he needs her support more than ever. Since her accession to the throne, Queen Sonia—whom Haakon stripped of the title “Her Majesty,” now simply Queen Sonia—has become a cornerstone of institutional and family support for the new monarch.

Beatrix of the Netherlands served as queen for 33 years.

At 88 years old, Beatrix of the Netherlands does not have a schedule as busy as those of Queen Sofía or Queen Sonja of Norway, but she has continued to attend institutional events and fulfill some official engagements since her abdication in 2013. King Willem-Alexander’s mother actively participates in award ceremonies linked to the Crown, such as the Appeltjes van Oranje awards presented by the Oranje Fonds foundation—awards whose bronze statuettes she designed herself and which she attends each year alongside King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima.

In addition, Princess Beatrix continues to make official trips to the Dutch Caribbean territories (such as her recent visits to Bonaire, St. Eustatius, and Saba) to preside over events dedicated to nature conservation, sustainable development, and education. She also continues to attend certain cultural and charitable events in her home country, such as the Dutch Ballet Gala hosted by the Dansersfonds Foundation, which she attended in mid-October.

Beatrix of the Netherlands, who now resides at Drakenstein Castle, was Queen of the Netherlands for 33 years, from 1980 to 2013. Following the coronation of her son Willem, she regained the title of princess, and today her official title is Her Royal Highness Princess Beatrix of the Netherlands, Princess of Orange-Nassau, and Princess of Lippe-Biesterfeld. Beatrix of the Netherlands remains deeply loved and respected by the people, and within the Orange-Nassau royal family, she continues to support and guide her son, King Willem-Alexander.

Princess Beatrix is a great role model for her granddaughter, Princess Amalia.

Queen Sofía, Queen Sonja of Norway, and Beatrix of the Netherlands all embody the key institutional values essential to preserving the monarchy in their respective countries. Loyal to the crown in one capacity or another and having dedicated their lives to public service for decades, all three are great examples of institutional loyalty for their granddaughters— Princess Leonor, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Amalia—who will one day become queens.

#3510. Rings of Power Episode 4 Ending Explained: What Happens to Galadriel, Celeborn, and Arondir?

A devastating betrayal, a long-awaited reunion, and a shocking death hit Middle-earth

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 sees Middle-earth in the midst of full-on war as Sauron (Charlie Vickers) continues his conquest. Yet he still hasn’t figured out how to forge the one weapon he knows will solidify his title as the Dark Lord: the One Ring.

The first batch of four episodes was released Nov. 11, bringing audiences back up to speed with many of the various characters and factions in Prime Video's sprawling Lord of the Rings prequel. As Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) grapples with the nature of his true purpose in Rhûn, both Numenor and Khazad-dûm are mired in political turmoil. Meanwhile the elves are struggling in the war as Sauron continues recruiting men to become his Nazgnagôl. (What about the Harfoots? We'll get to them later. Maybe.)

It all leads up to one of the show's most devastating moments yet at the end of The Rings of Power season 3, episode 4. What begins as a daring rescue mission inside the orc stronghold of Gundabad ends with an emotional reunion, a shocking death, and another demonstration of just how thoroughly Sauron corrupts those around him. Here's what happens at the end of The Rings of Power season 3, episode 4, and what it all means for the show going forward.

The episode's most important storyline unfolds as Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and the orc general Marnûkh (Adam Young) reach the fortress of Gundabad, where they hope to find an Elven smith they believe Sauron needs to forge the One Ring. Unfortunately, it’s all essentially a waste of time because Marnûkh and Arondir discover that the smith is already dead. But just across the way, in another cell, they find Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), Galadriel's long-lost husband, who has been held captive for centuries.

Celeborn proves instrumental in their escape, since Marnûkh’s knowledge of the fortress is a bit outdated. While Celeborn initially plans to flee by himself, once he hears them mention Galadriel, who has become separated from the group, he quickly helps them find her. After a touching reunion, they have to fight their way through the fortress to reach the roof. Galadriel’s plan involves lighting off a sort of flare with an arrow to call Landroval, the prince of the Great Eagles, who will carry them to safety. But with orcs closing in on them and firing arrows, Landroval has to hide until it’s safe for him to swoop in.

Then everything falls apart when one of the Nazgnagôl shows up and cuts Marnûkh down. Galadriel pleads with Arondir to run away, but he stands his ground. The Nazgnagôl encourages Arondir to flee and then takes off his helmet, revealing that it’s Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), the son of Arondir’s former human lover, Bronwyn (Nazanin Boniadi), who had died in season 2. For a moment, it actually appears like Arondir might be able to convince Theo to take off the ring, but then Sauron arrives. He commands Theo to kill Arondir, and the swift way the attack happens make it seem like Sauron was controlling him directly.

Celeborn drags Galadriel over the ledge where they’re caught by Landroval, but the episode ends on a shot of Arondir's lifeless face.

It's a particularly cruel end for a character who has spent his entire story protecting others. Arondir even risks his life to save Marnûkh, an orc he really doesn’t like to begin with, only to die because he refuses to give up on Theo. The scene also makes Sauron’s control over the Nazgnagôl abundantly clear, even before he forges the One Ring. Theo’s hesitation, however, indicates that this control isn’t absolute without the One Ring.

Season 3 also introduces Durin’s (Owain Arthur) older brother Thráin (Eddie Marsan), and though their reunion seems mostly cheerful at first, it quickly descends into outright betrayal. By episode 4, Thráin openly challenges Durin's authority after the other Dwarf-lords demand access to the Seven Rings. They believe the rings could help protect their kingdoms, but Durin rightfully doesn’t trust their influence after seeing first-hand how it drove their father mad.

Thráin cleverly turns that argument against him. If their father was no longer of sound mind while wearing the ring, Thráin reasons, then his decision to name Durin as heir may not have been legitimate. This leads Thráin to formally challenge Durin to a trial by combat. But Thráin wants the rings more than he wants the throne. Before the fight, he tries to manipulate Disa into getting him the rings.

Before Disa and Durin were married, they had a fight and briefly split up. During that time, she and Thráin had a brief romantic encounter. Thráin threatens to tell Durin unless Disa convinces Durin to give him the Seven Rings, and he promises to abandon his claim to the throne in exchange.

Rather than submit to the blackmail, Disa confesses everything to Durin, and he forgives her. For a moment, it seems like Durin just needs to beat his brother and all will be well. But right before the duel, Durin’s son Gamli tells his father that he saw Disa with Thráin. This sends Durin flying into a rage, attacking his brother, ultimately leading to Thráin winning. We don’t see the aftermath, but the implication is clear: Thráin now has the throne and likely control of the rings (if he’s able to find them).

A contingent of Númenorians — called the Faithful — including Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and Isildur (Maxim Baldry) have been working behind the scenes to defy Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) with the help of Eärien (Emma Horvath), who remains in Numenorian court. After she’s found out and dies at the end of episode 2, however, Pharazôn makes a play at kidnapping Elendil that ultimately fails when Elendil’s son Anárion (Andrew Richardson) saves him. All of this infighting is probably why, after the elves request aid from Numenor, Pharazôn sends them a rejection letter.

In episode 4, we see the elf leaders Círdan (Ben Daniels) and Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker) lamenting the state of the war in the aftermath of a battle against orcs. In a meeting with Elrond, he argues that the elves need to seek military assistance from Númenor. Elrond believes a personal appeal from the elven king might change the situation, and Círdan suggests that Elrond accompany him. Not only does Elrond have a great deal of experience in dealing with the other races, but his identical twin brother Elros was the founder and first king of Númenor.

That sets up a pretty clear trajectory for the show moving forward as some of these disconnected plotlines start to converge: Gil-galad and Elrond are heading to Númenor, while war continues to rage. Middle-earth history paints a pretty clear picture of where things go from here.

For now, however, the most immediate consequences of episode 4 are felt in Gundabad. Galadriel has finally recovered her husband, but Arondir is dead, Theo remains under the Dark Lord’s influence, and Sauron is inching ever closer to finally creating the One Ring.

Tony DiNozzo's return and subsequent promotion to Director of NCIS is the big story of Season 24. It was a surprising twist, and one that longtime fan and star Katrina Law told CinemaBlend she was amped for. It turns out she had a lot of questions about how Jessica Knight and Tony would interact, and she loved what the team came up with.

As NCIS continues its run on the 2026 TV schedule, I spoke to Law about the season thus far, as well as what we've seen. I talked about Michael Weatherly's big role in the new season, and she confirmed she was absolutely psyched to see the former vet of the show back in action:

I was geeked out. I've been an OG fan of the show, and Weatherly and actually Tiva has been my favorite part of the show, and I kept pitching all of these ideas of like, oh, what could Weatherly and Knight's relationship be?How do we meet? What's going to happen? And not once did I ever think I would be the informant for Ziva about his caloric intake. I love it. I think it's hysterical.

While she might've preferred to see her buddy McGee get the job as NCIS director, Jessica Knight has found good footing with Tony thus far. Granted, she's basically playing spy for his wife Ziva, but that kind of leverage can go a long way toward keeping her in his good graces.

I also had to bring up that Knight mentioning on camera that she's in contact with Ziva sets the stage for Cote de Pablo's eventual return to NCIS as well. Katrina Law confirmed she's optimistic we'll see Ziva before too long, and there's going to be a lot of fun stuff happening with her and Knight:

I fully expect Ziva to come onto our show and Knight and Ziva team up and just make Weatherly extremely uncomfortable, but then go off and like have a massive fight scene together to take down some bad guy.

She's been thinking about this team-up for a while, for the record, and I'm so excited for the day it finally happens. For now, she'll continue to solve crimes with her team and keep Tony on his toes with her occasional trolling of his eating habits.

Tony needs that so far, as he continues to look for ways to settle into his new role at the top of the NCIS team. He's tried to jump in and participate in the investigations, much to the chagrin of some of the agents. We'll see if he gets any better at taking a step back, letting them do their jobs, and watching from the sidelines and offering any support he can.

Being the director is not an easy job, and one that's filled with hazards. In fact, the past few NCIS directors have died, which may have fans sweating and wondering just how long Tony will sit in the role. Will he step away before he ends up in a body bag, or will he break the trend and end up staying at the top until retirement hits?

NCIS continues on CBS on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. Tune in for more of the team as they track down the bad guys and get to know each other better. I'm excited for more interactions between Jessica and Tony, and that eventual team-up with Ziva that's on the way.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

Despite its small size, it supports 4K streaming over Wi-Fi 6, along with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG for improved contrast and color on compatible televisions. What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. You can also use Alexa to search for shows, launch apps, or control compatible smart home devices. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. Still, if you're comfortable with Amazon's interface and don't need the missing Dolby formats, the Fire TV Stick 4K delivers responsive streaming and a useful remote for just $25.

#3507. VisionQuest: The Identity Of The Client, Explained

Spoilers ahead for "VisionQuest" Episode 8, "Forever."

Ultron (James Spader) may have no strings on him anymore, but someone has been manipulating the events of "VisionQuest" like a puppetmaster. That someone is The Client, who hired the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) to capture Vision (Paul Bettany). We've gotten glimpses of The Client all season, but only as a digitally altered voice or a faceless avatar ... until Episode 7, "Immolation."

At the episode's end, Vision and Ultron's gynoid lover Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) are delivered to The Client's doorstep. Out of said door walks ... someone who looks just like Ultron's human avatar. Huh?

"Forever" clarifies it. "The Client" is Virgil Horton, grandson of Phineas Horton (Bettany), the scientist who created the Synthetic Man/Human Torch (Bettany again) in the 1940s. As Virgil explains, the Synthetic Man's uncontrolled fire powers mean that Dr. Horton was considered a failure. Years ago, Virgil joined with Dr. Josephine Carrington (Miller) to perfect AI in hopes of redeeming the Horton family legacy. They scanned their own brainwaves to create the genesis of what Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.) completed.

Horton and Carrington also fell in love. After Carrington's death from a terminal illness, Horton revived her as Jocasta. As Virgil explains, he was one of the engineers hired by SWORD to rebuild Vision back in "WandaVision." After that, he created a robotic body for Carrington's mind-scanned AI. Jocasta being a recent creation helps explain why she looks like feminine Ultron, but why did Virgil then erase her memories of him and her creation?

Virgil believes the only worthy lover of a "goddess" like Jocasta is a god. So, he intends to delete Vision's personality and then upload himself into Vision's shell, so he and Jocasta can rule an Earth infected with Jocasta's hive mind nanites.

Virgil's borderline-incestuous romance plan echoes the central influence of Ultron: "Frankenstein," specifically when the Creature asks Doctor Frankenstein to make him a companion. Virgil's plan is rather similar to Kenneth Branagh's 1994 "Frankenstein" film adaptation, where Victor Frankenstein (Branagh) tries to resurrect his dead wife Elizabeth (Helena Bonham Carter) through the same process by which he made the Creature (Robert De Niro).

There's an implication that Virgil scanning his brainwaves for his and Josephine's AI embedded his personality into the AI code. That's why Ultron basically has his same flamboyant personality, his voice, and why Ultron wears Virgil's face as his human avatar. "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas has said giving Ultron a human form in "VisionQuest" was about getting the most out of Spader's performance. Now, we know, it was also essential to the pay off of this twist about the Client's identity. But "Forever" breaks out Ultron's robotic form, too.

Virgil's plan fails because Jocasta has fallen for Ultron and wants him to be her eternal partner. Using the nanites, Ultron recreates his physical form and crushes Horton to death with a hug. It's a very Oedipal move: Ultron's defining goal has always been killing his father, whether it be Hank Pym (in Marvel's comics) or Tony Stark (in the Marvel Cinematic Universe). He comes close to that by killing the man of whom he's an artificial echo.

Ultron being based on Virgil also explains why fell for Jocasta in the first place. This restores some of the mirroring of the creator and creation that's present in comics Ultron. In the "Avengers" comics, Ultron created Jocasta from the brainwaves of Hank Pym's wife: Janet van Dyne, the Wasp, and his spiritual mother. Since Ultron is based on Hank's personality, he inherited his father's affections for Janet though extremely twisted means. The same logic applies to Spader's Ultron falling for this Jocasta.

Now, it's worth noting that while Phineas Horton and his Human Torch originated in Marvel Comics, Virgil did not. Rather, he's an original creation of this series, and "VisionQuest" seems to be using him as a proxy for the original Dr. Horton. Previously, Steve Englehart and George Tuska's "Avengers" #135 tied Horton and the Ultron-Vision lineage together, with the issue revealing that Ultron had abducted Phineas Horton and forced him to rebuild the inert Human Torch into the Vision.

Keep in mind, Ultron and Vision debuted in 1968. At that time, it was plausible that a scientist active in World War II would be living in retirement. But not so much in 2026, where it makes much more sense to use a descendant of Horton in the present day. It's the same time creep that led to Captain America originally missing only two decades of time while frozen to awakening almost a century later.

#3506. The Subpoenas Are Coming, the Subpoenas Are Coming: Tech Execs Brace for Congressional Crackdown, Say Lobbyists

On Thursday, I was on the phone with a source when he suddenly sounded like he’d gotten the wind knocked out of him. We were in the middle of talking about antitrust policy when he exhaled and said, “Wow. Worst one-day destruction of value in history. Just got the Wall Street Journal alert.”

The tech world—and the markets built on top of it—is still figuring out how to feel about last week’s momentous Democratic midterm sweep. My Republican sources, unsurprisingly, reported that the vibes in their ranks are “horrendous.” Anyone who works with data centers is just about ready to throw in the towel on planet Earth and take their infrastructure efforts to space, with voters having opposed data center construction via 40 different ballot measures. And then there’s the more general rebuke of the future the tech industry is building, and the possible implications for an economy that’s increasingly come to revolve around it.

Indeed, it seems that the debate over AI has really, truly broken through to the mainstream this year: According to an NBC exit poll, 56% of voters called AI and data centers a “crucial or major factor” in their votes for Congress. Amid the free-for-all of President Trump’s first two years back in office, AI companies have been allowed to develop their technology largely free of regulatory oversight, but they may now be forced to pump the brakes.

In a lengthy interview with Ross Douthat on CBS’s 60 Minutes, Trump said he was open to working with Democrats to implement some AI guardrails. Still, no one I spoke to this week told me they expect to see sweeping AI legislation—unless, as two different tech Democrats suggested, there is an AI-caused catastrophe that “scares the shit out of us.”

Democratic Senators like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren have already begun making plans to investigate tech corporations.

In the absence of such an event, “we expect [new AI laws] to be narrow and bipartisan. Child safety, AI agent liability, and predeployment testing, for example, all have Republican cosponsors,” said Christina Ho, an executive at the financial auditing firm Oath Verified.

Meanwhile, even more explicitly MAGA-coded industries could see more concrete crackdowns. Those in “the crypto world,” who spent the first year of Trump 2.0 flying high, now “realize they’re screwed,” said an executive at a conservative think tank—especially as famed crypto critic Sherrod Brown makes his big return to the Senate with, as one Democratic strategist put it, an “axe to grind.”

Defense-tech founders and investors may also find themselves toning down their rhetoric as the testosterone-fueled “Department of War” era comes to an end with the possible impeachment of Secretary Pete Hegseth. In recent years, “dual use” has become a bit of a “dirty word,” said Cody Huggins, a partner at Scout Ventures. He suspects that promoting the commercial applications of military technologies, from satellites to drones, “will come back to be a little bit more sexy than it has been.”

Perhaps the biggest winners of the post-midterms period will be the DC law firms brought on to help manage the flood of subpoenas promised by politicians like Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. “AI executives might be called to testify,” said Ho, adding, “Companies would be wise to prepare their executives for the witness table before they prepare for any new laws.”

A Democratic tech lobbyist told me that one of his clients has already received a list of questions from a congressional committee. “They’re not waiting to have gavels,” he said.

Luther Lowe, the head of public policy at the start-up accelerator Y Combinator, is hoping to see a return to the antitrust revolution once promised by former FTC chair Lina Khan. “I think some of that stuff could come back online,” he said, referring to antitrust legislation that then Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer declined to bring to a vote in 2022.

In the future, tech executives who went all in on MAGA (right after going all in on woke) may want to consider some age-old advice: just be yourself. “Companies need to stop thinking about political outcomes as permanent conditions. Regulations change, governments change, and priorities change. That’s not new,” said Andrew Peek, CEO of the investing platform Tilt. “What’s different now is the sheer amount of money being committed to technologies whose economics are still evolving. If your entire strategy only works under one political scenario, that’s a pretty big risk to be taking.”

Still, there was one midterm fight in which the tech world definitively won out: the one over Proposition 40, or California’s so-called billionaire tax, which was defeated. Some suspect that the hundreds of millions of dollars spent by Silicon Valley billionaires to defeat the measure could backfire. “There’s a growing wave of anger and resentment from the working class that is coming for them,” said the Democratic strategist. The irony of spending so much money to fight the tax, he said, is that if it had passed, it could have “temporarily removed some of the pressure in the pressure cooker.” All that money having been spent to shut down the tax, he warned, “is gonna make things much worse.”

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. If you can do without cellular connectivity, the 45mm wifi model is also down by $100, now selling for a record-low $329.99 (down from $429.99). Plus, either one comes with 90 days of free Amazon Music. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. As for its health hardware, Google left it largely untouched, so you still get heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring, ECG readings, skin temperature, GPS, and sleep tracking, with reportedly accurate findings. The catch is that this remains an Android-only watch, requiring Android 12 or newer, and some of the better AI features work best with a newer Pixel phone.

Physically, the Watch 5 doesn’t stray far from its predecessor, keeping the familiar domed display under 3D Corning Gorilla Glass while adding new watch faces that curve around its edges—with the screen reaching up to 3,000 nits and adjusting to ambient light, so it should remain easy to read during a sunny afternoon run or in a dim room. As for its durability, its IP68 and 5ATM ratings mean you can wear it through a workout, at the beach, or in the pool without worrying about dust or water. And charging shouldn’t necessarily be a nightly routine, either, with the watch lasting up to 56.5 hours in testing. Heavier use will cut into that figure, but you should still have a good chance of making it through two full days with enough power left to track your sleep overnight.

For over 20 years now, the 2003 Mike Myers version of The Cat In The Hat has been the only version of the classic Dr. Seuss book to watch. However, this past weekend, it got the animation treatment, and it’s a blast of an adaptation. I even have an idea for a spinoff, and I ran it by some of the cast. SPOILERS ahead!

Look, I like The Cat, especially because he’s voiced by Bill Hader years after he played the character on SNL. But to me, the real highlight of the film are The Things. In my opinion, they are like much more likeable Minions, and the movie even explores what can happen to one when they get villainous. As we learn at the end of The Cat In The Hat, the reason why Thing 2 was missing is that he became The Something due to overusing the Go-Backer device. Oh, and of course there’s that meta line where The Cat tells The Things to wait for their own movie.

The Things are pretty mysterious characters, but I thought The Cat in the Hat did an excellent job of making them so fun and intriguing. I think it would be so much fun to see them on their own adventure after this movie earned a thumbs-up with audiences through an “A” CinemaScore. Though it’ll have to earn more money at the box office after Godzilla Minus Zero won the weekend.

When CinemaBlend spoke to the cast of The Cat In The Hat, I brought up the topic of a Things spinoff. Here’s what Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson, a.k.a. Sherrie from HR in the movie, had to say:

I wanna learn everything about them. This movie opening the crate, so to speak, on The Thing world, made me wanna know way more. I still have a lot of questions. Like, are they related? Are they from a planet? Is there offspring? Do they fall in love? Do they get married? I have a lot of questions. Why are they numbered? Do they have names beyond the numbers?

I love all these questions she has about The Things, because I had many of them myself. The Things have always been a memorable part of The Cat In The Hat book, but it would be so fun for a spinoff to explore who they are without The Cat. Here’s what Mr. Hoogeboom voice actor Giancarlo Esposito added:

I'm fascinated by The Things. I think they're on some advanced level of intellectual and emotional feeling. I just think that they're simpler, and somehow they communicate in a way that's clearer than any words could ever get.

I feel like a lot of kids are going to start learning Thinglish as is, and I wanted my own Thing plushy the moment I finished the movie. I even brought it up to the writer/directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni. Here’s what Carloni had to say about my idea:

If we're so lucky that the audience wants more of the characters we created, that would be very flattering. Give them what they want.

We’ll have to wait and see if this becomes a reality! For now, you can watch The Cat In The Hat only in theaters.

#3503. VisionQuest's Finale Finally Pays Off A Story Marvel Started In Avengers: Age Of Ultron

What is grief if not spoilers persevering? This article discusses major plot details from the season finale of "VisionQuest."

An argument could be made that the "VisionQuest" finale was a confrontation over a decade in the making. Clearly, the well-received Disney+ series has marketed itself as a "WandaVision" sequel and a trilogy-capper to the story continued in "Agatha All Along." But there's no way around its biggest and most pressing concern: providing a fitting epilogue to the 2015 blockbuster "Avengers: Age of Ultron." In an inspired choice, "VisionQuest" showrunner Terry Matalas understood there was still plenty of unfinished business between James Spader's megalomaniac robot Ultron and Paul Bettany's synthezoid Vision, which finally pays off spectacularly in the eighth and final episode of the show.

Once Vision and Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) realize that the mysterious Client dogging their steps is actually Virgil Horton (also played by Spader), the descendant of Phineas Horton (aka the mind behind the Synthetic Man, as portrayed by Bettany), this sets up the finale's most compelling battle. No, it's not Horton's toxic, twisted love for Dr. Jo Carrington and his desire to inhabit Vision's body so they may live forever together. It's the apparent murder of Ultron's lover Jocasta, setting off Ultron's malevolence towards humanity and one last showdown with Vision.

This is precisely the kind of potential that shared universes were meant to fully realize — not cameos and references for the sake of it or disposable narratives to throw on in the background as white noise, but as meaningful additions to ongoing arcs for viewers willing to take the time to explore them. That may go down as the greatest accomplishment of "VisionQuest" in its finale, delivering the perfect button on the Ultron saga that "Age of Ultron" simply couldn't pull off.

Amazing what eight hours of storytelling can do that studio-meddled blockbusters never could, eh? In spite of its obvious shortcomings and compromises, we here at /Film are long-suffering defenders of "Avengers: Age of Ultron." Arguably the last time the Marvel Cinematic Universe was able to be as weird and messy and introspective as the comics themselves, the movie still managed to find moments of quiet poignancy amid all the mind-numbing spectacle. To no surprise, that's something showrunner Terry Matalas and his writers have carried over into "VisionQuest," and nowhere is that more confidently on display than in the finale.

We're not only talking about the moment when a dying Jocasta merges Ultron with the horde of killer nanobots and allows him to regain his physical form, fighting Vision in a well-staged battle that ought to be many a nerd's dream come to life. What puts the finale over the top is when it somehow combines the best of "Age of Ultron" with "WandaVision." Vision traps Ultron inside a sitcom-set mindscape where the two artificial beings can hash out their differences without throwing hands and trading particle beams at each other. If previous episodes filled in some Ultron-centric plot holes, then this one brings us back to their best moment of all — when, in the midst of Sokovia's destruction, the two land in an idyllic forest to talk about humanity's doomed fate, the grace found in their failings, and the fact that nothing beautiful is meant to last forever.

Here, the big climactic fight becomes a treatise on Ultron's all-consuming grief, his unresolved malevolence towards human beings, and, deep down, his debilitating fear of being alone.

To the credit of "VisionQuest," this season-long epilogue suggests there's more to his emotional journey than a single movie could ever explore. The finale digs even deeper to prove this, completing Ultron's transformation into something much more human by giving him someone to love. Despite the changes made to the comics' origins, the Ultron/Jocasta romance is a defining moment in Ultron's portrayal in the MCU. Finally, he can understand Vision's own progression to becoming an individual in his own right, along with all the joy and loss and humanity that comes with it.

That's probably why, even after he retreats back to his old ways and attempts to cause our extinction again, "VisionQuest" posits that Ultron isn't beyond redemption. Sure, it isn't until he's confronted with his own mortality that he finally decides to spare the world's population. But even that is as human as it gets. Vision helps him come to terms with what life has to offer. And when we leave him, eager to appreciate human art and perhaps even rebuild Jocasta, it's a perfect period to the end of his sentence ... or, perhaps, an ellipsis.

"VisionQuest" is now streaming on Disney+ in its entirety.

#3502. Why Prince William Is Reluctant to Become Head of the Commonwealth

Following King Charles’s successful nine-day tour to the Caribbean, the future of the Commonwealth has become a much debated subject. At last week’s Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, Charles, who was designated Head of the Commonwealth, a role he assumed after his late mother Queen Elizabeth, told assembled leaders he found the voluntary union of 56 nations to be a “source of enormous encouragement and pride.”

However, Buckingham Palace has made it clear this weekend that Charles will only serve as monarch in the Caribbean realms “for as long as they wish” and that the monarch is open to change. According to The Times, Charles is “fully open” to those realms removing him as head of state.

While Charles was in the Caribbean, there was ongoing debate about slave trade reparations, which the monarch addressed in his speech to CHOGM. Describing it as a “monstrous injustice” he expressed his “profound personal sorrow” but fell short of making a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade. (Since King Charles is a ceremonial head of state, he is unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless the government sanctions it.)

Amid calls for reparations, there are questions about the future of the Commonwealth and who its next head should be. In conversation with Vanity Fair, constitutional expert Ed Owens, author of After Elizabeth: Can the Monarchy Save Itself?, discusses what’s in store for the future.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

King Charles reacts near Antigua and Barbuda flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda on November 2, 2026 in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda.

Vanity Fair: Prince William has made it clear that he does not necessarily expect to follow his father as head of the Commonwealth, saying that the decision belongs to the Commonwealth itself.

Ed Owens: Prince William hinted after his difficult 2022 tour of Belize, the Bahamas, and Jamaica that he wasn’t focused on following his father as head of the Commonwealth. A couple of weeks ago The Times of London confirmed that the prince’s position was unchanged on this issue. Crucially, the position of head of the Commonwealth is not hereditary. King Charles got the role because his mother and predecessor, Queen Elizabeth II, actively lobbied Commonwealth heads of state to ensure that the role would pass to him when he became monarch, following her death. But it will not automatically transfer to William when Charles dies.

What is the Commonwealth and how significant is that statement?

The Commonwealth of Nations (as it’s officially known) is a voluntary association of 56 independent member states. Most of these member states were once colonies in the British empire. Decolonization began after World War II and most newly independent states—though no longer part of the empire—became part of the new Commonwealth. This new international body represented change but also continuity, enabling Britain to maintain a global (but mostly symbolic) presence at a time when its real geopolitical power was rapidly in retreat. The Commonwealth also provided a stage for the monarchy to continue to exercise an important international role. George VI was the last emperor and first Head of the Commonwealth. The latter role was invented by the British government to replace the former and allowed the monarch to maintain a semblance of global prestige while helping to facilitate the process of decolonization.

Although most member states have historical ties to Britain, any country can apply to join the Commonwealth—exemplified by recent members like Rwanda, Mozambique, Gabon, and Togo. Members commit to shared principles outlined in the Commonwealth charter, including democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and sustainable development. In reality, though, many member states have failed to live up to these principles, and the Commonwealth has, in recent years, felt morally directionless.

William’s reluctance to take on the mantle of Head of the Commonwealth isn’t that surprising: He and his advisers want to future-proof his reign. One way to do this is to identify potential problems in order to avoid them. The Commonwealth is one such potential problem, and William seems to have calculated that the headship of this organization likely represents more trouble than it is worth.

Does it represent a fundamental shift in the monarchy’s attitude toward the organization, or simply an acknowledgement that the old imperial relationship is no longer sustainable?

We have to remember that 15 members of the Commonwealth (including the UK) are also “realms”—i.e. their head of state is King Charles. I think it’s clear even to the current king that his position as monarch of the 14 realms beyond Britain is unsustainable. Eventually all 14 nations, and perhaps the UK too, will opt to become republics, cutting their ties with the crown. Those nations most likely to become republics soonest—owing to the fact that they have surging republican movements—are the Caribbean realms, two of which (the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda) King Charles visited during his recent tour to the Caribbean. Indeed, we can even interpret the tour as the king and his courtiers preparing the ground for this transition to republics. This is because, though former realms will no longer have as their head of state the incumbent monarch, they will almost certainly remain members of the wider Commonwealth.

What King Charles was trying to do with his latest tour was to inject energy and meaning into the idea of the Commonwealth, more than attempt to reinvigorate the personal bonds that connect him to his peoples in the Caribbean. In loudly acknowledging the injustices of the slave trade in which Britain was, for a long time, complicit, while also reminding his hosts that Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish and oppose slavery—the king has sought to address and ease concerns in ways that might enable the Commonwealth to function more cohesively in the future, irrespective of whether the UK’s monarch remains in post as head of the Commonwealth.

When Charles eventually leaves the throne, could the Commonwealth decide that it no longer needs a British monarch as its figurehead? What might replace that role? Will the Commonwealth continue?

I absolutely think [the] Commonwealth nations will look to replace the British monarch with a new figurehead. My sense is that many nations would already prefer to have a different kind of figurehead, for example a head who belongs to one of the 56 member states and is elected by member states for a set term. Alternatively, there could be some kind of “rolling” headship, whereby every member nation is invited to elect an official who will take a 12-month turn as head of the Commonwealth.

Whether or not the Commonwealth will continue is more difficult to say. Certainly one of the reasons it has survived until now is because of the energy and engagement of two British monarchs—Charles and Elizabeth II—who have viewed it as a potential force for good in the world. Without its connection to the British monarchy, it may lose what is left of its momentum. However, its survival also depends on wider geopolitical shifts: If individual governments within the Commonwealth view it as [a] useful arena for bringing together states who could benefit from closer association—be that economic, political, or military association—then it may continue long into the future.

There is an increasingly difficult conversation about Britain’s colonial past, slavery, and reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over the slave trade, but the question of a formal apology remains politically and constitutionally complicated. How much freedom does the king actually have to address these issues, and could William take a different approach?

The king has very little freedom to apologize unless his government specifically sanctions and encourages such an apology. As the recent Caribbean tour made clear, I think Charles would prefer to strike a more nuanced line, reminding audiences that, despite the UK’s colonial past and its involvement in the horrors of slavery, Britain was one of the first major powers to abolish slavery and that it played an important role in bringing to an end the maritime trade in human chattel. Whether William takes a different approach will depend entirely on the UK government’s approach to formal apologies and reparations. My sense is that no government—at least not now or in the near-to-medium-term future—will agree to financial reparations, because historians, philosophers, and politicians are increasingly pushing back on such a solution, questioning why UK taxpayers (already under huge strain) should fork out huge sums for the wrongs committed by some of their ancestors more than two centuries ago.

What would Queen Elizabeth II make of this? She saw the Commonwealth as her father’s legacy and her second family.

I think she would probably be relatively relaxed, recognizing that times change and institutions have to evolve. Let’s not forget that as queen she oversaw many key alterations in the way both the monarchy and Commonwealth functioned through her long reign, as was required by shifts in politics, economics, culture, and social norms. While the Commonwealth was of emotional importance to her—not least for the way it connected her back to her father and predecessors—by the end of her reign it was already a shadow of what it once had been and she would have known that it was likely to continue on a trajectory of decline. William has decided that given the challenges and changes of the mid-20th century the monarchy and royal family’s future is likely to be stronger without the post-imperial baggage of the Commonwealth. I think his grandmother would have respected the way he is putting the family firm first in this instance.

#3501. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3500. Dragon Quest Creator Says New Game Will Capture the Series' 'Unmistakable Feeling'

Dragon Quest RPG will come out worldwide in 2027

The Dragon Quest series has taken players on countless journeys over the past four decades. Next year, fans will be able to embark on a new Dragon Quest adventure using their smartphones with the launch of Dragon Quest RPG The Cursed Tree and The Chosen Isle.

RPGs come in all shapes and forms, but if you're looking for an old-school turn-based JRPG, Square Enix is taking Dragon Quest back to its origins with a classic adventure in Dragon Quest RPG The Cursed Tree and The Chosen Isle. Wright Flyer Studios, a Japanese developer known for smartphone games such as the Another Eden series and Heaven Burns Red, is developing the mobile title.

In this next installment in the Dragon Quest series, players will fight monsters and explore the land as they rebuild Yyghaven, after a goddess named Belusha entrusts them with the sacred branch of a tree. To succeed, they must lead a party into hundreds of turn-based battles, hone their fighting skills and powers, and build a secure home base where they make weapons and cook with ingredients they find in the overworld. Based on the trailer, the main side characters are called Theodore and Etica.

Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii has expressed his excitement for the launch of Dragon Quest RPG The Cursed Tree and The Chosen Isle. While few details are known about the game, Horii's words imply that this will be a traditional Dragon Quest game, unlike the franchise's other mobile ventures. Horii said that the game's goal is to "capture that unmistakable Dragon Quest feeling" that comes with "exploring towns, meeting new allies, gearing up and steadily growing stronger," which is why they put "RPG" in the name. As he puts it, Dragon Quest RPG is "the same classic adventure, brought to your smartphone." And who better to claim this than the series creator himself?

Dragon Quest RPG The Cursed Tree and The Chosen Isle is in development and is expected to release in 2027. A closed beta test will take place from Dec. 8 through Dec. 15, so players can get a feel for Dragon Quest RPG and provide feedback that will be vital to its improvement.

Square Enix is accepting applications for the closed beta test on the Dragon Quest RPG website until Nov. 23 at 9:59 a.m. EDT. Up to 25,000 players will be selected to participate in the closed beta testing for Dragon Quest RPG. Entry will be granted using a lottery system. However, for better performance, the iPhone 14 with 6 GB RAM or an Android 13.0 device with Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 — or better — is recommended.

I would like to begin this story about Julie Chen Moonves commenting on the future of Big Brother by noting the longtime host of the CBS reality series is not planning an exit anytime soon. There will, well likely, be no goodbye episode for her in the near future, but given the show’s popularity, I’d be willing to bet she’ll retire before Big Brother is off the air. She’s seen the conversations surrounding her exit, and she’s honestly in agreement.

So, first let’s talk about the fan speculation. As recently as three months ago, some fans were speculating they think Julie Chen Moonves will leave Big Brother after Season 30. Season 28 just wrapped with Rick Devens as the winner, and the show airs in the summer, which would give her a couple more seasons on the TV schedule before bowing out. Of course, this is complete speculation, and the reality host has not said anything either way.

In other threads, fans have mentioned thinking that Big Brother and Amazing Race contestant, and Big Brother: Unlocked star could be the ideal choice. Honestly, it’s been a bit divisive, with some fans noting:

Even though the issue is apparently divisive, I know in general Big Brother fans can be haters and in many ways Hale would be an obvious and solid choice. The people worried about her being too polished in particular I think are reading into it hard. Chen Moonves herself is polished, professional and deeply unemotional as the host. I guess what I'm saying is it's impossible to make everyone happy, and Julie Chen Moonves is not a hater when it comes to Taylor Hale. In an interview with Variety, the interviewer casually mentioned the possibility of Taylor Hale taking over, and this is what Chen Moonves had to say.

I’ve wondered that too because, to me, she would be perfect.

But then I don’t know how the network would feel about, ‘Is it too close to home that they’ve walked in their shoes? Does that put them too much in a position of judgment?' Part of me feels like maybe you want to keep the air pristine and have someone who comes from a news background. I got hired because I know how to do live interviews.

At the time, it was heavily a social experiment as much as a reality show, and her background fed into that.

It would change things if Julie Chen Moonves were to leave, but I do think another contestant would be close enough to the franchise to step into her shoes flawlessly, and Taylor and Derek in particular do have the background to potentially do so.

Of course, this is if and when she ever steps down. She previously told EW she was "playing a game of chicken" with CBS' Jeff Probst and Phil Keoghan and would stick it out as long as they would. (Note: Jeff and Phil are also both older than the 56-year-old star is at 65 and 59 respectively.) We'll have to wait and see what happens, but I'm just saying, don't expect an announcement tomorrow.

#3498. The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3 Opening Credits Have A Hidden Connection To HBO's White Lotus [Exclusive]

As viewers make their long-awaited return to Middle-earth in Season 3 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," they will inevitably find things a bit different compared to where they last left off. The war that was teased at the conclusion of Season 2 has finally arrived, led by Charlie Vickers' Sauron unmasked in all his Dark Lord, uh, lordliness. A five-year time jump has reset the board considerably, putting heroes like Elrond (Robert Aramayo) and Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) on their back foot. But, as of Episode 2, fans will notice a significant tweak has been made to the opening credits sequence — one which contains an unseen connection to another popular streaming series.

Prior to the premiere, I recently attended the press junket for "The Rings of Power" and spoke with co-showrunner Patrick McKay about the third season. In our limited time together, I wanted to address the noticeably darker edge to the title sequence this time around and whether there might be any Easter eggs worth paying attention to, as has been the case in the prior two seasons. The creative team worked with studio and creative consultant Plains of Yonder, who crafted the sand-based vibrational look for the opening credits of "The Rings of Power" and apparently pitched a new approach for Season 3. Here's a behind-the-scenes featurette showcasing their previous work:

But observant fans may recognize the fingerprints of another haunting title sequence. Fans of HBO's "White Lotus," this one's for you. As proudly displayed on their website, Plains of Yonder was also involved in everyone's favorite dramedy about "when everybody goes to the hotel" (as McKay hilariously put it in our interview) and, specifically, the wallpaper-focused title sequence with some seriously unsettling imagery. Not surprisingly, the designers pulled a similar trick with "The Rings of Power."

In keeping with the theme of Season 3 of "The Rings of Power," Patrick McKay explained that Plains of Yonder pitched a different approach for the episodes to come. Where Seasons 1 and 2 contained hidden references and symbols pointing towards specific events of the story, the designers felt called to go in another direction. "They're really serious artists," McKay told me with obvious admiration for their skills. "They're really wonderful people to work with. I mean, we find [their work on Season 2] hypnotic."

Episode 2 provides our first glimpse of the newly-revamped opening credits sequence, with the familiar-looking particulates now taking on a much darker color palette as they reform into all sorts of different visuals: evocative landscapes, elemental imagery, and plenty more examples of abstract art. According to McKay:

"Season 3, they're like, 'We want to do something different. We want to change the entire thing. We want to revisit the concept and make it feel like this season feels [emotionally], rather than reference things that happen in the season.' So it's a little different this time. It's a little more dramatic, has a little more darkness to it."

The visuals certainly help strike a different tone for Season 3, although the stirring musical theme by "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy composer Howard Shore remains perfectly intact. This seems to suggest that, even in its darkest moments, Middle-earth always retains a glimmer of hope. New episodes of "The Rings of Power" stream on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3497. Loose Lips Sink Chips: Silicon Valley Reacts to the (Alleged) Spy Who Shagged Jensen Huang

I remember asking my parents when I was a child why it was such a big deal for a politician to have an affair. They explained to me the many layers of possible compromise beyond the simple breach of morals and propriety. Extramarital affairs, my parents explained, could expose politicians to blackmail, undue influence, and the temptation to give up vital state secrets over pillow talk.

Maybe someone should have that explain-it-to-me-like-I’m-five conversation with investors like Shaun Maguire and Bill Ackman, who rushed to the defense of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this weekend following his shocking confession that he’d been involved in an affair with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. (A Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson has called the spy allegation “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”)

Sure, Jensen Huang is not a head of state. But he’s arguably someone even more powerful. He’s the man in command of the world’s largest company—and its most coveted technological infrastructure: high-performance GPUs required to train artificial intelligence systems.

For years, tech-world observers scratched their head when he insisted again and again that his company should have the right to supply those elite chips to China—even as Americans were told that letting our most formidable adversary gain any advantage in the AI race would spell doom for the Western world. When Huang took the number four spot on our New Establishment list this fall, I wrote that his commitment to fighting these export controls could become his Achilles’ heel. And boy, has it. Nvidia has now launched an independent investigation into his affair, while the government continues to assess the blast radius of the scandal.

There are “three big national security implications from this,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, told me this week. “The first question is whether Chinese intelligence has succeeded in obtaining any sensitive nonpublic information about Nvidia, about its products or—I think what’s being overlooked—its customers of massive quantities of GPUs, like large AI labs.” The second, he said, “is whether Chinese intelligence may have succeeded in indirectly obtaining information about President Trump or people close to him,” given Huang’s unusually close relationship with the president. And third is “the question of whether Mr. Huang’s personal relationship with his customer might have motivated the company’s decision to sell large numbers of computer chips to Megaspeed, a company that has been under investigation by the Commerce Department for violations of American law.” (A Megaspeed rep told The New York Times that the company was “conducting an internal investigation into allegations of chip diversion,” the subject of the US probe, and that it had “repeatedly offered to cooperate with the US government.”)

According to the Times, the US government has been aware of Huang’s relationship since at least 2025, prompting many more questions about why this knowledge was not made public until it was uncovered piece by piece by the killer investigative team at the Times—notably, right after the midterm elections.

“Someone in the national security establishment clearly decided that they were sick and tired of the president playing this game with Jensen,” said Dennis Wilder, a former senior intelligence official who now teaches at Georgetown’s School of Foreign Service.

Of course, investors have plenty of reasons to turn a blind eye to Huang’s misdeeds. His company has also played a keystone role in keeping the entire economy afloat, taking many investors’ portfolios along for the ride on its seemingly never-ending bull run since 2023. Many are wondering if dethroning him from the company he built from the ground up could also send our entire economy over the edge.

Fedasiuk thinks the decision is worthy of a bit more nuance. “I think investors and the American people have to remember that there is actually a distinction between the personal interests of Mr. Huang and the corporate interests of Nvidia, a $4 trillion company that is the backbone of the intelligence revolution,” he said.

Mentioned in this issue: Dario Amodei, Sherrod Brown, Whoop, Culper Research, Daniela Amodei, Holden Karnofsky, Brian Chesky, Ramp, Sean Parker, Tilt, Kalshi, Modal Labs, Lina Khan, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren.

I’ve always felt a kind of kinship with short sellers—would-be investigative journalists who’ve decided to use their skill set to make real money. Kudos to the investment-research firm Culper Research for publishing a brief back in May detailing its short position on Nvidia, taken, in part, due to Jensen Huang’s “uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang.”

Next time you log your weekend party habits, remember that Whoop sees you, and it’s judging you. “LSD and ketamine use were associated with bedtimes over an hour later and Recovery scores about 9 points lower. Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3495. 32 Years Later, The Santa Clause's Line On Believing Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote

Ah, "The Santa Clause." The holiday classic where Tim Allen (making his leading man debut in a movie) accidentally murders Jolly Old Saint Nick, featuring a title that tricked an entire generation into misspelling "Santa Claus." In the 1994 film (which ended up having to cut a risque joke), Allen plays Scott Calvin (Get it? His name has the same initials as SANTA CLAUS!), a divorced, work-obsessed marketing exec spending the holidays with his son, Charlie (Eric Lloyd).

Christmas Eve rolls around, and when the real Santa accidentally falls off Scott's roof and dies, Scott is forced to become the new Santa. Scott doesn't like this idea, especially when he starts growing a magical beard and a magical fat belly. It doesn't help that everyone around him — except Charlie — thinks he's gone insane. The film then unfolds over a year leading up to the following Christmas, where Scott has to come to terms with his new career.

Will Scott learn to be a better father, embrace the Christmas spirit, and thrive as the new Santa Claus? Of course he will, and then they'll make a string of sequels (and a streaming TV series reboot as well)! Happy holidays!

"Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing."

"Seeing is believing" is an age-old saying, but "The Santa Clause" flips this a bit. When Scott becomes Santa, he ends up in the North Pole, where the Elves who toil away in the workshop try to give him some help. One of those elves, Judy (Paige Tamada), utters our quote of the day: "Seeing isn't believing. Believing is seeing." This quote is later embraced wholeheartedly by Scott's son Charlie, who has to keep reminding Scott that all he has to do is look around to witness the reality of his new magical life.

Belief is a big part of "The Santa Clause." Scott has to believe in himself, while everyone around Scott has to believe he's really the new Santa. The hard-headed realists of the world understandably have trouble with all of this, and that includes Scott himself. He's a gruff American businessman! He doesn't believe in Christmas magic, gosh darn it! All Scott needs to do is open his eyes, both literally and metaphorically, to see the reality of his new situation. And isn't that what Christmas is all about? That and drinking way too much nog? Thank you,"The Santa Clause," for making us believe in Christmas.

#3493. Where are all the rings in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3?

As the name of the series implies, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is focused on how the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forged the Rings of Power as part of a scheme to control all of Middle-earth. As of season 3, the three Elven Rings, Seven Rings for the Dwarf-lords, and the Nine Rings for Mortal Men have all been made, while Sauron is working endlessly to complete his project by building the One Ring to rule them all.

That's a lot of magic jewelry to keep track of! If you need a refresher, we’ve put together a list of where the rings are and who is currently wearing them.

This story contains spoilers for the first four episodes of The Rings of Power season 3

While in disguise and calling himself Halbrand, Sauron inspired the elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) to create three rings that would save the Elves of Middle-earth from losing their immortality. He forged them in the season 1 finale using mithril Elrond (Robert Aramayo) received from his friend Durin IV (Owain Arthur), combined with a knife made of gold and silver from Valinor.

Even though Sauron didn’t have a direct hand in creating these rings, Elrond feared Sauron would use them to manipulate the Elves. So he stole the rings and took them to Círdan the Shipwright (Ben Daniels) in the Elven capital Lindon. Círdan is the oldest and wisest elf in Middle-earth and he offered to throw the rings into the ocean. But after actually seeing them, he changed his mind and donned the ring Narya. He brought the other two back to Lindon, where Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) put on Nenya and the High King of the Elves Gil-galad (Benjamin Walker) donned Vilya. Their power was able to restore the Great Tree of Lindon, which is tied to the vitality of the elves of Middle-earth.

As of season 3, all three of those elves are still wearing those rings, which are the only things that seem capable of stopping Sauron’s advance across Middle-earth. Galadriel is protecting Rivendell, while Gil-galad and Círdan preserve Lindon. Meanwhile, Sauron is scouring Middle-earth for information on how Celebrimbor crafted the Elven rings so he can forge a ring of his own that would bind all the ringbearers to his will.

With just a touch, Sauron was able to corrupt the seven rings that Celebrimbor made for the Dwarves. Durin III (Peter Mullan) wore one in season 2, and it made him paranoid and greedy. He didn’t listen to his son’s pleas to take off the ring even as Khazad-dûm was plunged into darkness. He only realized how much the ring was affecting him when he unleashed the Balrog while digging for mithril. He then took off the ring, gave it to Durin IV, and sacrificed himself to seal the Balrog away again.

As of the beginning of season 3, Durin IV has possession of all the Dwarven rings and has hidden them away, refusing to give them to the other Dwarven lords who paid Durin III for them. Durin’s older brother Thráin (Eddie Marsan) came to Khazad-dûm along with some of these lords, and while he’s acting like he has his brother’s best interests at heart, he’s actually in league with Sauron.

When Durin tells the Dwarf lords that the rings drove his father mad, Thráin points out that the king was wearing a ring when he decided to make Durin his heir. Arguing that their father was not of sound mind, he challenges his brother to a duel for control of Khazad-dûm. He wins and becomes the new king, but he still needs to find those rings.

Sauron was directly involved in the construction of the Nine Rings for Mortal Men and has the most control over their wielders. As of the beginning of season 3, he has already distributed three of them, and these Ring-servants (or Nazgnagôl) are fearsome warriors capable of dark magic.

In the season premiere, the Gaudrim (Men from the desert lands of Rhûn) come to Mordor to accept his proposal of an alliance with the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds). Sauron makes them fight among themselves and gives one ring to the winner, Khamûl the Easterling (Zubin Varla). The ring’s power cures him of the Dark Wizard’s flesh-warping curse and he returns to Rhûn to usurp his former master. While the Dark Wizard demands that Khamûl surrender his ring, the Nazgnagôl refuses and shows off his new power by almost breaking the wizard’s staff.

Sauron also offered a ring to the Men of Númenor, who ignored his missives. Instead, the invite was answered by a group of Men from Pelargir, including Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin) who were looking for an alternative to toiling for their colonial lords. Once again, Sauron made them fight for a ring. This time, he intervened after seeing a scar on Theo’s arm that came from the magical sword hilt used to cause a volcanic eruption in the Southlands and create Mordor.

Sauron uses necromancy to contact Theo’s father, Faldred, son of Hammethreg, explaining that he was a steward of Mordor and that Theo’s mother killed him when she discovered his dark nature. Sauron then offers Theo a ring as a way to claim power for himself as a conqueror, a sorcerer, and a king. Theo dons the ring and accompanies Sauron to Gundabad, but tries to allow Galadriel, Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova), and Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) to escape. Sauron demonstrates his control of Theo by forcing him to kill his surrogate father, Arondir.
