#3492. VisionQuest's Avengers: Doomsday Post-Credits Scene Explained: [SPOILER] Returns

This article contains spoilers for "VisionQuest" Season 1, Episode 8, "Forever."

The season (series?) finale of "VisionQuest" teases that the Vision-Maximoff family still has a future in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. There are two post-credits scenes in "VisionQuest." One is vaguer: Ultron (James Spader), now free and convinced not to kill all of humanity for now, has a backup drive of Jocasta (T'Nia Miller). So, yeah, it looks like this isn't the last we've seen of the Living Automaton in the MCU.

Towards the end of the episode, Tommy Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica) asks Vision (Paul Bettany) if they'll ever see his mom, Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) again. The second post-credit scene all but confirms, yes, they will.

The scene replays the climax of 2022's "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," where Wanda buries herself under the rubble of Mount Wundagore to destroy the grimoire, the Darkhold. But then the scene shows green energy telekinetically lifting the rubble away, as a shadowed, hooded figure stands over Wanda. "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine," he says in a European accent as green light bathes Wanda, and her eyes shoot open. Three guesses who Wanda's savior is and the first two don't count. (But you will get a hint — his name rhymes with "zoom.")

This basically confirms Olsen will be appearing as Wanda in "Avengers: Doomsday," and as a servant of Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) This scene also aligns rather well with a post-credits scene included in the "Avengers Endgame: Encore" rerelease earlier this year, which depicted Doom freeing Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) from imprisonment after the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

Many now vindicated Marvel fans refused to believe that Wanda was really dead after Wundagore's destruction. Elizabeth Olsen had previously said she was open to returning as Scarlet Witch, and it seems Marvel must've given her a call.

In "Avengers: Doomsday," Doom will have at least three "Latverian witches" under his command, and they will wear steel masks much like their boss does. That'll be a fitting homage to the three Brides of Dracula — Doom, as a caped, castle-dwelling Eastern European king, is very much a villain modeled in Dracula's image. But there's also rampant speculation the witches' masks hide familiar faces, including Wanda's. This "VisionQuest" post-credits scene all but confirms it.

(In the "Time Runs Out" storyline that "Doomsday" is loosely adapting, Doom had all female acolytes called Black Swans serving him. The Latverian witches might be a simplified version of that concept.)

While I'm hoping Marvel doesn't make Doom, their greatest villain, a literal variant of Tony Stark, the fact is Robert Downey Jr.'s casting means a lot of the audience will read Doom as "evil Iron Man." There'd be some fitting narrative symmetry then if Doom has corrupted Avengers, like Hulk and Scarlet Witch, on his side.

Doom has manipulated Wanda before in the comics, too. "Young Avengers: The Children's Crusade" by Allan Heinberg and Jim Cheung revealed that, after Wanda's infamous "No more mutants" crash-out in "House of M," Doom sheltered her in Latveria to try and gain her powers. This is the storyline that reunited Wanda with Tommy and Billy as well. With how "VisionQuest" leaves the Maximoff boys, and with Marvel Studios having planted the seeds for Young Avengers, I think a "Children's Crusade" adaptation is in the near future.

#3491. 10 Years Later, Billy Bob Thornton's Forgotten War Movie Is the Perfect Weekend Watch

Molly DeCastro is a New York-based emerging film and entertainment journalist with a personal passion for poetic prose and impactful storytelling. She graduated from Pace University with a degree in English and a concentration in creative writing. While film analysis is at the heart of her work, she is especially interested in exploring cinema through an anthropological lens and in examining how creative themes reflect cultural identity. She aims to forge a deep connection between audiences and film through thoughtful and evocative writing. She also enjoys keeping up with all things film! That means specializing in industry news, emerging directors, and stand-out projects.

Surprisingly, despite being widely considered a classic must-watch, Billy Bob Thornton's 2016 war-dramedy Whiskey Tango Foxtrot is a rather polarizing film. That said, with comedy legend Tina Fey and, at the time, emerging starlet Margot Robbie at the helm, it's hard to imagine why. It's a classic odd-couple pairing, following Fey's Kim Baker, a mild-mannered, bottom-shelf news outlet reporter, and Robbie's Tanya Venderpoel, a fierce foreign TV war correspondent. The two stumble into one another when, struck by the desire to be a real boots-on-the-ground journalist, Kim takes up a station in Kabul, Afghanistan. The supporting cast, including Billy Bob Thornton as a rough-around-the-edges marine general and Martin Freeman as a hard-drinking Scottish photographer, help round the film, and in some way defines its charm.

Notably, the film is loosely adapted from Kim Baker's memoir, The Taliban Shuffle: Strange Days in Afghanistan and Pakistan, with Fey's character portraying a fictionalized version of the actual journalist. Similar to the film, the novel is a candid, comedic dissection of the post-9/11 "forgotten war", as told through the eyes of a journalist who was present there. Fey's portrayal of the character is quippy yet grounded in her undying pursuit of journalistic greatness.

There's no doubt Tina Fey is a comedy legend. She has a stacked repertoire of both acting and writing props to back it up. From Mean Girls to Baby Mama, watching Fey truly command a scene with such effortlessness is a never-ending pleasure. With that being said, her role as Kim Baker allowed audiences to see a new angle on her capabilities. Her character is in a vulnerable position, both internally and externally. She's essentially a half-failed journalist, putting her career and life on the line, completely dependent on her counterpart, Tanya Venderpoel. Fey's portrayal of this vulnerability, as well as her cohesion with Venderpoel, was wonderfully and warmly executed.

Kim arrives in a chaotic, male-dominated war zone and is quickly thrust into a world of intensive work, high-risk reporting, and heavy partying. Something in particular that this film captures well is the deep bond between women in a male space. Tanya's entrance into the film is disarming in some way, especially when juxtaposed next to Thornton's General Walter Hollanek, who initially intimates Baker but eventually develops a begrudging respect for her. The depth of Baker's experiences doesn't stop there. As she grows comfortable in this space of danger and risk, she eventually finds herself hooked on the high. This forces her to confront not only what she wants out of her career, but also her life. Fey's portrayal of this internal battle is refreshing next to her typically comedic roles.

As stated prior, the supporting cast provided an astounding cushion of extra depth to the foundation of the film. Thornton's character, in particular, added extra motivation not only for Baker but also for the plot itself. His role fills the typical brooding mentor trope, which makes his eventual softening all the more satisfying. In a conversation with Kim, she asks for a quote about the war and the current state of combat. Hollanek replies with a sobering thought: "This war's like f**king a gorilla; you keep on going until the gorilla wants to stop." At that moment, he sees Baker as an inexperienced nuisance. Over time, their dynamic shifts as Kim keeps proving her grit, leading to a pinnacle moment when she uses her skills to lead a large-scale rescue mission.

Martin Freeman's Lain MacKelpie is exactly the opposite. He's a warm, charming, romantic-leaning colleague to Kim. His character provides a lightness to the plot which is otherwise pretty gritty. Together, their scenes break up the chaos and provide a dynamic pace to the story. He's a wisecracking, heavy-drinking guy, and as the two grow closer, he becomes incredibly lovable as a character. Overall, each of the respective supporting characters helps build the story into what it is.

Two horror stars are ready for deployment.

In summary, Whiskey Tango Foxtrot ​​​​​​is a thrilling, bumpy ride. Each moving part of the film breathes so much life into the story. Though it at times relies on cliché tropes, the expert performances from Fey, Freeman, Robbie, and Thornton helped differentiate it from the masses. It's gritty, fun, and a wonderful combination of the best of each genre it pulled from.

#3490. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3489. Ryan Gosling's R-Rated 2016 Comedy Is Officially Apple TV's Biggest Streaming Hit

I have never seen an actor resist Hollywood stardom more stubbornly than Ryan Gosling. Three years after his 2001 breakout performance as a Jewish skinhead in Henry Bean's incendiary "The Believer," (for which he should've been nominated for an Academy Award), he was transformed into a big-screen heartthrob via his portrayal of Noah Calhoun in Nick Cassavetes' "The Notebook." Gosling could've dined out on hunky leading men roles for the next decade, but, over the next few years, he chose instead to play a freebasing high school teacher in "Half Nelson," a self-destructive husband in the soul-hollowing "Blue Valentine" and an emotionally remote getaway driver in "Drive." "Crazy, Stupid, Love" was a bright box-office spot, but it wasn't the showcase he needed. If he wanted to be a star. Which, in 2011, seemed to be in question.

In 2016, Gosling made a play to become a star on his own off-kilter terms as alcoholic private detective Holland March in Shane Black's "The Nice Guys." The legendary screenwriter behind "Lethal Weapon," "The Last Boy Scout" and "Kiss Kiss, Bang Bang" cooked up an elegantly seared filet mignon for Gosling, and he savored every moment. "The Nice Guys," which pairs Gosling with an over-it Russell Crowe (as a Yoo-hoo swilling enforcer) is an audience movie, but the audience, for whatever reason, didn't show up in 2016.

28 days after "The Nice Guys" went live on Apple TV, it's now the service's most watched movie. I'm thrilled that more people are discovering this shaggy detective classic 10 years after its release, but under Ellison's Skydance rule, Warner Bros. isn't trying to resuscitate commercial misfires. This is it. That said, it's got more going on in its 116 minutes than the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe oeuvre.

I read "The Nice Guys" when it was pitched as a network television pilot by Black and Anthony Bagarozzi (one of these men had the pleasure of watching a stray kitten urinate on my lap). It was sharp, hilarious and fertile ground for a series – if the writers could get around CBS' standards and practices. Not since "The Monster Squad" had Black written with such ease and eloquence at a PG-ish level.

When "The Nice Guys" got greenlit as a film, producer Joel Silver starred it up with Gosling and Crowe. The idea seemed to be that Crowe, a major movie star and Academy Award-winner, would play straight man to Gosling's goofball PI, and the film would sell itself. This just didn't happen. Set in the late 1970s, Black's stumblebum neo-noir is a skillfully plotted romp that finds Gosling and Crowe trying to piece together the disappearance of anti-pollution activist Amelia Kuttner (Margaret Qualley).

Gosling is dopey perfection as Holland March, a single father who's battling against a boozy haze to solve a case that could save his profession and his life. He's funny and heartbreaking in this role. As is Black's wont, you're left with a wacky, whimsically moralistic Donald Westlake riff with blockbuster trimmings. Gosling and Crowe are scrambling to take down men who abuse women. Spoiler: they get their dastardly dudes, and you'll shed tears along the way.

I'm thrilled that Gosling is now an A-lister making films for Lucasfilm, and he was wonderful in "Project Hail Mary," but we've yet to see his best. I just want to watch him blossom.

#3488. 15 Years Ago Today: Henry Cavill Starred In An Epic Fantasy Movie Before Superman

With now-former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran's version of the DC Universe coming to a premature end, it's times like these when we would do well to look back at what has worked, and what hasn't worked, when it comes to DC's films. One thing that kinda worked was Henry Cavill, a great Superman who never got a great Superman movie during his run in the DC Extended Universe. Without doubt, the actor had both the charisma and physicality to make you believe a man can fly.

And yet, just two years before debuting as Superman in "Man of Steel," Cavill made audiences believe a man could battle gods with a sword. It was November 11, 2011, and Indian director Tarsem Singh Dhandwar had just released his film "Immortals," an epic fantasy movie inspired by Greek mythology.

In the film, Henry Cavill plays Theseus, a humble stonemason with the physique of a Kryptonian who is chosen by Zeus himself (Luke Evans) to lead humanity in their resistance against Hyperion (Mickey Rourke), a tyrant king wreaking havoc on Greece in search of a mythical bow that would allow him to free the Titans and overthrow the gods of Olympus. No, this movie isn't really based on any particular myth. Rather, it borrows from a number of legends and blends them together in a nonsensical yet very cool tale full of superhero-like action, incredible costumes, and some of the most stunning imagery in any fantasy movie out there.

Back in its day, critics generally praised "Immortals" for its stunning visuals while admitting its story left a lot to be desired. Nowadays, though, the movie represents an underrated entry in Cavill's body of work, as it showed he was ready to be a star and lead a franchise (or two).

"Immortals" is, admittedly, not a well-written movie. And yet, Tarsem Singh Dhandwar went about crafting this movie like it was going to mark the last time he ever set foot on a film set, leaving it all on the screen. Case in point, he tapped Eiko Ishioka ("Bram Stoker's Dracula") to design the movie's impossibly flamboyant costumes, which make the human characters look so extravagant that they almost overshadow the literal gods around them.

Then there's the film's visual style, which Singh once described as "Caravaggio meets 'Fight Club.'" He wanted to make a hardcore action flick in the manner of a Renaissance painting, and it shows, resulting in a movie that blends the desaturated colors and slow motion of something like "300" with a striking painterly aesthetic. When it comes to its spectacle, "Immortals" similarly combines gods with mythical weapons that tear down city walls and intimate, grounded sword clashes, making its violence feel huge in its scope and scale. Indeed, the first scenes involving gods are especially stunning, as they move at full speed while the humans they're reducing to smithereens are slowed way down. It's a great way to illustrate the awesome powers of these deities.

Speaking of awesome powers, "Immortals" is further bolstered by Henry Cavill, who very much proves his ability to carry a big-budget movie ihere. To be sure, his performance matches the wild tone of everything else around him, all while bringing some needed humanity to Theseus. It's enough to make you more than a little excited for Cavill's return to the realm of outlandish fantasy movie adventures with his upcoming "Highlander" reboot.

Joining Mercer in this charity one-shot are fellow founders Ashley Johnson and Sam Riegel, along with an incredible lineup of musicians, including Tom Morello of Rage Against the Machine, K.Flay, Blake Roman, THOT SQUAD, and Wayne Brady, who also appeared in The Legend of Vox Machina as the magnificent Taryon Darrington.

If you like your media industry dramas to be based in reality but still can’t resist a salacious power struggle, “Ink” might be the movie for you this holiday season.

Danny Boyle‘s Netflix thriller dramatizes the beginnings of Rupert Murdoch’s empire, following the future mogul when he was just a young Australian newspaper man. When he launched The Sun alongside former business partner Larry Lamb in 1969, the two men effectively created the modern tabloid and figured out that audiences were hungry for a lot more than just truth. Their sensationalist approach to journalism would come in handy on many of Murdoch’s future business endeavors, and the film draws a very clear line between his editorial preferences and the 2026 world he helped create for us. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? Guy Pearce stars as Murdoch alongside Jack O’Connell as Lamb, with James Graham handling the writing duties on the adaption of his hit West End and Broadway play.

“Ink” was the opening film for the 2026 Venice International Film Festival, where critics praised its entertainment value while acknowledging that it treads some familiar territory.

“That ‘Ink’ begins as a story of Larry Lamb and Rupert Murdoch launching the tabloid newspaper The Sun in 1969 and ends with a montage including Trump and Elon Musk tells you all you need to know about Danny Boyle’s new film: This is a vividly directed if overcooked political parable about How We Got Here Now,” IndieWire’s Ryan Lattanzio wrote in his review. “If you’ve seen ‘Nightcrawler’ or ‘Network,’ there’s nothing new to take away about the if-it-bleeds-it-leads newsroom mentality, but Jack O’Connell (who also starred in Boyle’s ’28 Years Later’) is terrific as an editor obsessively addicted to winning — and willing to mow down lives in the process.”

The original “Ink” play premiered on the West End in 2017, with a Broadway run following in 2019. Boyle spent years trying to make a movie out of the material, and recalled the lengthy process of convincing actors to remain on board during an interview with IndieWire at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival.

“I begged Guy to hang on,” Boyle said. “I apologized to Guy because it wasn’t like I’d offered it to him, but I’d said ‘I want you,’ and bless him he hung in there for us.

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters on Friday, December 11 before it streams on January 8. Watch the full trailer below.

#3484. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: up to 15 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks when I tested it. The company says some users are finding the latest software update extends battery a bit further.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

Updated 11/10/2026 to note that the Ultrahuman Ring Pro's stated battery life is up to 15 days, not 8-10 days.

#3483. We Officially Ranked the 8 Best HBO Shows of All Time

HBO is responsible for creating some of the best television shows of all time. Originals like Sex and the City, The White Lotus, and Euphoria have changed television as we know it, and were responsible for many stars' breakout performances. Actors that fall under this success list include Sarah Jessica Parker, Sydney Sweeney, and Idris Elba.

The network has produced over 200 shows since 1983, many of which became award winners, cult classics, or both. Its pattern of skyrocketing celebrities' careers appears to be never-ending, and it is only a matter of time when new stars will enter the spotlight following the debuts of upcoming shows. In the end, some shows are better than others, and here is our list of the 8 best HBO shows of all time.

The Wire focussed on a specific issue in Baltimore for each of its six seasons, and its connection to law enforcement. While the first season focuses on ceasing the illegal drug trade by the Barksdale family, Season 2 shines light on how deindustrialization affects labor unions, particularly the Baltimore docks. Other issues addressed during the show include city government, public school systems, urban reform, city politics in the media, and the Baltimore Sun newspaper combined with the decline of journalism.

The crime drama's choice of not making anyone a true main character is a rare thing on television, but it was a smart decision for this show, as it doesn't take one or two main characters to initiate change all the time. The characters needed to do the work, and not just have determination and passion to improve Baltimore, and The Wire did a phenomenal job in proving that to viewers who were looking to make a difference. Unlike most shows on this list, The Wire did not receive many awards following its universal praise, but its plot lines and diverse cast were groundbreakers that changed television for the better.

The Gilded Age has become one of HBO's top television shows following its series premiere in 2022. The historical drama is set in the 1880s, and begins with Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) moving in with her aunts, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski), and Ada Forte (Cynthia Nixon), following the death of her father. What she didn't expect to witness was tension between families that came from new and old money, along with the things that aquaintances would do to be one step closer to climbing the Manhattan social ladder.

The show's characters are an accurate representation of the New York elite in the 19th century. Not only do the actors portray their characters with grace, but they also fully embrace the time period, and make each scene feel like a piece of history one won't read in a textbook. The drama is currently airing its fourth season, and like its previous seasons, it received universal acclaim from fans and critics.

Larry David was known for co-creating Seinfeld before starring as a fictionalized version of himself in Curb Your Enthusiasm. In the show, Larry is a semi-retired television writer who finds himself in hundreds of unusual circumstances. Those situations and resolutions helped make the show an instant success, and featured a string of celebrities portraying characters or fictionalized versions of themselves, including John Hamm, Lin-Manuel Miranda, and the late Catherine O'Hara.

Unlike most popular HBO shows, Curb Your Enthusiasm aimed to make viewers smile from beginning to end rather than have them fear something dreadful would happen. It brought out the whacky sides of every actor who appeared on the show, and provided a new level of comedic relief to fans who needed it. Even though Curb Your Enthusiasm concluded its 12-season run in 2024, the award-winning show is still missed by fans looking to laugh before going to sleep.

The must-see fantasy drama of the 2010s was Game of Thrones, which featured a long list of celebrities portraying complex characters in their breakout roles. The show featured several story arcs during all 8 seasons, including political conflicts between noble houses and fights to reclaim power that characters believe they deserve. The impressive plot lines and actors' performances alone were enough to score higher viewership, but its frequent nudity and fight sequences prevented it from ever being something appropriate for young children.

Although the show's final season wasn't a favorite amongst fans, it does not take away from the excitement it provided them throughout the first seven seasons. It reignited the popularity of fantasy, and turned a nerdy genre into a global sensation for adults who believed fantasy was only for kids. The iconic show also inspired HBO to create two spin-offs: House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms.

HBO had originally billed Big Little Lies as a miniseries, but the show's overwhelming praise led to the network renewing the show for a second season. Season 1 begins with the arrival of Jane Chapman (Shailene Woodley), a single mom who befriends Madeline Mackenzie (Reese Witherspoon) and Celeste Wright (Nicole Kidman). As the season progresses, the darkness in their lives comes to light, and it leads to deathly consequences they, along with fellow moms Renata Klein (Laura Dern) and Bonnie Carlson (Zoë Kravitz), must face throughout Season 2.

Every actress in Big Little Lies showed audiences that no matter how hard one tries to pretend everything is fine, nothing is ever perfect. Fans could feel the guilt, sadness, and fright each character had, and even though it took time, the women showed viewers the perfect example of an unbreakable bond. The emotions and chemistry portrayed by the actors contributed to the show's Emmy and Golden Globe Award wins, and fans are antsy to learn when full production of the show's upcoming third season will begin.

Succession is a prominent HBO classic that showed viewers what happens when a family is ruined by greed. The show centered around the Roys, and the fight to take over the family-owned company, Waystar RoyCo. The three frontrunners in the takeover were Kendall Roy (Jeremy Strong), Roman Roy (Kieran Culkin), and Siobhan "Shiv" Roy (Sarah Snook), all of whom were children of the company's CEO, Logan Roy (Brian Cox).

The race for the CEO position was terrifying to watch, as viewers watched the children ruin their own lives for the possibility of a fancy job. In the end, Logan's third son, Connor Roy (Alan Ruck), was the sibling with the happiest ending, and the only one who wanted nothing to do with running the company. Although none of Logan's children became the CEO, the actors portraying them did win Golden Globes for their performances, and they taught audiences throughout the show's four-season run that no life of privilege is worth ruining one's life or family over.

Fans immediately fell in love with Dr. Michael "Robby" Robinavitch (Noah Wyle) within the first five minutes of the series premiere of The Pitt for his hardworking demeanor. The show centers around Robby and the events of his shifts at the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center's ER, which he and his co-workers call The Pitt. Some of the cases were minor, others were life-threatening, but what they all had in common was the ability to surprise viewers who believed every patient would have a happy ending.

Critics and medical professionals praised the show for its realistic depiction of the lives of ER doctors and nurses. It gives audiences the gift of understanding what an ER is like in real life, and even though some cases are truly heartbreaking, it's the reality of the medical field that fans aren't used to seeing. The show has already won Emmy and Golden Globe Awards, and its third season is set to premiere next year.

The Sopranos is not only the best HBO series, but it's also one of the only mafia shows where audiences have trouble despising members of the mob. The show introduced viewers to Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), a mob boss who managed to balance work and family life in his own twisted way. Tony committed heinous crimes with friends and relatives, but after six seasons, it was impossible to hate or want him in jail.

The diabolical behavior of some of these mobsters never got boring, and the show always found ways to add twists to pivotal plot points throughout all six seasons. No one can imagine a criminal getting away with everything forever, but this show made fans hope the members of Tony's crime family were immortal. Even though audiences will never know if Tony Soprano lived or died, the character will always be one of the most inspirational and evil protagonists of all time.

#3481. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3480. 10 Biggest Changes Rings Of Power Season 3, Episodes 1-4 Make To Tolkien's Story

Warning! Spoilers for Rings of Power season 3, episodes 1-4 ahead!

Prime Video is back at it with Rings of Power season 3! The platform was kind enough to premiere with four episodes, which will ultimately be exactly half of the complete eight-episode season. We've therefore covered quite a bit of ground in a short amount of time, and Rings of Power has absolutely delivered on all the thrilling intensity that was promised. Of course, as was expected, not all of this is strictly in line with what J.R.R. Tolkien wrote in his various works.

Rings of Power has taken a lot of flak for its various changes to canon, but that's not always exactly fair. The Second Age of Middle-earth was never written about within a novel or traditional narrative. Instead, Tolkien described these events as an impartial historian would. This ultimately meant that large gaps in the details had to be filled in. For this reason, there's no point in listing all the ways brand-new characters like Arondir or Theo don't have a place in canon. Still, there are a good handful of elements in Rings of Power season 3 that do specifically contradict that canon version of the story.

Tolkien didn't describe in much detail the actual process of Sauron creating the One Ring, nor did he ever mention whether the Dark Lord faced any significant failures or challenges. In Rings of Power season 3, however, we pick up with the understanding that Sauron has been at this for quite some time. The show establishes that Celebrimbor kept a key secret from Sauron and that he needs to discover what it is to create a ring that can control not just all the others but the Three Elven Rings as well. It's an entertaining struggle, but certainly not canon.

In canon, Sauron had possession of the Three Elven Rings and gave them to the Elves, even though he didn't craft them himself. It therefore doesn't make sense that he would need one back to study it and create the One Ring.

Rings of Power's orcs have been rather controversial across the board. Last season, we saw orc parents with their baby, which, though frequently challenged, is not out of line with the Tolkien canon. Season 3 takes things a bit further, however, and we see what the showrunners are calling an "orc with an arc." Marnûkh seemingly betrays Sauron to help the Elves prevent the creation of the One Ring. There's absolutely no mention of such an event in Tolkien's works; neither is there any orc that ever went good.

We now know that the Stranger is actually Gandalf the Grey, and Rings of Power season 3 has officially revealed that the Dark Wizard is one of the Blue Wizards. More specifically, he is Pallando. This makes some sense in canon, since one of Tolkien's explanations for what happened to these wizards is that they formed magical cults in Rhûn. What the author never wrote about, however, is this idea that Pallando murdered his companion, Alatar, and that this is what caused Rhûn to become a desert wasteland.

In Tolkien's legendarium, there was a King Durin III who ruled Khazad-dûm around the time that Sauron's Rings were created. However, he did not have a son named Durin IV who lived at the same time. The name "Durin" was given to dwarves that were believed to be incarnations of Durin the Deathless, so there couldn't be two at once. Durin IV ruled generations later, during the Last Alliance of Elves and Men. All of this means that the family drama seen in Rings of Power season 3 between Durin and Thráin absolutely did not happen.

While it's conceivable that Tolkien would have written about brotherly rivalry among the dwarven heirs, the dramatic misunderstanding about Disa and Thráin's relationship feels less like something that would ever appear in his works.

Rings of Power season 3 hinges on the idea that none of the Elven Smiths survived the fall of Eregion. In the show, Sauron specifically ordered that all of them be executed and Celebrimbor's records be burned. This bites him in the butt, since he now needs answers that only an Eregion smith would have. This wouldn't necessarily have been an issue in canon, since it's specifically noted that several smiths (Gwaith-i-Mírdain) were among the elves that escaped to Rivendell. Whether Sauron could have gained access to them is another matter, but they certainly existed.

Sauron's entire process of handing out his Rings of Power is quite different in Prime Video's TV show compared to Tolkien works. According to canon, Sauron intended for all of his rings to go to elves, but they proved too difficult to corrupt. He had to gather them all back up again before ultimately deciding to redistribute them to Dwarves and Men. As for the Nine specifically, Sauron chose men of influence and power—the Great Kings of Men. There's no real reason to think that he had ordinary men fight one another to the death to claim rings for themselves.

The idea of Elendil leading a group known as the Faithful is absolutely canon. It didn't really happen until much later, when Pharazon embraced Sauron's cult, and Númenor began worshiping and giving human sacrifices to Morgoth. Even then, however, the Faithful were a peaceful resistance to the new practices. They simply refused to participate. Rings of Power portrays the Faithful as being an army in training that plans and carries out assassinations and other forms of violence. This is, once again, far more dramatic, but not a part of Tolkien's story.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

It's no big secret that Rings of Power invented the implied romance between Galadriel and Sauron. While it's certainly possible that the Dark Lord would have wanted Galadriel on his side, perhaps even as his queen (pretty much everyone fell immediately in love with Galadriel), there's no concrete proof. Moreover, the idea of Galadriel having nightmares about Sauron being in her bed doesn't fit with anything we know about these canon characters. Galadriel was among those who were never fooled by Annatar, and while she knew Sauron was dangerous, she never had this traumatized fear response toward him.

When Gandalf faces the Balrog in The Fellowship of the Ring, he announces that he is a servant to the Secret Fire. Rings of Power has incorporated this idea, but with some odd twists. The Secret Fire is the source of all life in Tolkien's works, and the only being with access to it is the supreme god, Eru Ilúvatar. When Gandalf says he is a servant to the Secret Fire, he means that he serves Ilúvatar's will for life. There's no reason to think the wizard could ever speak to the flame directly, or that the flame could ever talk back. If this is just meant to be a vision that Ilúvatar used to communicate with Gandalf, then perhaps it works.

Rings of Power had already headed in its own direction regarding the character Celeborn, since it was claimed by Galadriel in season 1 that her husband had died. We all knew that couldn't possibly be true, and Rings of Power delivered in season 3 with the reveal that Celeborn had just been taken captive. Galadriel finds him at Gundabad, but it's hard to imagine he was kept there for the several thousand years since the First Age. It's all a big oddity, but we will have to see where this non-canon story goes as Rings of Power season 3 continues.

#3479. All Zelda: Ocarina of Time Dungeons, Ranked From Worst to Best

While every moment of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is memorable, it’s the Nintendo 64 game’s dungeons that really stick in your memory. Each one is a tightly constructed puzzle box built around the tools you collect inside, culminating in an often-excellent boss fight. The game’s terrific Switch 2 remake doesn’t mess with that strength; it only refines some of Zelda’s best dungeons in tasteful ways.

It was a joy to revisit those dungeons during my playthrough, not just to experience some nostalgia, but to appreciate some timeless Nintendo design. Since I left the remake with some strong opinions about which ones are best in class, I’ve decided to definitively rank the eight primary dungeons in Ocarina of Time from worst to best. (I’ve left out side-dungeons like the Gerudo Training Ground and the Bottom of the Well, though those contain some killer bits of puzzle design, too.)

On paper, the Shadow Temple sounds fantastic. It’s a dungeon that fully realizes Ocarina of Time’s underlying horror by forcing Link to face off with Gibdos, Like Likes, and Dead Hands. In reality, it’s a fairly straightforward temple that revolves around a gimmick that sounds cooler than it is: a ghost ship ride. The remake misses an opportunity to make that sequence more exciting, leaving it feeling like an amusement park ride. The one saving grace here is Bongo Bongo, a bizarre boss that comes totally out of left field to make for one of Ocarina of Time’s most delightfully weird combat encounters.

Like the Shadow Temple, Jabu-Jabu’s Belly is an iconic temple that doesn’t quite hold up to its reputation. Don’t get me wrong: It’s perhaps the most creative dungeon in the entire game. Link gets swallowed by a giant fish and has to cut his way out of it by attacking its electrified uvulas. But the reality is that it’s a fairly small dungeon with an underexplored Princess Ruto escort gimmick and the least memorable boss in the entire game. It still deserves all of its flowers for being a funny, gross-out idea, though.

Dodongo Cavern is by no means a weak dungeon. It’s a fun, early-game area that gives you a lot of room to play with bombs. (That ends with you feeding them to King Dodongo, one of Zelda’s most classic boss mechanics.) It’s more that it’s outclassed by the Fire Temple later in Link’s adventure. The only way that Dodongo’s Cavern really stands out is in its central room, which has a massive skeleton looming over it. Dropping bombs in its eyes to unlock the route to King Dodongo remains a great final puzzle, as does setting off a bomb chain reaction to knock down a staircase.

Depending on who you ask, the Water Temple is either an abomination or the best Zelda dungeon. The truth is that it’s neither: It’s just a pretty good dungeon held back by some repeated backtracking. The idea of unlocking new areas in a flooded temple by changing the water level makes for a great gimmick that adds some clever spatial reasoning to the mix. The remake even makes it easier to navigate, thanks to better visual signposting and streamlined controls. Even with those changes, it’s still easy to get mixed up and wind up trekking back through routes to reset the water. The Longshot is a bit of a cop-out key item too, but the area’s pair of standout bosses in Dark Link and Morpha more than make up for that.

Even though it’s little more than an introductory dungeon, The Great Deku Tree is a perfect bit of Zelda design. The opening section, which has you climbing webs and avoiding Skulltulas, is a unique bit of vertical exploration that makes it special. Falling through the big web at the center of the dungeon to get to the bottom floor is a magical moment, too. And then there’s Gohma, a top-notch first foe that’s easier than ever to appreciate with the remake’s control tweaks. It’s a little small and the puzzles are simple, but it’s a delightful first challenge for Link.

As a dungeon that lands right near the midpoint of Ocarina of Time, the Fire Temple does a great job of (ahem) heating things up. It’s one of the more complex dungeons in the game, combining high-stakes platforming with a Goron-searching throughline that really shakes up the linear dungeon design at just the right time. It also features one of the best items in the game, the Megaton Hammer, which is especially satisfying to use in the remake. Volvagia might just be the most spectacular boss fight in the entire game too, aside from the final showdown. Top to bottom, it’s a meat and potatoes dungeon that nails all the essentials.

Key item: Silver Gauntlets, Mirror Shield

As the last dungeon in the game before Ganon’s Castle, the Spirit Temple makes for a great final exam. Its defining feature is the fact that it’s a dungeon in two parts, as Link needs to explore it as both a child and an adult to complete it. It’s the kind of ingenious idea that you would find in a game like Link’s Awakening, and it’s a little surprising that Ocarina of Time doesn’t play with that time-travel dynamic more elsewhere. That unique hook makes it feel like two dungeons in one, as you solve puzzles with both the Silver Gauntlets and the Mirror Shield. The final battle against Twinrova is a high point too — especially in the remake, which does an excellent job turning the witches into lovable foes. It’s a wonderfully creative way to send Link on his way to his journey’s end.

Zelda dungeons don’t get much better than the Forest Temple. Really dialing into Ocarina of Time’s spooky side, it’s a literal ghost house where Link has to track down and defeat four Poes. That quest sends him through twisted hallways and flipped rooms that require just enough spatial reasoning to feel gratifying without being a headache. Using Link’s arrows to shoot Poes out of picture frames, reorient rooms, and light torches makes for a strong puzzle dungeon that gives you multiple uses for your newfound item. The fact that it all ends in the memorable Phantom Ganon fight, a battle that brilliantly teases the ending encounter, makes it that much stronger. It’s a quintessential Zelda dungeon, and Ocarina of Time wouldn’t feel as magical as it does without it.

#3478. ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

The so-called villains of our childhood stories aren’t so bad when you look at things from their points of view. It’s a lesson that 21st century pop culture has taught us on a constant loop ever since “Wicked” kicked off an Oppenheimer-esque chain of tragedy that has seen everyone from Maleficent to Cruella de Vil humanized with their own origin story. It was inevitable that Cinderella’s allegedly wicked stepsisters would get their own mainstream version of the formula at some point (the Norwegian body horror movie exists in a separate, more ambitious category). If Hollywood can try to make us emphasize with someone who lives to kill puppies, anyone could have guessed that someone would slap a generational trauma label on literal children who grew up under the same evil matriarch as Cinderella. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

We’re long past the point where reimagining the classics from other characters’ perspectives earns you any credit for originality. If anything, those of us who have lived through the past two decades of pop culture might feel like stories where fairy tale side characters get to reclaim their agency are more omnipresent than actual fairy tales. But those original stories have endured in part because there’s always a new generation arriving to be wowed by them, and there’s no reason that the same principle can’t apply to the reimaginings, too.

Nobody whose age contains multiple digits needs to seek out “Steps” for any reason other than potentially entertaining their own children. But those young enough to be unfamiliar with the tropes it employs might be entertained or even moved by the material. “Cinderella” was an appropriate story to use for the purpose, as the beloved story of wish fulfillment doesn’t contain nearly as much emotional depth as better fairy tales like “Beauty and the Beast” or “The Little Mermaid.” Maybe it’s all part of a healthy cycle in which young kids can watch “Cinderella” and slightly older ones can watch “Steps” before graduating to stories and re-imaginings that have more to say. But on its own terms, the animated film comes across as little more than disposable corporate entertainment.

Directed by Alyce Tzue & John Ripa from a script by six credited writers (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, and Felicia Ho wrote the screenplay and Kate Micucci also has a story credit), “Steps” is a well-meaning entry into the subgenre that follows the blueprint competently enough to avoid being offensive or memorable. It literally opens on an old storybook with a stereotypical voiceover narrator reading the text about Cinderella being mistreated by her wicked stepsisters — before Lilith (Ali Wong) slides into the frame yelling “Whoa whoa whoa” and declares that the fairy tale is “character assassination.” From there, it’s only a matter of time before the contemporary pop needle drops start.

“Steps” has no choice but to expand the thin mythology of “Cinderella” before it has a chance to tell the other side of the story. In this version, the stepmother isn’t wicked at all — she’s just an Asian dressmaker who constantly moves her two daughters Lilith and Margot (Stephanie Tsu) wherever the work takes her. When her marriage takes them to the kingdom of Alouette, all three of them see it as a chance for some much-needed stability. More than anything, the girls are excited to hang out with their new stepsister, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried).

Yes, they started out as friends! (Where have you heard that one before?) The initial villain in “Steps” isn’t Cinderella, but the all-Caucasian kingdom where she lives. The newly blended family has fun sharing their cultural traditions, but Lilith and Margot quickly learn that everyone else sees them as outsiders. And when mean girls at school like Nikki Glazer’s Priscilla start freezing them out, Cinderella doesn’t do enough to stand up for them. Thus a sibling rivalry is born — turns out that Cinderella is also the mean stepsister that somebody else hates.

Lilith decides that if she’s not going to be accepted, she might as well rebel. Like a lot of pre-teens, she’s torn between an impulse to reject the social hierarchy around her and the unavoidable fact that she still defines herself by it. She’s more interested in destroying what she hates than figuring out what she likes, so she steals a magic wand from the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler) and sabotages the royal ball, significantly complicating things for the Prince (Daniel Radcliffe) and sending the kingdom into free-fall. It isn’t long before she and her loathed step-sister have to take a journey through the forest to set things right.

From its unpleasantly slick animation to its picture-perfect storytelling — Cinderella thinks Lilith is mean and Lilith thinks Cinderella is dumb and ditzy, but they both learn there’s more to the other than meets the eye — “Steps” is an example of how you can do everything “correctly” and be left with a film that’s too smooth around the edges to resonate. There’s enough for kids to enjoy, but this won’t be one that parents find themselves unexpectedly invested in.

For all its modern cliches, “Steps” still contains a few moments of genuine pathos that tug at the heartstrings. We can all relate to being bullied as kids and the cosmic importance that our young brains assign to being left out, and the film handles those early scenes admirably well. But nothing in the movie is strong enough to transcend the fact that it’s packaged in a tired formula that has lost any subversiveness it once had. These villain-led reimagnings were introduced as a way to counteract the two-dimensional nature of fairy tales, but it’s starting to feel like we replaced those Happily Ever After endings with something equally superficial.

“Steps” streams on Netflix beginning on Friday, November 20.

#3477. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3476. Taylor Sheridan Star Officially Addresses That Devastating Season 3 Finale Death

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 'Lioness' Season 3If there's one thing Taylor Sheridan has demonstrated throughout his television career, it's that getting attached to his characters can be something of a poisoned chalice because, whether it's Yellowstone, 1923, or Lioness, Sheridan isn't exactly a fan of happy endings, and that's especially true when his characters all find themselves caught up in situations where survival is anything but certain. And one of the main characters in his spy thriller felt the sharp end of his pen.

Elizaveta Neretin, who portrayed Oleksandra in Lioness Season 3, has officially spoken out on her character's death in the season finale, saying that she understood Sheridan's decision even though she obviously hoped it wouldn't happen. Speaking about the storyline, Neretin also discussed the decision to have the character die off-screen, a creative choice that left viewers confronting the aftermath rather than witnessing the moment itself. Speaking with Fox News Digital, Neretin explained:

"I thought it was going to happen. So when he called, and he told me, I was like, 'Yeah, I get it.' I'm sad for Oleksandra and what Oleksandra represents, but I understand the choice. It does serve this. It serves to show how the whole system is. Like American or not American, the whole system and the people that work in the system. It's all sharks, you know, so it just demonstrates how people are."

Surprisingly, we don't even see the murder. Instead, the finale shows two Delta Force operators removing her from a safehouse before a later scene reveals that a jogger has discovered her body near a trail. For a series that has never been particularly shy about depicting violence, it's an odd choice but Neretin believes there may have been a good reason for leaving the character's final moments to the imagination. Speaking with Decider, she added:

"We didn't film her actual murder, but I wonder if that's more of a question for Taylor. He writes some pretty gruesome things... Good writing means you don't write the things that are obvious. The viewers already knew she was going to die. So, what would be the purpose of showing her being murdered? Every scene has to have a purpose. Again, I don't want to speak for Taylor, but perhaps that's why the audience only saw her dead body. That's all they needed to see."

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

#3475. ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 21, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

Winifred Notty is the sanest person she knows, or so the heroine (or anti-heroine, depending on how you might see it) of Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” is quick to tell anyone who will listen. Or not, as star Maika Monroe delivers that damning and darkly funny insight into Winifred’s soul via a prim voiceover that seems to exist for her own benefit as much as the audience she seems to imagine.

That’s tangled enough, but there’s also this: Winifred doesn’t really know that many people, mostly because just about everyone she’s come across in her life is dead. Still, sane! Ish. Well, it’s not called “Victorian Psycho” for nothing. Related Stories Want a Full Scholarship to One of Our Film Festival Intensives? IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Video Contest Is Now Live Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Adapted for the screen by novelist Virginia Feito from her own work, the book comes recommended alongside its predecessor, “Mrs. March,” for anyone drawn to entertainment with “psycho” in the title.Beloved scream queen Maika Monroe (“It Follows,” “The Guest,” “Longlegs”) may be switching sides here, offering a twist on who horror fans root for once the blood starts flowing. (Hint: it’s the psycho.)

When we first meet Winifred, the Victorian-era governess is bound for her next assignment to teach the children of Mr. and Mrs. Pounds (Jason Isaacs and a sneaky-great Ruth Wilson, respectively) at their sprawling Yorkshire estate. “This won’t be like the other times,” she tells herself, winking mightily at how all those other times turned out. Our Winifred sports dead eyes and a rictus grin she works so very hard to fix in place. It’s even better when she attempts to imitate those around her, all the better to approximate “being human.”

No question, there’s something very wrong with Winifred. But what? You’ll find out soon enough. Possessed of “a darkness” she cannot shake, Monroe’s Winifred practically vibrates with the need to hold things together. It does not always work for her, but it is nearly always funny, deliciously and dementedly so.

Wigon and Freito don’t balk at the “psycho” promise of their story, as Winifred happily whacks away (often literally) at everyone icky, from gardeners to nurses (Thomasin McKenzie) and, yes, at least one baby. Killing scenes are elegantly, amusingly cut by editors Dustin Chow and Lance Edmands and designed for maximum gasps. Blood flows, then spurts, then pools. Sometimes it gets on Winifred’s face or her collar. She moves on, grimly and happily.

Cinematographer Nico Aguilar brings a similar energy to his work, shooting in and through keyholes, swinging his camera like a clock pendulum, even briefly adapting the perspective of a swallowed (redacted, for spoilers) as it travels into Winifred’s belly. It’s playful and gross, wholly fitting the material. Mostly, it’s so dark and fucked up you can’t help but laugh. OH! Did they do that? Yes, yes they did.

Possessed by the notion that she’s meant to be a part of the Pounds family (who would want to be? these aristocrats are monstrous), Winifred continues to fray. Bloodlusty audiences will be charmed by her go-for-broke attitude (more like go-for-the-throat), plus a steady stream of visual cues as to her current state. Dreams and nightmares merge, she’s haunted by the Pounds’ family mascot of a wild boar (particularly in an ever-morphing tapestry), and she simply can’t stop sneaking into places to stare at people while they sleep.

Clocking in at a tight 90 minutes, some changes to the also-slim book are smart, while others dilute its darkest impulses. Gone is the countdown to a Christmas massacre, which frames the novel; hell, gone is the whole Christmas massacre. Freito’s script leads up to a different sort of celebration, doing away with many of the most colorful supporting characters in the process (Mrs. Fancey, we hardly knew ye!).

That choice isn’t disastrous, although the execution of the big! final! event! is oddly watered down. Here it’s imagined as a battle of Winifred’s wills… but, erm, what wills? The book and the film each offer enough reasons for why our heroine is the way she is, Wigon’s film oddly bisects her spirit by implying she’s not fully on board with all the evil she commits.

For fans of the novel and its wonderfully unrepentant star, this choice might rankle; it’s also odd that Freito would go this route with her own adaptation. “Well, that’s not my ‘Victorian Psycho’ — and she’s not. That’s such a shame because for much of the film, she’s even better. By tempering her impulses and inner monologue, the film ends with less of the giddy gore that makes the rest of it such a dark treat. Dare we say it? We would have loved for this one to go full, ahem, boar.

“Victorian Psycho” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release it in theaters on Friday, September 25.
