#3474. My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic Is Back, And It's Better Than Ever

BOOM! Studios’ November 2026 My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic series opens with a story that understands what makes the Mane Six an entertaining and beloved group. Their personalities are funniest when they collide, but their differences also give them room to help one another. Written by Seanan McGuire, illustrated by Amy Meberson, and colored by Joana Lafuente, issue #1 reunites the familiar cast for a messy, friendship-focused adventure.

Rather than introduce a sweeping threat or a new corner of Equestria, the premiere starts with a party gone wrong. Pinkie Pie’s attempt at a prank leads to an accident involving something Twilight Sparkle treasures, and the friends have to work out how to make things right. The setup is light, but the damaged object gives the issue a question to explore.

The comic establishes its comedic rhythm through Pinkie and Rainbow Dash’s antics in Twilight’s castle. Pinkie’s contraptions and confidence repeatedly create problems, while Rainbow’s impatience adds another layer of chaos. Applejack gets caught in the mess, and the frosting-covered mishaps turn the opening pages into a lively showcase for the cast’s timing. Meberson’s expressive poses and Lafuente’s vivid frosting splashes make the chaos easy to read.

That slapstick is not just background decoration. The accident leaves the castle library in disarray and damages a book Twilight had been studying. The Mane Six clean up together, with Rainbow using her speed, Applejack pitching in, and Rarity bringing her standards to the task. Their teamwork gives the opening a recognizable Friendship Is Magic feel, while keeping the pace moving.

The story becomes more interesting when Twilight explains why the ruined book matters. It is her only known copy, and its author disappeared after completing it. The book is a friendship story, but not a simple celebration of companionship as it examines how a friendship can fracture. That premise gives Twilight a personal reason to recover it, beyond its rarity.

McGuire connects Twilight’s interest in the book to Fluttershy’s news that she has made a new friend. The parallel is gentle rather than heavy-handed. While the Mane Six prepare a surprise party for Fluttershy, the comic shows how good intentions, distraction, and Pinkie’s enthusiasm combine into an unintended disaster. The conflict suits the series’ focus on relationships.

The comic’s history adds a wistful note. Its author, Posey Pan, once lived in Seaward Shoals with her best friend, Merry Weather. The panels show the two fillies sharing books before their futures pull them apart. Twilight wants to understand what happened and preserve the lesson, making the missing volume more than a rare collectible. The flashback gives the adventure an emotional mystery.

ScreenRant has the exclusive first look at Hasbro's My Little Pony Kayou Friendship in the Cards for San Diego Comic-Con 2026.

The issue turns that emotional thread into a concrete adventure. The friends learn that another copy might be found at Rainbow Falls Trader’s Exchange, then head toward Picca-Filly Circus, a gathering place for traders. Because the search has barely begun, the debut feels more like a promising setup than a complete adventure; issue #2 of the My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic comic is advertised for December 2026.

#3472. Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

The Producers Guild of America (PGA) has announced that Casey Bloys, the newly instated co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance Direct-To-Consumer, will be honored with the Milestone Award at the 38th annual Producers Guild Awards on Saturday, February 27, 2027, at the Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles.

The PGA’s Milestone Award is meant to honor individuals or teams who have made historic contributions to the entertainment industry. Past recipients include Louis B. Mayer, Walt Disney, Alfred Hitchcock, Steven Spielberg, Sherry Lansing, James Cameron, Bob Iger, Donna Langley, Ted Sarandos, George Lucas and Kathleen Kennedy, Charles D. King, Dana Walden, and Jason Blum. Related Stories Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’ How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

“Considering Hollywood’s recent history, no one is more deserving of the Milestone Award than Casey Bloys. Over the last decade, Casey has had a front row seat to all the disruption and consolidation facing our industry. All the while he has remained a true and steadfast champion of the creative process,” said recently elected PGA presidents Donna Gigliotti and Mike Farah in an official statement. “He is a friend to producers, writers, actors and everyone who has dedicated their lives and careers to entertainment. Casey and his talented team help shepherd television that shapes our culture, stands the test of time, and protects the originality of storytellers. While Casey is never one to seek the spotlight, the Producers Guild of America is proud to recognize the breadth and depth of his exceptional career with the Milestone Award.”

“Receiving the Milestone Award is an incredible honor, particularly from an organization that represents so many of the people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside throughout my career,” said Bloys in his own statement. “I’ve always believed our job is to create an environment where talented people can take risks, tell ambitious stories and do their best work. I’m enormously grateful to the Producers Guild for this recognition and to all of the producers, storytellers and colleagues who have been part of that journey.”

In his new role at Skydance, Bloys oversees all original programming for HBO Max and Paramount+ in addition to strategy, operations, communications, and performance across the company’s streaming platforms.

Since becoming President of HBO in 2016, Bloys has led the development and production of award-winning and critically acclaimed series like “Succession,” “Euphoria,” “Barry,” “Girls,” “Veep,” “Insecure,” “Mare of Easttown,” “Big Little Lies,” “The Pitt,” “The White Lotus,” and many more. That has resulted in HBO and HBO Max’s original television programs receiving 21 Emmys across eight original programs this past year, as well as several other industry awards. Seven of Bloys’ current original series also saw cross-platform audiences averaging a milestone number of more than 15 million U.S. viewers per episode.

#3470. ‘The Rings of Power’ Just Confirmed Our Biggest Theory About the Dark Wizard

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episode 3.

After years of speculation, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has finally granted fans an answer about the true identity of the notorious Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds). Ever since we first encountered this desert ruler, who holds sway over the eastern land of Rhûn, there have been many theories about which Istari he might be. Season 3 finally confirms that this Dark Wizard of the East is none other than one of the famed Blue Wizards sent to Middle-earth before Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) himself.

Season 3's reveal probably won't surprise diehard Tolkien fans, even if the particulars are a bit surprising. Previously, Tolkien wrote that only five Istari made their way to Arda in physical form. Given that viewers have already met Gandalf and know the fates of characters like Saruman the White and Radagast the Brown, that left only the two Blue Wizards. Between them, Tolkien wrote very little, with most of the material coming from Unfinished Tales, but The Rings of Power fills out the story in Season 3's third episode as Gandalf communes with the Secret Fire. "He was once called Pallando," Gandalf hears, "one of two wizards sent to protect these lands, but he wanted more. So, he betrayed and murdered his partner, an act so evil that it laid all of Rhûn to waste." Thus, it is due to Pallando's lust for power that the east was cursed, destined to never be made right.

Although the decision to kill off Alatar (the other Blue Wizard) is certainly shocking, this development (as well as their arrival in the Second Age) isn't beyond the realm of possibility when examining Tolkien's legendarium. In The Peoples of Middle-earth, the Blue Wizards are described as having been sent to Middle-earth likely around the same time as Glorfindel during the Second Age. "Their task was to circumvent Sauron," Tolkien explains, "to bring help to the few tribes of Men that had rebelled..." These tribes were meant to be some of those furthest from the Kingdom of Númenor. Interestingly, Tolkien concludes that, while the Blue Wizards most likely failed in their efforts, they had some hand in reducing Sauron's potential allies by the time of the Third Age. Even so, their failures would have major ramifications, giving the Dark Lord a true hold over that part of the map.

The cast and creators break down the show's most personal storyline yet for Tolkien's most iconic wizard.

"I suspect they were the founders or beginners of secret cults and 'magic' traditions that outlasted the fall of Sauron," Tolkien added in a letter collected in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien. While there has never been anything written about one wizard killing the other, it's certainly not implausible, especially since neither of them appears in any form during the climactic events of The Lord of the Rings. After all, even Tolkien himself continued to shift and change their backstory, including their names, which he altered to Morinehtar and Rómestámo near the end of his life. Since Tolkien appeared to believe that both wizards failed in their task, Pallando's betrayal could absolutely work within the context of The Rings of Power.

However you slice it, the Dark Wizard's biggest reveal has been a long time coming. The Rings of Power spent way too long teasing the Stranger's true identity as Gandalf over the first two seasons (despite it being quite obvious), and it's clear that the show's creators have no intention of leading fans on any further here. Indeed, intersecting the lives of Gandalf — who, unlike the Blue Wizards, really shouldn't be around in the Second Age — and Pallando is certainly an interesting direction. His new divinely-inspired mission to redeem his wizard brother is a compelling idea when seen in light of Saruman's eventual corruption during the Third Age. As the Secret Fire tells the Grey Wizard, "Only together can you prevent the armies of Rhûn from joining Sauron."

Whether Gandalf succeeds or not, The Rings of Power continues to dive deeper into Tolkien lore this season, and it's about time. Some page-to-screen translations may leave a bit to be desired (Tom Bombadil should be much jollier), but the route the show is pursuing with the Istari seems to be the right — or at the very least, fascinating — direction. Would it have perhaps been more lore-accurate for Gandalf to be a Blue Wizard? Sure, but it's great to see the show finally exploring one of these lesser-known sorcerers. With the Harfoots out of the story, this reveal comes at just the right time to offer more hope for the future of Middle-earth.

New episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power are available for streaming Wednesdays on Prime Video.

#3469. ‘The Rings of Power’ Season 3 Review: Amazon’s ‘Lord of the Rings’ Series Is Just Going Through the Motions

The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth. Related Stories Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not.) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir (for now, at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door. Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god, these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.

#3468. This Bose Portable Bluetooth Speaker Is 33% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

#3467. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel Gets Official Update For Skyrim's Anniversary

After eight extremely long years since its initial announcement, The Elder Scrolls VI finally broke cover the other day to give the waiting masses a title for the game they've been so desperate to see more of. Sentinel, as it is now known, is likely taking us back to Hammerfell, and it will be really interesting to see the important region in a modern game from the series.

Outside of that, though, we still don't really know anything about the game, or what it will look and play like. That's because it is almost certainly still a couple of years away from being in our hands at a minimum, and the announcement of the title was likely just to placate us for as long as they can, for the most part.

Unfortunately, it seems as though we have now had confirmation that nothing is coming for a while, and it comes from the developer themselves.

As first reported by ComicBook.com, a post on Reddit is drawing attention right now as it has attracted Bethesda themselves, who stopped by to put pay to a particular rumor that's circulating. Specifically, several members of the community felt that a full reveal could be on the way to mark the 15th anniversary of the release of Skyrim, which actually dropped today (at the time of writing), November 11, 2011.

Unfortunately, that's absolutely not going to be the case, as Bethesda's official Reddit profile shared the following response to quash that burgeoning speculation:

"Hey everyone, wanted to pop in to say that we aren’t going to have any big announcements tomorrow. We’re excited you’re excited but we will not be sharing anything new on Sentinel for some time," the comment read.

As you might expect, that led to humorous conspiratorial responses from the community, who felt as though this was simply Bethesda obfuscating their plans.

"This sub getting so unhinged the last few days that Bethesda has had to literally step in has made me so proud lmao." one comment read.

While another added, "I'm reading this as 'Wanted to let you know we are launching tomorrow. We are excited to keep you busy in Sentinel for some time'".

The recent teaser for the game gave us a look at a titular Elder Scroll being revealed from underneath sand which, while it doesn't reveal much on the face of it, could provide certain clues. One leading theory is that it symbolizes the Alik'r Desert, which stretches across the northwestern part of the province of Hammerfell, and could easily serve as a hidden location for the scroll.

That said, there is lots of existing lore around the Elder Scrolls that should mean they aren't able to be simply wielded by the player, or anyone else for that matter. It will be interesting to see how Bethesda puts them at the center of the narrative in Sentinel, as it relates to our character, without overriding much of the lore that made them compelling in the first place.

#3466. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3464. How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

Jordan Firstman knew that the success of “Club Kid” hinged on finding the perfect preteen actor to play his character’s long-lost son, Arlo.

It was a demanding role that had a lot of boxes to check off: A British kid, whose hard-partying mother had just committed suicide, finds himself dumped in New York City, where he struggles to break out of his protective shell to bond with his party promoter dad, Peter (Firstman, who wrote and directed the film, in addition to starring in it ). But the perfect candidate had to project an effortless coolness that allows him to organically blend in with his newfound father’s social circle of hard-living, LGBTQ+ clubgoers, whose lives revolve around their love of music, dance, and drugs. Related Stories ‘Victorian Psycho’ Review: Maika Monroe Scares Up a Very Different Kind of Final Girl ‘Steps’ Review: A Disposable Fairy Tale Reminds Us That Cinderella Is Someone’s Hated Stepsister Too

“[Arlo’s] not just cool, he’s empathetic and wise; there’s a lot of stuff about that kid that was on the page that needed to be there,” said Firstman, who on this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, called the casting search the most “nerve-wracking” part of making “Club Kid.”

“Club Kid” had the right casting director for the job. Carmen Cuba has a legendary track record of finding child stars, including the original “Stranger Things” ensemble. But as Cuba pointed out while participating in IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable of Casting Directors, “Club Kid” was different from those previous assignments.

“I do six-month searches for kids,” said Cuba. “On ’Stranger Things,’ ‘Starfighter,’ you have time and money, and this was a small film.”

The $6 million production could not afford a lengthy search. It didn’t even have the money for Cuba to fly to London with Firstman for auditions. She would be reliant on a UK casting team, working within a limited budget, to help her find a needle in a haystack.

“I was very nervous about just sort of the plan of attack, because I was going to have a UK team, and you need a British kid who looks like he’s half-Jordan,” said Cuba.

Right before jumping into “Club Kid,” Cuba went on her yearly vacation with a group of close casting director friends. As the holiday wound down, Cuba tried to work through her upcoming casting dilemma with some of her closest colleagues.

“I [said], ‘How am I going do this?’ just trying to map it out for myself before I left to go start it,” recalled Cuba of the conversation. “And one of those friends is Lucy Bevan, who had just finished her ‘Harry Potter’ search, so she so generously said, ‘Why don’t I share some of the names.’”

To cast the first season of the $200 million-plus upcoming HBO series — based on the first Harry Potter book, “The Philosopher’s Stone,” in which Harry turns 11 — Bevans had just finished her own six-month search. She had auditioned thousands of young British actors to play the next generation of Harry, Hermione, Ron, and their Hogwarts classmates.

“This is just a testament to our relationship because Lucy would not normally do UK casting on a tiny movie,” said Cuba of the prominent British casting director, whose credits include “Barbie,” “F1,” and “The Batman.”

“She had just seen 40,000 kids,” said Firstman of Beaven, who early on showed him a photo of Reggie Absolom. “I saw his face and I was like, ‘that is the face that I’ve seen in my head.’ Even in the script, he’s supposed to be a quarter Indian – “Innit Babes” [Peter and his friends’ nickname for Reggie’s mom based on her favorite expression] is supposed to be like half Indian — and Lucy [said], ‘Let’s not focus on that. That’s not going happen.’ And Reggie’s a quarter Indian. Every single thing that I had asked God for, this kid came to me in Reggie.”

In total, according to Cuba, Bevan showed Firstman 90 kids, with a wider range of ages — Cuba and Firstman went back and forth about how old Reggie should be, with the character originally skewing younger than 10 — but Firstman never wavered from Absalom, whose résumé included roles in “Silo” and “The Other Bennet Sister.”

“Lucy was so generous. They had no money to fly me to London to do the session in person, so she hosted the callback session there,” said Cuba. “Jordan is incredible with kids, he was like, ‘Let’s not do it in this casting office, let’s take it outside.’ So suddenly Lucy’s assistant is outside with the camera, and they’re walking and talking. I rewatched that audition recently, and it’s just amazing. Jordan’s brain, and how he connects to everyone that he casts. I think that’s what you feel in the movie; it’s so familial.”

On the podcast, Firstman talked about how beyond his decade of drug-fueled clubbing in Europe and New York City, one of the inspirations for “Club Kid” was the bond he formed with one of his close friend’s child, something he felt would be essential to replicate with Absolom.

“The reason kids like me is I don’t treat them as kids,” said Firstman. “They’re surprised at my candor, or the inappropriate things that most adults wouldn’t be willing to say in front of a kid. I know what Reggie sees on the internet. I’m not going to say something too much, but I can push it a little bit.  I think he always appreciated that in me, and once he understood that I liked to be made fun of too, everything shifted. Once he got permission to make fun of me, the whole dynamic shifted, and we just got so much more comfortable around each other.”

Much like his unorthodox, take-it-outside, walk-and-talk callback audition with Absolom, Firstman quickly realized, after casting the young actor, traditional preparation wouldn’t work.

“We tried doing traditional rehearsals, and it was awkward,” said Firstman. “I [said], ‘Let’s just keep hanging out, and keep having pizza together, and keep talking about music, and keep talking about TikTok clips we’ve seen, and send each other TikToks,’ and that’s how we bonded.”

An A24 release, “Club Kid” is now in New York City and Los Angeles theaters, and will expand on Friday, November 13.

#3463. Netflix Officially Revives One of the Worst Fantasy Remakes Ever Made

Tom Cruise has spent most of his career making the impossible look ridiculously easy, whether that's hanging off airplanes, jumping motorcycles off cliffs, or somehow finding increasingly dangerous ways to save the world as Ethan Hunt. But even Hollywood's most committed action star has the occasional misfire. Nearly a decade later, however, it's getting another opportunity to find its audience.

The Mummy has returned to Netflix's Top 10 movie rankings, bringing Cruise's much-maligned fantasy adventure back into the streaming spotlight. The 2017 release earned approximately $410 million worldwide, a respectable-sounding figure that wasn't enough to make the movie the franchise-launching success Universal had envisioned. Intended to launch an entire cinematic universe of classic monsters, the movie instead became a rather expensive reminder that audiences aren't always interested in another big-budget IP.

Thought safely entombed in a tomb deep beneath the unforgiving desert, an ancient princess whose destiny was unjustly taken from her is awakened in our current day, bringing with her malevolence grown over millennia and terrors that defy human comprehension. The movie takes us on a globe-trotting adventure from the sweeping sands of the Middle East through hidden labyrinths under modern-day London, in a new world of gods and monsters.

The movie stars Tom Cruise (Mission: Impossible) as Nick Morton, Sofia Boutella (Kingsman: The Secret Service) as Princess Ahmanet, Annabelle Wallis (Peaky Blinders) as Jenny Halsey, Russell Crowe (Gladiator) as Dr. Henry Jekyll, Jake Johnson (New Girl) as Chris Vail, Courtney B. Vance (The People v. O. J. Simpson) as Colonel Greenway, and Marwan Kenzari (Aladdin) as Malik.

Crowe's Dr. Jekyll was intended to help connect the movie to a wider world of supernatural creatures, with Universal announcing plans for future installments involving characters such as Frankenstein's Monster and the Invisible Man. Yes, they also planned to bring in the likes of Javier Bardem and Johnny Depp for a new Dark Universe.

Despite Cruise’s star power and a big marketing push (remember that awkward cast promo image with him, Bardem, Depp, and Crowe?), the film bombed critically and commercially, earning dreadful reviews and losing an estimated $100 million for Universal. The entire Dark Universe crumbled before a second movie could even shoot.

#3460. CBS Is Officially Ending NCIS Series' Undisputed Best Run

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Ana has also covered a wide-spread of topics in the past — from franchises like, the MCU and Star Wars, to classic TV favorites, such as Frasier and MASH.

Ana brings clarity and enthusiasm to every story she tackles—whether reporting on new releases or offering deep dives into fan-favorite franchises. Her coverage translates complex entertainment developments into engaging, audience-focused content.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for the NCIS franchise.The NCIS franchise has been a hit on all cylinders this cycle, but one series is ending its best run disappointingly earlier than the rest. Donald Bellisario and Don McGill's famed procedural has been a staple of CBS's programming since 2003. Since then, the flagship has created the franchise, birthing multiple spinoffs along the way. In CBS's fall 2026 slate, the Eye Network strengthens its commitment to the universe with its revamped Super Tuesday lineup, which groups all the Navy-related projects in one night.

Each show in NCIS's active lineup has something fresh and interesting to offer viewers. NCIS season 24 marks the beginning of a new era with the return of Michael Weatherly's Tony Dinozzo; NCIS: New York sees LL Cool J's Sam Hanna leading his own team, and NCIS: Origins gets Mark Harmon's Leroy Jethro Gibbs out of retirement in Alaska. While everyone has their favorites, it's arguably fair to say that the way David J. North's prequel series has been the best in terms of storytelling among the three. Unfortunately, CBS is ending its run earlier than its peers.

Ahead of the ongoing network TV cycle, CBS announced that NCIS: Origins season 3's run will be significantly shortened — slashing its episode count from 18 to just 10 episodes. Thus far, the prequel has already released five episodes, which means that it has officially arrived at the midpoint mark of its run. The decision to slash its output stems from CBS's scheduling, slotting NCIS: Sydney season 4 to the same timeslot once the winter season rolls around — something that is becoming more popular among traditional broadcasters.

That said, the verdict came long before the public found out about what's in store for the period series for its junior year run. Bolstered by Harmon's full-time return as Old Gibbs, not to mention the string of beloved franchise characters coming back, all on top of the procedural aspect of the series from its '90s timeline, and NCIS: Origins season 3 has been such a delight to watch every week. So much so, that there was hope that somehow, CBS might have a surprise twist regarding its run with a last-minute extension in any form. Sadly, that isn't the case, as NCIS: Origins season 3 is re-affirmed to be ending early as originally planned.

With only five episodes left before NCIS: Origins season 3 ends, expect that long-running stories introduced early on will have some sort of resolution. It has already been confirmed that CBS is bringing back three more key people from Gibbs' story — Roma Maffia, Muse Watson, and Joe Spano as Old Vera Strickland, Frank Gibbs, and Tobias Fornell. They join Weatherly and Emily Wickersham as Dinozzo and Ellie Bishop in this modern arc for Old Gibbs.

Six years after their final appearance, the original young Gibbs is officially recast in the NCIS franchise playing a more interesting character.

Considering the major reveal that Lala Dominguez didn't die in that plane crash that Old Gibbs previously revealed, it's safe to say that Vera and Mike's respective comebacks will have something to do with that. As for Fornell, his storyline might be tied to the bigger conspiracy at hand. In any case, seeing them back would be a big treat, not just for fans of NCIS: Origins, but also those who have followed Harmon's character from his days in the NCIS flagship.

#3459. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3458. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3457. ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’

Jack O’Connell was feeling a little bashful. Seated outside for coffee, taking in the fresh fall air at the remote Salamander Resort in Middleburg, Virginia, the actor revealed that communication between him and Oscar-winning filmmaker Danny Boyle began long before he was cast as the lead in the director’s latest film, “Ink.”

“I used to write to Danny a lot. I wrote all the directors that I admire,” said the 36-year-old star from Derbyshire, England. “Not cap in hand, trying to get anything out of them, just letters of appreciation, lovely stuff that’s affected me and inspired me. ‘I hope we get to do it someday.’ And, in Danny’s case, we did.” Related Stories How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star Casey Bloys to Receive the Milestone Award at 2027 PGAs

Technically “Ink,” in which O’Connell plays influential newspaper editor Larry Lamb after he’s recruited by outcast media magnate Rupert Murdoch to take over The Sun tabloid in 1969, is the second time the actor has worked with Boyle. The pair first officially met when he was brought in to play antagonist Jimmy Crystal in last year’s “28 Years Later,” directed by Boyle, and more prominently in January’s “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” directed by Nia DaCosta.

“It was right before I went and shot ‘Sinners,’” he said, referencing another major turn as a villain that loomed prominently over cinema this year. “The initial meeting wasn’t an audition. I just didn’t have the role. It was a meeting discussing the role with Danny and Nia.” It was the first time Boyle had acknowledged O’Connell, though he had a sneaking suspicion that he had been on the director’s radar for a while, having starred on the same iconic British teen drama “Skins” from which Boyle had found the star of his Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire.”

“Listen, he cast Dev [Patel]. He knew about ‘Skins.’ I think his daughter put him onto ‘Skins’ in the first place. So whether or not he stuck it out for our generation, I don’t know,” said O’Connell.

It’s been almost two decades since he first played fan favorite Cook as part of the second generation of the trailblazing E4 series, which ran from 2007 to 2013. “Skins” still stands out as an experience that helped shape his ethos as an actor. “I certainly felt like we were on the coolest show around. It was so amazingly written. The directors we had were brilliant. The whole model of the way that you audition en masse and then they find their characters. I love that,” said O’Connell. “It’s really quite pure, isn’t it? People are just getting the roles because of ability.”

The “Ink” star first trained as an actor at a free program in Nottingham called the Television Workshop, which eventually helped lead to his first breakout film role in the coming-of-age drama “This Is England.” However, it was “Skins” that felt like a “crash course” continuing education. “You’re doing all the heavy stuff, the tough stuff, the really laborious side of doing a TV show like that. But also the fun and the joy that gets provoked by all the art, the amazing writing and everything else,” said O’Connell. He’s quick to remind that notable “Skins” alumni include not just Patel, but also writers like Emmy winner Jack Thorne and Tony-nominated playwright Lucy Kirkwood.

But free programs like the Television Workshop are increasingly hard to come by, meaning there are less and less egalitarian-type opportunities in the United Kingdom for an actor from a working-class background like O’Connell’s to find their own “Skins.” Asked what he would tell the next generation of artists, the “Ink” star said, “I wouldn’t know what advice I would give nowadays, which is a shocking indictment.”

What attracted O’Connell to playing Lamb in “Ink,” a role that has brought him to the Middleburg Film Festival to receive the Spotlight Actor Award, was the opportunity to address how the UK, and the world in general, reached this place of inequality. “We see this man just excavate his morals, and his soul, and his decisions, and this newspaper. Being the best-selling newspaper, he’s had to part with what makes people more human. To me, it’s a comment on capitalism,” said the star. “The beginning of hyper capitalism, post-war England, and individual opportunity versus looking after everyone else and your responsibility within society. That was all just getting ripped up.”

“Ink” is an adaptation of James Graham’s 2017 play of the same name, with Graham also serving as the screenwriter of Boyle’s film. Another major factor in O’Connell’s decision to play Larry Lamb was working with the playwright and the director, who had come from a similar background. With Boyle, “I came to his work as a fan first, before I knew I was going to try and be an actor,” he said. “I remember watching ‘The Beach,’ and that made me want to go and see the world. And watching ‘Trainspotting’ and that made me want to never take heroin. But also the amazing soundtrack that’s in there and the fucking unforgettable performances.”

With “Ink” they were preparing to tell what O’Connell sees as a quintessentially British story, and “what [Danny’s] films have meant for British cinema and British culture as a result is undeniable. Thank fuck for Danny Boyle. He is an artist by every stretch of the word. I would argue that his films have perhaps meant the most to us as a collective growing up. His work at the Olympics opening ceremony makes you tingle to watch it. It is fucking monumental.”

Boyle is why O’Connell, an outsider to the film and TV industry in the same way Lamb was to the publishing industry, could still envision himself becoming an actor one day. “His style has been able to make you feel part of the film. It takes you along. You feel like you’re in the movie somehow. You don’t feel like an observer, like a spectator. They give you a feeling and mood as well,” he said.

As for Graham, “We’re not too far from each other in a particular pocket of the UK. And although my town and his town famously don’t get on — that’s all to do with football and Brian Clough and whatever else — but he is a dramatist. He’s also interested in analyzing culture and the culture around him and examining it,” said O’Connell. “He’s a great spokesman for under-representation in the industry at home because eight percent of the entire industry are from our background.”

The actor added, “Once he knew that I was somebody that could be trusted with his words, not someone who was going to try and fucking destroy them, we really hit it off.”

Here the three were, as what some would call a band of outsiders, telling a story about these insurgents to the distinguished Fleet Street, where the most esteemed newspapers like The Daily Mirror were published. Playing Lamb was a bit of an exercise in what would happen if O’Connell’s comeuppance led him toward the dark side. “The intoxication of power is something that really interests me. And Larry, he began as a socialist, voted Labour, celebrated socialist politicians. He left Fleet Street having been knighted by Margaret Thatcher. … Talk about excavation, a whole U-turn politics there, colluded with Rupert Murdoch in tearing up the unions and workers’ rights. Sold his soul,” said O’Connell.

“There’s a great contradiction with Larry that he begins as an outsider. Even within the duration of our film, he’s trying to become an insider. He wants to be part of that gang. In fact, that’s where he ended up, Sir Larry. So there’s a great contradiction in the man. So I can’t afford to go all the way ‘outsider with a chip on his shoulder,’” said the actor.

With “Ink” following the successes of “Sinners” and “28 Years Later” so quickly, O’Connell has a newfound feeling of security and sense of becoming that sought-after leading man. “It probably is my most mature role to date,” he said. “I look back on my career and I just feel so fortunate. There’s not a single regret. So if this is a new era, yeah, brilliant, bring it on. A lot of my heroes, a lot of their work that I really celebrate, were around my age, so maybe that is inspiring and gives me cause to kick on.”

Netflix will release “Ink” in select theaters across the United States on Friday, December 11. The film will debut on the streaming service on January 8, 2027.

#3456. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

To read Counterpoint’s full report, follow this link.

#3455. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3454. Spawn Returns Today With New Sequel Ahead Of Movie Reboot

Every Spawn fan is on pins and needles as we await news about Todd McFarlane’s upcoming live-action reboot. Many will remember that McFarlane first announced his partnership with Blumhouse to develop the reboot in 2017, and that Jamie Foxx was officially announced as Spawn in 2018. However, it has been a grueling, near-decade-long wait, with still no end in sight for when we might finally see the movie. Thankfully, today is still a great day for fans, as the first installment of a two-part Spawn sequel has officially arrived.

’Tis the season for Santa Claus, serial killers, and Spawn! Arriving today is the highly anticipated sequel to last year’s acclaimed Christmas horror story, I Saw Santa: A Spawn Universe Story. Titled I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale, this sequel will be a two-part special, just like its predecessor. With issue #1 launching today, fans can expect the second and final issue to arrive on December 16, 2026.

Last year, Chris Killian, Andrew Sanders, and artist Thomas Nachlik brought us a horrifying tale about what happens when one disturbed child takes offense to Santa's gift of coal and makes it his life's mission to torment Jolly Ol' Saint Nick for the rest of his life. The two-part special also answered the question of who you call when naughty kids take their misbehavior to diabolical levels: Spawn, of course!

2027 is already a huge year for Witcher fans, and now Geralt and Jaskier are returning for another release set in the franchise's golden era.

Now, Killian and Sanders return, this time alongside artist Todor Hristov, for the official sequel to this story. For a spoiler-free idea of what happens in the first issue of I Saw Spawn, check out the official synopsis: "The North Pole is shaken by a gruesome massacre that bears the signature of serial killer, Charlie Kohl. As Santa Claus investigates, dark forces begin to corrupt Santa's workshop from within, and it’s clear Spawn is the only one who might be able to put a stop to this terribly twisted Christmas."

While the 48-page I Saw Spawn: A Twisted Christmas Tale #1 is available now for $5.99, we highly recommend checking out I Saw Santa #1-2 first. Not only is this the proper reading order and a way to elevate your reading experience, but the original two-part story is also a PHENOMENAL read. This story gives a whole new meaning to the Christmas song "Santa Claus Is Coming to Town," especially the jingle's famous warning: "You better watch out."

This story is perfect for those who love a smorgasbord of genres. Here, you'll find a collision of Christmas, horror, mystery, and a surprising amount of nonstop fun. However, this is far more than just a brutal Christmas story, as the writing for this two-part special is superb. Don't believe our praise? Then check out I Saw Santa: A Spawn Universe Christmas Story #1 on League of Comic Geeks, where readers gave the story an "exceptional" 4.5-out-of-5-star rating.

With Killian and Sanders returning for the sequel, readers already know the quality they can expect. And while Nachlik's artwork was perfection in last year's special, fans will likely appreciate Hristov's work just as much. So, if you're starting to feel that Christmas fever and want to experience the holiday spirit through the brutal lens of the Spawn universe, then bump this holiday special to the top of your TBR.

I SAW SPAWN A TWISTED CHRISTMAS TALE #1 from Image Comics is available now!

#3453. 8 DC Characters Who Should Make Their DCU Debut on TV

While the DCU has seen some success in cinemas with the likes of Superman and Clayface, they've actually been doing just as well on television—some even arguing they've been doing better. With Creature Commandos and Lanterns both being critical smash hits, it's clear that the DCU will not be having the Marvel Cinematic Universe's television problem moving forward.

This is good because the DCU actually has a lot of plans for television in their upcoming slate, and that means even more great stories to come. Through the previous two series, audiences got introduced to Clayface (before his cinema debut), the Creature Commandos, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), and so many more iconic characters. With this and these upcoming announced projects in mind, there are some legendary DC Comics characters that should most definitely be making their DCU debut on television.

While not well-known to the general public, anyone who's seen the ever-beloved animated series, Young Justice—and the more niche-but-critically-acclaimed Mister Miracle (2017) comic—knows exactly who Granny Goodness is (played in that series by Deborah Strang). With how important of a character Granny Goodness is to the story of Mister Miracle, it'd be an incredible disservice to the DCU iteration of the hero (to be played by Josh Hutcherson) not to have her be included.

She is a master brainwasher, but most importantly, she is the top recruiter of the planet Apokolips' militaristic forces. This, of course, makes her very close to the Thanos of the DC Comics world . . . Darkseid. Audiences already know the terrifying villain will be making his first appearance in Mister Miracle, but with how important Granny Goodness is, it would feel odd not having her around at his right hand.

Fans of the Scarlet Speedster—both in comics and the television show, The Flash—are well aware that the classic Flash villain, Gorilla Grodd, will be making his DCU entrance in The People v. Gorilla Grodd. The show will follow reporter Jimmy Olsen (Skyler Gisondo) as he investigates the murder of Grodd's father, of which Grodd himself is wrongfully convicted of. If Olsen is going to truly investigate something like this, he needs to look into other potential suspects and those who have similar enemies that Grodd does—aka, other Flash villains.

Audiences have already come across a major rumor that Flash villain, Weather Wizard, is going to appear, so why not have one of the greatest Flash villains up there, with Grodd, also make an appearance—the one and only Captain Cold? Aside from the Reverse Flash, this Cold Gun-wielding baddie is one of the most recognizable Flash foes of all time. It would be a dang shame if audiences didn't get to see him find a place in The People v. Gorilla Grodd.

If anyone has ever heard of Booster Gold, they know of his close relationship with Blue Beetle—Ted Kord, not Jaime Reyes. With the latter finally being added to the DCU and getting his own animated series, Xolo Maridueña's Jaime Reyes still acts as the perfect hallway for Booster Gold to enter the cinematic universe. Despite the gold-clad hero being a good friend to Ted Kord, he's still teamed up with Jaime from time to time.

Not to mention, with the Blue Beetle film itself not being confirmed to be DCU canon, and only Xolo's iteration, there's a very good chance Kord could have a place in this new animated story regardless. If they choose to include Jaime's predecessor in some way, then Booster Gold is the perfect addition to this series—especially for comedic relief. Now, all that DC Studios needs to do is listen to the fans and get Shayne Topp on the cast for the iconic character.

As stated, with Xolo's Blue Beetle only being canon as a character and the movie itself not being canon (at least not yet, anyway), the disappearance of Ted Kord in that film may not end up being canon. So, this means audiences could finally see the old Blue Beetle in the DCU. This iteration of the hero differs vastly from Jaime's.

While the younger hero has the Scarab to power him up, Ted Kord is more of a gadget-based hero—almost in a Batman sense, just not dark and gritty. He's a funny, relatable, and a bit of an outsider in the DC Comics universe. He would be a perfect addition to the animated series and, as previously said, would be a great way to bring in Booster Gold, too.

Another character extremely important to the Mister Miracle mythology is his adoptive brother, Orion. Fans of the classic animated series, Justice League Unlimited, might recognize him. He is a living contrast—being born into a world of war and violence, but chooses to embrace light and heroism regardless. He's very compelling for this very reason.

Everyone loves a hero who has some darkness within them and Orion is a great example of this. There's no question he'll be appearing in Mister Miracle, and hopefully this means he'll be sticking around in the DCU moving onward post-Mister Miracle. These two brothers have a great dynamic, so adding Orion to the cast of characters currently in the cinematic universe is perfect.

The major question regarding the Flash in the DCU at the moment is whether the main mantle-holder will be Barry Allen or, the once Kid Flash, Wally West—who became the Flash in the comics after Barry's death in Crisis on Infinite Earths (1985). Regardless of if he's the main Flash, Kid Flash, or still powerless, though, Wally could be a perfect addition to The People v. Gorilla Grodd, thanks to one of the main locations within said series.

If the young hero is still, well, young, he could be perfect to have at the college that Grodd attends at one point in the show. If he isn't younger, and is the main Flash at the moment, it would only make sense for the hero to make an appearance to help Grodd—or believe that he's still evil and try to prove Jimmy wrong. Wally (as Flash) was one of the most popular characters in the Justice League and Justice League Unlimited animated shows, so it'd be a shame not to see him in the DCU soon.

With Lanterns being successful enough to warrant a greenlight for Season 2, one can only hope that the DCU continues to expand the Green Lantern corner of the universe. Unlike the cinematic universe, though, the comics have multiple Green Lanterns from Earth, and a fan favorite just so happens to be the likes of Kyle Rayner. Where John Stewart is more tactical and precise with his constructs and heroism, Kyle has always been one of, if not the most creative, Green Lanterns.

While John still needs a lot more time to be Earth's Green Lantern on his own for a bit, Lanterns Season 2 is still a great opportunity to introduce this fan favorite green-suited hero. It wouldn't be the best choice to make him a Green Lantern right away, but bringing him into the fold in some way, to being building him up to eventually be a hero, would be an excellent move on DC Studios' part.

If it isn't already clear—based on what was already stated about Wally West—it would be a gigantic missed opportunity to not have the Flash help out or be an antagonist in some way, shape, or form in The People v. Gorilla Grodd. While Wally would be cool to see, it actually makes far more sense to include Barry, as he has a direct connection to matters like this, being a CSI, and someone who has faced Grodd multiple times in the past—the gorilla has always been more of a Barry villain.

It's genuinely so difficult to believe that Barry wouldn't use his CSI work as a way to insert himself in the investigation and learn more. Flash is a hero that typically believes in redemption for his villains, meaning he would definitely want to get behind what actually happened between Grodd and his father—if anything even did. Honestly, if Barry—any Flash, really—doesn't show up in The People v. Gorilla Grodd, it'd be a bit absurd.

#3452. Apple expected to bid for F1 streaming rights in more countries, says Formula 1 CEO

On the latest earnings call for F1’s parent company Liberty Media, the CEO of Formula 1 Stefano Domenicali said that both parties are happy with the US deal, and he expects that Apple will bid for rights in more countries as the opportunities become available.

F1 has previously expressed that they are not currently looking for one media partner to take global broadcast rights for the sport; they want a portfolio of deals, picking the best partners for each geographic market.

We have already seen this play out in the United Kingdom, with broadcaster Sky renewing its deal for F1 rights through 2034, seemingly locking Apple out of that region. So, despite the apparent demand, Apple will not be able to just walk in and take over the future of the sport’s worldwide distribution.

However, it seems the league is open to striking more deals with Apple in certain markets.

On the earnings call, in response to a question from an investor about Apple’s interest, Domenicali said “this is part of our discussion, if there are opportunities that can be in other markets, they will do it … they’re going to do it as soon as these opportunities will be open for them”.

Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang said they continue to think about what new innovation they can bring to the product side, and noted that “Apple as a potential bidder in other markets is helpful” for their business.

As a reminder, all Formula 1 races are available to watch live and on-demand with an Apple TV subscription, in the United States. The company recently launched a Dolby Atmos audio track for its F1 streams, as well as expanded support for Multiview on more platforms, including iPhone Duo.
