#3451. Why Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg Built a Therapy Circle for Hollywood’s Next Generation in Texas

Talent labs and mentorship programs are plentiful for aspiring filmmakers — but where do you turn when your career has already started, after your first movie or on the precipice of one, and especially when filmmaking can be such a lonely enterprise?

Enter Square Peg Social, the Austin, Texas-based filmmaking summit launched by Lars and Amy Knudsen and Ari Aster that offers four days of singular community-building: brutally honest advice, commiseration, and idea exchange shared among 35 participants, with the program now in its second year.

A weekend of panels, discussion, and camaraderie designed for filmmakers at the early stages of their career, this year’s talent-incubating event was even crashed by the likes of Zach Cregger and Richard Linklater — both of whom were down to get frank about their filmmaking highs and lows. (In fall 2025, IndieWire did a deep dive into Square Peg Social’s first year, just to show how much the event has already grown.) Related Stories ‘Ink’ Star Jack O’Connell on His ‘New Era’ as a Leading Man: ‘Thank F**k for Danny Boyle’ How Casting the New ‘Harry Potter’ Helped ‘Club Kid’ Find Its Adorable 10-Year-Old Star

But the program’s stable of 2026 mentors and panelists — i.e., filmmakers keen not only to open up to new filmmakers about their own struggles, but also to scout new talent — also counted “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything” director Lance Oppenheim, “Sing Sing” filmmaker Greg Kwedar, “The First Omen” director Arkasha Stevenson, and “Mother Mary” director David Lowery among them.

The closed-door, off-the-record, noncompetitive summit opened to applicants in May, later unfolding from September 17-21. Partners including the Austin Film Society, Belvedere, and Airbnb offset the cost, besides a modest application fee, for participants to hole up for four days and nights at Soho House that don’t promise job opportunities — but instead, the kind of lasting industry connections that can take years (and many starts and stops) to build. Also, no job opportunities isn’t entirely true. Take last year’s Square Peg Social mentee Yona Strauss, who’s now working for Knudsen and Aster’s Square Peg.

Just a sampling of this year’s participating producers and directors: producer Annie Huang, who worked on franchise IP like “Barbie” and “Wicked” at major studios; Jack Auen, co-founder of the filmmaking collective Cosmic Salon, which this year directed the New York critics’ favorite “Chronovisor”; Emmy-winning director of the Netflix short “The Turnaround,” Kyle Thrash; SXSW 2026 Neon Auteur Award winner Oliver Woolf; and many more who have their foot in the door, but are ready to cross the threshold.

IndieWire spoke to Lars Knudsen and Aster (who also co-founded the production company Square Peg, which this year backed “The Drama” and “Primetime”), plus Stevenson, Oppenheim, and Kwedar, along with three participants, to replay the on-the-ground experience in Austin. Late nights, early mornings, and vulnerabilities abounded across a long (but in some ways too short) weekend of intimate panels, small group sessions, and candid remarks from established filmmakers about the times they were trying to hold their own projects together with Scotch tape and paper clips. Think of it like a mini summer camp devoted to obsessive ambition.

“When you’ve been doing it for this long, sometimes it feels like you’re just a little bit going through the motions. You’re going from movie to movie to movie, and you sometimes forget why we do this thing that we do. We’re in this world working with these artists where they don’t have a plan B. Having now worked with 30, 40 filmmakers, I realized that when my wife brought up the idea of doing something because she has her own aversions to the industry, and that there isn’t really — it sounds cliché — but there just isn’t a lot of kindness or compassion or openness in our industry.

“There’s a lot of fear, there’s a lot of rejection. We wanted to create a space for filmmakers where there’s radical transparency and where it was truly, truly focused on a selfless thing: helping young filmmakers navigate the industry at a time in their career where things can either take off or not, and really demystifying the process of making movies, especially during the stage where they’re often in the back seat, which is financing or casting. Because for all these filmmakers that I work with and all the filmmakers that we’ve invited there, even the producers, it’s the first thing to think about when they wake up and the last thing to think about when they go to bed. Nothing is more important. I wanted to create an event where that is treated with the utmost importance, almost like it’s a life-or-death thing because it is all they want to do.”

“When Lars and Amy first broached the idea with me, I realized that it was something that I wish I had when I got out of school [at AFI], because I really did have to navigate that on my own. I was making a lot of shorts with whatever money I could raise and writing screenplays and trying to get one screenplay going. When that failed, writing something else and really looking for any sort of mentorship or guidance, It’s a very demoralizing process, and it was very, very hard for me to find traction, and it hasn’t gotten easier. It’s as bad as it’s ever been. There’s just so much uncertainty right now in the industry, not just for filmmakers. Even the lives of these studios are suddenly in danger and in question.

“There are a lot of filmmakers that Lars and I have been championing and films that we’ve been trying to get financing for that have proven almost impossible… It felt like a good thing to create a space where filmmakers can come together and commiserate and share experiences and connect. More important than even the connections that are made between the mentors and the mentees here are actually the relationships made among the people who are attending. A lot of them end up working together because we have producers and directors coming in. Last year proved really successful, and I would just say it was refreshing for us, too, that it galvanized us to keep doing this. Because last year it was almost an experiment: Will this work? How will we feel having done this? … Everybody walked away feeling good and feeling like it was a really useful and positive experience.”

“I’ve never really had the opportunity to just hang out with so many great filmmakers, not only just working filmmakers whose work I’ve loved, like David Lowery, who I’ve idolized for so long, but there’s so many filmmakers that were actually in the program as participants whose work I also have really admired. So having a space where we could all just kind of talk and vent and really nerd out on stuff that you never really get the opportunity to do.

“Because this was so filmmaker-driven and filmmaker-led, it encouraged the spirit of vulnerability [where] everyone really went there. I felt like maybe I should go back to therapy or something, but I felt like this was a great opportunity to therapize and also dump all of my feelings into a forum where you could just be open and honest about the process of making films… Most people had made features before, and were in the process of making features. It felt much more like we were at a film festival and everyone was able to connect with each other in a much deeper way, more than anything I’ve been to before.

“The first night I was there, I stayed up till like three in the morning, and I went on one of those electric scooters, the limes with Lars and Christian [Vasquez], my producer, and a producer from the event, too. We went to Whataburger and just kept talking. I think that was sort of the vibe. I don’t know. I guess everyone was encouraged to hang out for as long as they wanted to and to kick back and relax. There was another night we closed down the Soho House lounge bar, and Amy was like, ‘Let’s keep hanging out.’ So we were outside the bar, and everybody pulled together all of the drinks in their mini bar, and we created an ad hoc bar outside of the Soho House, and we kept drinking and hanging.”

“I don’t think you can really do film if you have a plan B because there’s always an escape hatch, and film requires every single atom of your body, mind and soul. It naturally becomes a very therapeutic place. I think because we’re all in this constant state of obsession, that can get really tiring, and it can get really lonely. … [The industry] attracts very sensitive souls. [With Square Peg Social] I didn’t even realize how badly I needed it until the first year. I’d known Amy and Lars before that, and Amy said that she wanted to start a Social. … I thought it would be much smaller, smaller. It ended up being this great big thing where, yeah, it does feel like a therapy circle, really.

“Everyone was really struck by the safety of the event. There was this unspoken agreement that everybody would be checking your egos at the door, and that this would be a very safe place to share your personal vulnerabilities, which is exceptionally rare in film because resources are so limited, and it’s just naturally a very competitive industry. Letting yourself be very, very vulnerable in front of your peers is something you were, in a sense, trained not to do but sometimes desperately need. At Square Peg, also, the line between mentee and mentor blurs quite a bit, which is why I think it’s so beneficial for everybody who goes there.

“It kind of reminds me of summer camp a little bit because you’re up until two or three in the morning talking to people, and then you’re up at eight again.”

“I always think of this term, like, whenever you take an elevator up, if you get to the top floor, send it back down for someone else to get on. [Square Peg] is one of the busiest production companies working today. To dedicate this weekend for emerging artists to have a forum where they can come and feel completely comfortable being very vulnerable with their ambitions, but also the things that they’re afraid of, and to hear that echoed from industry mentors who are being just as vulnerable about their ambitions and the things that they struggle with and the heartbreaks they’ve had, it’s an amazing table that’s set.

“I had ulterior motives in the, in the sense that Clint [Bentley] and I have started this new company, Ethos, and we have a deal at Netflix to finance films from emerging artists, and so I was also there … to look for talent. We’ll be following up with a lot of these artists to just hear more about the films they want to make. One thing that I appreciated about it was that it wasn’t like a pitch fest. You’re not there to pitch your project. You’re there to soak it in and learn.

“It had this healthy blend of these panels, and not the normal kind of panel. One was a panel of filmmakers led off by Ari and Lars, telling a very, very brutally honest story of how hard one of their films was to make. That kind of created a pathway for how the rest of the weekend would unfold.”

“I think the whole reason anyone works in film is that we were once kids making videos in the woods with our friends, making with a shitty camera. And there’s nothing else in this world, and I think I probably speak for everyone, where I can’t imagine film is the only thing that’s our main passion and hobby and something we can also make a career out of. So there was never a plan B at all. Whenever someone asked me, ‘What do you think you’d do if you couldn’t do anything film-adjacent?’ I have literally no idea, maybe a teacher or something. That’s super nice that Lars and the rest of Square Peg was saying that there is no plan B. There’s only: If it takes longer to get to Plan A, then it takes longer to get to Plan A.

“I remember on the very first day before we even properly began, Lars did a little speech with Ari, and Lars was like, ‘We’re going to be 100 percent transparent with you guys.’ And I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that’s cool, but I wonder how transparent.’ And by the end of it, I was like, ‘Fuck me, that was transparent.’ There really was nothing off the table.”

“It was definitely something that I’ve never experienced before in this industry, to experience that level of candor and to hear these traumatic experiences that they have gone through in not a sensationalistic way, but almost in a very personal and almost relatable way, despite me having never experienced that level of millions of dollars of movie budget making — but on a personal level of how the heartbreaks had felt for them individually and the hardships of filmmaking. Coming into this program, there are so many people within our cohort who are incredibly talented, who have accomplished so many things. And coming into it, oftentimes you’ll have a fear of: ‘OK, how do I compare in relation to their accomplishments?’ But in hearing Lars and Ari talk about their own hardships, I think that’s what influenced me to really share some of mine coming up in the industry and producing independently.

“Some of the traumatic experiences that I have also faced are ones that I feel like I have to not talk about or hide from people, for fear of them looking like mistakes or of me looking like I’m not good enough to be doing this. And we were able to share that, like Ollie [Woolf] and I, in our own little producer’s therapy session with the mentors, with Lars. That was really healing for me.”

“[Ari, Lars, and the mentors are] on, not a different level, but they’re all going through similar issues and this and that, whether it’s a low budget or a higher budget type of ordeal. Everyone’s going through the same thing in their own way, in a sense. Just to know the people that I’ve been looking up to for a very long time, the reason in large part why I got into making films, to know that they’re going through similar things and just keep going, and it’s fine. No matter what level we’re going to be at, there’s still something to navigate. So I thought it was very cool to see, over the course of five days, to hear these individual experiences and stuff and how you could relate it back to what we’re going through right now and where we are.

“It was information overload in the best way possible. At a certain point, I hope I’m retaining everything that was said over those five days because it was nonstop, all useful information. I wasn’t even taking notes at a certain point because I’m like, ‘I can’t write all this stuff down. I’m just going to try and soak it all in.'”

#3450. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

#3449. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

#3447. WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

Select WhatsApp users on TestFlight and in the main app are now seeing the option to expand an image in the app’s photo editor. Here are the details.

iPhone users with access to Apple Intelligence have a native AI-powered photo expansion tool called Extend, which lets users pinch or drag to expand an image beyond its original borders.

This feature, which is also present on AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and image-editing platforms like Photoshop, is now also making its way into WhatsApp.

According to WABetaInfo, the platform is rolling out a Meta AI-powered image expansion tool, though it is currently limited to select users, primarily those in WhatsApp’s beta program via TestFlight.

When users select a photo in their chats, WhatsApp opens the drawing editor. Here, they can choose to apply some AI effect to improve it. Among these, users can find a new option to expand their photos. Once users select this option, Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the expanded version. Once the process is complete, WhatsApp shows the expanded photo in the drawing editor, and users can choose to send it. Note that this feature is also compatible with status updates.

The site notes that if the user isn’t happy with the result, they can tap an undo button to revert to the original and then try using the tool again to generate a different result.

As is usually the case with beta features on WhatsApp, there is no telling when it might become widely available.

That said, given that it has also rolled out to users in the Android beta and some users on the public iOS version already have access, a broader rollout might not be too far off.

#3446. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3445. How Harry Potter’s New Snape Will Compare To Alan Rickman Addressed By HBO Star

New Harry Potter star Paapa Essiedu explains how his take on Severus Snape compares to Alan Rickman.

Except for Warwick Davis as Filius Flitwick, the cast of HBO's Harry Potter series is completely different from the eight movies that were released from 2001-2011. This has naturally led to comparisons between the previous and new actors playing the iconic fantasy characters created by J.K. Rowling, from Daniel Radcliffe and now Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter to Rickman and now Essiedu as Snape.

In an interview with Vanity Fair, Essiedu explains that he is not trying to erase the films or imitate the performance of Rickman, who he calls "an icon" and "a legend," but is instead focusing on fully fleshing out Snape amid all the character's contradictions and complexities. Essiedu feels that whether he has done the character justice cannot be fully assessed until the series is complete, and also expresses appreciation for the "goodwill" and those who were close to Rickman reaching out to him. Check out his comments below:

The guy is an icon. He’s a legend. Anyone who’s ever met Alan or spoken to him or been friends with him have all reached out to me and spoken about what Alan would’ve thought about my casting. There’s so much goodwill, and I really feel him with me. There are people who have got such a tight and deeply felt connection to something that they believe is theirs, and it feels like somebody is trying to take their thing and break their thing. I know that’s not what I’m trying to do. I’m not trying to break anybody’s nothing. After this, we’re not going to burn the books. We’re not going to remove the DVDs of the films. It’s not the end of that. That all still exists. I’m very clear-minded in my head about what I want to do and what I’m trying to achieve, and the potential of it. [H]opefully I get the opportunity to pull the contradictions and the unexpected masks of Severus so that eventually we get a human being that is fully fleshed [out] and living and breathing. That was my ambition, and is my ambition. And you can judge me sometime—in 2039 or whatever it is—as to whether it’s been successful or not.

While Essiedu is focused on his interpretation of the character, he also shared that he's read the books, but hasn't watched the movies, so he has not seen Rickman's performance for himself: "To be honest, I never watched the movies when I was younger. I still don’t think I really know what happens in Deathly Hallows because I read it so quickly that it didn’t really seep in."

Essiedu's mention of not being able to judge the success of his performance until 2039 is a reference to the show's ambitious plan, which is to make one season for each of the seven Harry Potter books. Given the scale of the high-budget HBO fantasy show, it will likely take over a decade to fulfill the plan of making seven seasons that adapt the full book series.

While season 1 took several years to make, season 2 is already in production, which is meant to avoid overly long hiatuses in the coming years, but it will still end up being a lengthy process.

With seven seasons, which as of now are eight episodes each, as opposed to eight movies, Essiedu is poised to end up having more scenes as Snape than Rickman ever did, including potential additions to the character's story that go beyond the source material and the films.

At the same time, his response emphasizes that the show is not overwriting the movies, which will continue to exist and be celebrated for their adaptation of the novels, and Alan Rickman's performance is an integral part of that legacy. Rickman passed away at the age of 69 in 2016.

#3444. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. #3443. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

Since it's actually two, opposite, single line command states;

Why can't it simply be an on/off button, in Settings?

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

To read Apple’s full support article, follow this link. And make sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the new MacBook Pro.

#3442. Prime Video’s Star Wars Replacement Is Hailed as the Best Space Show of All Time

Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other big events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

Space may be the final frontier, but you don't need to go to galaxies far, far away to find some good space adventures. In fact, the best one is set right here, in our very own Solar System. Over its six seasons, Prime Video's The Expanse has quietly built its reputation as the best space series on television, surpassing even mighty sci-fi franchises like Star Wars and Star Trek, and amassing quite a following among fans of the genre. Having debuted in 2015, it was even brought back from cancellation, proving how beloved it really is — fans just wouldn't let go. All that wouldn't have happened with just any series, of course, so what is it that makes The Expanse so special, even among titans?

Although it is set right here on our cosmic doorstep, The Expanse also takes place roughly some 200 years into the future. It's a time of war, with three main factions fracturing the Solar System: the United Nations of Earth and Luna, the Martian Congressional Republic, and the Outer Planets Alliance. The latter comprises all the planets and stations working in the asteroid belt, which have been part of Earth, but are now fighting for independence. Tensions are at an all-time high, and the tiniest mistake can lead to all-out war.

At the center of all that is an unlikely group of heroes and their aptly named gunship, the Rocinante. Led by James Holden (Steven Strait), they start out working hauling ice to the dwarf planet Ceres, but a distress call from a derelict ship in the middle of nowhere suddenly puts them in the middle of a conspiracy that threatens the whole system. With a sort of "found family" dynamics, the Rocinante crew is at first only looking to stay out of trouble, but, as it often happens in these stories, they quickly grow into heroes.

Meanwhile, on Ceres, the disappearance of a young woman has police investigator Joe Miller (Thomas Jane) rattling some cages that are dangerously close to making the planet the place where the war actually starts. With resources like air and water being rationed because of all the tension, everyone is on edge, and, unbeknownst to everyone, the thread Miller finds himself pulling ties all that together. As this soon-to-be-very-hot war gears up, there are still some people on all sides trying to work a way through it.

Star Wars and Star Trek have a much wider scope than The Expanse, granted, as they deal with a galactic scale, while the latter stretches as far as the asteroid belt, at first. Still, after a while, distances don't seem to matter as much when you have technologies like hyperdrives or warp drives. In The Expanse, however, there is no faster-than-light travel, so distances actually matter. This is one of the ways in which the Prime Video series uses space to its advantage, making it feel much more real than any other sci-fi galaxy.

Considering this, it's only natural that there would eventually be a divide between Earth and Mars, as well as a secessionist movement in the belt. It's precisely there that the most interesting effects of space life are felt. So far away from the two other planets, life in space turned Belters almost into an ethnicity of their own, with physical differences and their own language, Belter Creole. Because of that, they are usually seen as a lower caste by both Earth and Mars, hence the OPA's struggle for independence.

Who doesn't want to hear a Deep Purple cover in a sci-fi dialect?

To go with this rich worldbuilding (or spacebuilding?), The Expanse also pays a lot of attention to production design, particularly ships and space stations. Instead of flat rooms and hallways, ships are built more like skyscrapers, with decks serving different purposes. This allows for acceleration to create a gravitational pull that's small enough for the human body to feel comfortable with, and maneuvers like "flip and burn" turning, and the effect of G-forces on the crew also make The Expanse the most scientifically accurate space series around.

All that makes The Expanse one of the best sci-fi adaptations on TV. Its six seasons adapt only two-thirds of James S.A. Corey's book series, though, so, despite Prime Video having concluded the series with Season 6, we still can't say we've gotten the whole thing. But it could have been even shorter, because, in 2018, The Expanse was cancelled by Syfy after only three seasons for its poor ratings on TV and its complicated business and distribution model.

However, the audience wasn't ready to say goodbye, and they made their feelings known. The resulting #SaveTheExpanse campaign quickly became one of the most memorable fan movements in recent TV history, including crowdfunding efforts, targeting Amazon executives and even Jeff Bezos directly, and even getting an airplane to fly a banner over Amazon Studios. It also helped to have notorious celebrity sci-fi buffs like Wil Wheaton, George R.R. Martin, and Patton Oswalt join in.

This kind of loyalty and dedication isn't seen often, proving just how good The Expanse really is. Amazon picked it up for three more seasons in 2018, raising the bar with production value and consolidating the series as a sci-fi phenomenon. Few series have managed to pull off what The Expanse did in terms of worldbuilding and storytelling in this genre, and, right now, it doesn't look like any other will any time soon, either. Not even Star Wars or Star Trek.

The Expanse is available to stream on Prime Video.

#3441. Stacy Keach, ‘Fat City’ and ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Dead at 85

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life.” Related Stories How Nicholas Britell Packs Conflicting Emotions Into the ‘Jay Kelly’ Score Adam Sandler Looks Back on His Early Days in Hollywood at IndieWire Honors

She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

#3439. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3438. Apple confirms $7.5 billion bond sale following strong investor demand

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

#3437. Apple Is Already Getting The Mistborn Movie Casting Right After Brandon Sanderson's Update

The upcoming Mistborn movie has revealed its casting strategy, and it's the perfect choice for what could wind up being one of Apple TV's biggest franchises. With adaptations planned across movies, television, and even board games, Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere could become one of the biggest series ever seen on big and small screens alike.

All of this is set to begin with Mistborn, a huge feature film based on the popular 2006 novel Mistborn: The Final Empire. Crafted with a complex magic system, the novel depicts a deeply atmospheric dystopian world where a group of the oppressed must band together to resist the tyrannical leadership of the Lord Ruler.

The Mistborn franchise has the potential to be enormous. Three novels explore the original setting and characters, while a whole additional series of Mistborn books is set hundreds of years later. Brandon Sanderson continues to write novels in the series, with a new trilogy of Mistborn novels planned for release in the coming years.

While it is already too late for the most popular Mistborn casting to happen, it is still important that great performers take on the iconic roles of Vin and Kelsier in the upcoming film.

And while stars as big as Millie Bobby Brown and Henry Cavill have routinely been fancast for the lead roles, the film's strategy appears to be looking for different kinds of stars.

A new update from Brandon Sanderson recently revealed the casting strategy for the upcoming Mistborn movie, and it looks to be the right choice. In a mailbag video on the author's YouTube channel, Sanderson revealed that the plan for casting Vin and Elend in the upcoming film will be to "look for talented new actors."

This immediately disqualifies many of the most popular fancasting choices for the roles. Virtually every dark-haired young actress has been suggested for the part of Vin, from Dafne Keen to Jenna Ortega, while names like Louis Partridge have been suggested for Elend. However, this revealed strategy is a much stronger proposition.

In the first novel, Vin is a teenager, while Elend is in his early twenties. With that in mind, many of the proposed names are already too old for the roles, and even those who might be the right age now will likely have aged out of it by the time that filming begins.

With that considered, it makes much more sense to look for lesser-known faces.

Like roles such as Katniss in The Hunger Games, or Edward and Bella in Twilight, Mistborn's most important characters, Vin and Elend, have the potential to be career-defining parts. Securing actors who do not have too much baggage or awareness already attached to them makes sense, although the film will still need the anchor of at least one star.

In the same video, Sanderson revealed that "the only big name" cast in the film will be for the role of Kelsier. As the leader of the skaa rebellion, Kelsier works as an excellent entry point into the larger story for Vin, and using him in that same fashion, to draw general audiences to the Mistborn film, also makes sense.

Doing this with a strong and familiar performer is the right move. Fancasts for Kelsier have suggested a plethora of names, many of which could be a good fit for the role, including John David Washington and Charlie Hunnam.

While it is also necessary to recognize that Kelsier is 38 years old in the first novel, his exact age is not as important as Vin's. So long as Kelsier is old enough to serve as a mentor to Vin, it is possible that he could be cast younger or older than he appears in the novel.

Casting a big name as Kelsier also makes sense because the character's role in the sequel novels is significantly reduced. With this in mind, the part is not nearly as much of a franchise commitment as roles like Vin and Elend, who go on to become the faces of the Mistborn trilogy.

Getting the right star for Kelsier is an important move for the Mistborn movie. The film has the potential to be one of the biggest and best fantasy movies ever made, and casting the roles well will go a long way in securing a rich future for the Cosmere on the big screen.

The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3433. The 5 Strongest Opening Chapters in Stephen King Books

Few writers are as prolific, well-regarded, or popular as Stephen King. The iconic author is a certified legend of the horror, thriller, and supernatural genres, producing banger after banger with such consistency that fellow authors like George R. R. Martin have openly expressed their admiration for his speed. Indeed, King has written many of the most beloved and enduring classics of the last 50 years, covering a wide range of genres and introducing some of modern literature's most iconic characters. Not every King book is the same, though, and some stand out because of their strong opening chapters.

In the author's words, "there are books, and there are books," and most of the latter benefit from instantly impactful openers that not only capture the reader's attention but also set the stage for what's to come. Here, we list the five King books with the strongest opening chapters, the ones that immediately compel you to pay attention and keep the pages turning. They benefit from strong prose, confident worldbuilding, and a distinct sense of atmosphere that cements King as a master of his craft.

It might be King's best-known novel, and for good reason. The book follows the Losers' Club, a group of eleven-year-olds living in the town of Derry, Maine, where children mysteriously disappear. The Losers eventually discover the existence of the creature responsible, a mysterious being who commonly assumes the guise of Pennywise, the Dancing Clown, and uses fear as a weapon against them. 27 years later, the adult Losers reunite in Derry again to finish the job they couldn't as children.

The opening chapter is well-known by now. In it, Six-year-old Georgie Denbrough chases after his paper boat on a rainy afternoon, eventually reaching a sewer where Pennywise awaits him. Their seemingly sweet conversation quickly takes a turn, and Pennywise rips Georgie's arm before killing him. It's a brutal and profoundly creepy opening even before the gore. The opening line lets you know that the main evil won't be defeated for another 27 years, if ever, making the chapter feel all the more ominous. King is a master at crafting atmosphere, and here, he makes Georgie's last minutes feel like an entire odyssey.

Now on to something a lot grander. The Dark Tower is probably King's magnum opus, a sprawling saga that began in 1982 with The Gunslinger. The story focuses on Roland Deschain, the last gunslinger, and the years-long pursuit of his nemesis, the Man in Black. Here, King balances multiple genres, most notably Western, fantasy, thriller, and science fiction.

The opening line of this book is probably King's most celebrated: "The man in black fled across the desert, and the gunslinger followed." There's such a haunting quality to this line; it may seem simple at first glance, but it packs so much in just a few words, hinting at the backstory behind these two characters and painting a vague but instantly compelling picture of what's to follow. From there, King makes the desert feel alive in its scarcity, depicting a vague and endless land that threatens to overwhelm with its nothingness. Few chapters are as immersive or atmospheric as this one, and it's quite surprising how little of the larger plot it concerns itself with.

Desperation is among King's scariest yet most underappreciated efforts. The plot centers on a couple traveling the Nevada desert, who are kidnapped by Collie Entragian, the deputy of the remote mining town Desperation. Along with other victims, they realize that Collie has been possessed by a dark entity that controls the desert and wildlife. The entity must also change hosts, meaning they are all trapped in Desperation and subjected to becoming the being's next target.

Desperation's opening chapter is among the tensest, most discomforting things King has ever written. A masterclass in buildup and escalation, the chapter sees Entragian slowly take command of the situation, as the helpless couple slowly realizes, along with the reader, that the situation before them will be far darker than they could imagine. From there, Desperation tells a truly bleak and brutal story full of violence, gore, and supernatural danger. It's probably King's last truly horrific work, and it all begins with a remarkable opening chapter. An upcoming movie adaptation is in the works, which hopefully will live up to the source material's eeriness (the 2006 ABC version is pretty solid).

Now we move on to the book with possibly the best opening line in any King work: “The world had teeth, and it could bite you if you bothered it. Trisha McFarland discovered this when she was nine years old.” The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon is a survival story centered on Trisha McFarland, a 9-year-old who gets lost in the wilderness during a hiking trip with her mother and older brother. With only a Walkman to keep her company, Trisha hallucinates a version of baseball player Tom Gordon and becomes convinced a being she names The God of the Lost is after her.

The book wastes no time going into the thick of it. In the first chapter, Trisha escapes a complicated family dynamic by trailing off for a bathroom break. Strong character work sets the background for Trisha's story, but the main attraction is how King writes this girl's inner thoughts: it's intimate, childlike, but never dumbed-down. King has enough respect not only for his audience but, most importantly, for his creation. The most important relationship — that of Trisha and Tom Gordon — is also established here. Then, she's lost in the woods, and King's prose gets us as confused and disoriented as the girl herself.

Lastly, we finish with one of King's strongest late-career works. The book chronicles the aftermath of an attack in which the mysterious driver of a Mercedes S-Class drives into the crowd at a job fair in the Midwest, killing eight people and injuring fifteen. Months later, retired, suicidal cop Bill Hodges receives a taunting letter from the perpetrator, dubbing himself Mr. Mercedes, and decides to investigate the crime.

A classic hard-boiled detective novel, Mr. Mercedes is among King's best thriller efforts. As expected, the book opens with the attack, with King putting us in the eyes of Augie Odenkirk, a hopeful who rides the last bus to camp outside a job fair that opens in the morning. Augie is kind and sympathetic, quickly striking up a conversation with desperate single mother Janice Cray, who is there with her young daughter. In just a couple of paragraphs, King makes us care about these two characters before Mr. Mercedes arrives and runs over the crowd twice, killing Augie, Janice, and her daughter. It's a harrowing, unforgiving opening that sets the tone for the rest of the book.

#3431. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

If Ada Forte (Cynthia Nixon) makes good on her idea, The Gilded Age will beat Downton Abbey to the modern world by 28 years. The Gilded Age season 4, episode 2 ended with George Russell (Morgan Spector) confronting the man who shot him, Will Morris (Will Pullen). Russell spared Morris' life after a dramatic confrontation. Across East 61st Street, Agnes Van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is jumping through hoops from The Heritage Society as she prepares to host a dinner for President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan). Aunt Ada also has another plan to inject a symbol of modernity into the Van Rhijn and Forte house.

Her sister responds that someone eventually will. The matter was left there, but Ada is likely to follow through on her desire for a telephone. When she has it installed, The Gilded Age will beat Downton Abbey to owning a telephone by 28 years.

The Gilded Age returns for its fourth season with supreme confidence and a renewed focus on family drama and testing its huge cast of characters.

The Gilded Age season 4 is set in 1886, four years after the series began with Ada and Agnes' niece, Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson), arriving in New York as George and Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) move into their newly completed East 61st Street palace. Downton Abbey began with the sinking of the Titanic in April 1912, and season 1 ended in August 1914, when England entered World War I.

Downton Abbey's season 1 finale saw two telephones installed in 1914, one upstairs in the main house, and one downstairs in Mr. Carson's (Jim Carter) office. The telephone in Downton Abbey changed the life of Gwen (Rose Leslie), one of the maids. Thanks to Lady Sybil (Jessica Brown Findlay), Gwen was hired by Mr. Bromidge (Sean McKenzie) to work for the telephone company. This lifted Gwen out of service, and she eventually married and became Mrs. Harding.

A telephone in The Gilded Age's Van Rhijn home would truly one-up Downton Abbey, which takes place in the early 20th century. One of Downton's themes is how slowly and begrudgingly the Crawleys let go of Edwardian tradition and embrace the modern world. Meanwhile, Ada is remarkably progressive for a woman in 19th-century New York society, and it fits her character to embrace something as modern as a telephone.

The Gilded Age season 3 garnered record ratings on HBO, and it became the most-watched streaming show in the world with The Gilded Age season 4's premiere on November 1st. The Gilded Age has captured the hearts of audiences, many of whom originally sampled Julian Fellowes' HBO series because they were already Downton Abbey fanatics.

After four seasons, many servants in The Gilded Age remain underdeveloped.

While The Gilded Age has come into its own narratively and is as addictive as Downton Abbey was at its peak, the predecessor series is still superior at balancing its lords and ladies with the servants who toil for them. After four seasons, many servants in The Gilded Age remain underdeveloped, like butlers Church (Jack Gilpin) and Bannister (Simon Jones),

In Downton Abbey, the servants were equally important as the Crawley family, and their stories carried the same weight. Indeed, the Crawleys and their servants' lives were inextricable. This is much harder to achieve in The Gilded Age, with two households, the Van Rhijns and the Russells, having two sets of servants. There isn't enough screen time in an hour-long episode to service everyone.

As a tale set in America, The Gilded Age also feels more immediately relevant than Downton Abbey, despite its posh 19th century trappings. The haves and have-nots in The Gilded Age, with its greedy millionaire tycoons, feels like a mirror to today.

Aunt Ada installing a telephone is just one step closer to The Gilded Age embracing the 20th century, which Downton Abbey tried to avoid for as long as possible.

#3426. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3423. iOS 27.2 adds Apple Photos invisible watermark feature, here’s how it works

iOS 27.2 arrived last week, and among its changes for Apple Photos, the update adds an invisible watermarking feature when you use certain editing tools. Here’s how it works.

In the age of AI, what looks like a genuine photo might actually be a fake—or partly fake. That’s why tools like SynthID have been used to apply invisible watermarks to AI-generated content.

Starting with iOS 27.2, Apple now uses SynthID watermarks when you make AI-generated edits to photos in Apple Photos, or create all-new images with Image Playground.

Starting with iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2, some Apple Intelligence tools will add an invisible SynthID watermark to images that you create or edit:

Image Playground generates entirely new images, so it’s more what the average person would consider an “AI image.”

However, as Apple notes, the SynthID invisible watermark is also applied to genuine photos in your Apple Photos library if you use the AI-powered Clean Up, Extend, or Spatial Reframing tools to edit them.

It’s worth emphasizing the word “invisible” here. You won’t see evidence of a watermark anywhere on your photos, nor will others unless they explicitly check the image with a SynthID detector.

If you do want to check for the watermark, Apple recommends going to synthid.com, where you can upload an image and see its result.
