#3347. Aura Ink 10 review: A digital photo frame that looks (almost) like a real picture

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Aura Ink 10 is a second-generation ePaper photo frame that’s smaller and less expensive than the original, and can display a few more colors. If you’re looking for a digital photo frame you can hang on your wall without any wires showing, this is the one to get, though it is more expensive than most other frames, and overall it's less vibrant than a traditional digital photo frame.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

A year ago, Aura introduced the Aura Ink, the first ePaper photo frame; this device, while not as vibrant as a traditional digital photo frame, had the advantage of letting you hang it on a wall — no power cord required — for up to three months at a time without needing to be recharged.

The company is back with the Aura Ink 10, the first in the second generation of ePaper style photo frames. This frame can show more colors, and at $349, is also less expensive, albeit still well above some of the best digital photo frames. So, is the premium worth it?

The Aura Ink 10 went on sale on November 10, 2026, for $349 at Aura's website. It’s offered in just one size, and with just one matte color (black). The original only came with a white matte; I wish the company offered both options.

The frame itself is very thin, at a little less than an inch, and comes with both a stand for placing it on a table, as well as pins so you can mount it on a wall. Three buttons sit inconspicuously on the back edge of the frame, and let you switch photos and get the frame ready to go. Overall, it’s a very subtle design, and it’s unlikely that anyone would recognize it as a digital frame at a glance.

The Aura Ink 10 uses an E Ink Spectra 6 display, which can produce nine colors (black, white, red, yellow, blue, green, off-white, mustard yellow and orange), up from six on the original Aura Ink. That means it can show more nuances in pictures, though don’t expect true-to-life fidelity that you would get from a traditional LCD picture frame. The 10-inch frame also has the same resolution as the 13-inch model, which means greater pixel density.

To see the difference in Aura Ink generations, I placed the 10-inch Ink next to the 13-inch Ink, and then displayed the same photos on each.

The 10 inch model tended to show photos a little darker, but with better transitions between light and dark areas. For example, in an image of a girl jumping off a sand dune, there was less obvious pixelation from the sun-drenched stretches of the beach to shaded areas.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In another photo of a girl in front of a blue and white wall, the blues of the wall were a bit deeper, but shadows were more pronounced, making it more difficult to make out features in her face and neck area.

The Aura Ink 10 has very gentle lighting that only turns on if it senses someone in front of the frame. Again, it’s not something you’d notice unless you see it turn on, but it helps bring a little more vibrancy to the photo.

Aura says the Ink 10 will last up to three months on a charge, assuming it changes photos just once per day. Once it runs low, you simply have to plug it into a USB-C for a little bit.

Aura also updated the manner in which the frame refreshes; on the original model, the screen kind of flashes randomly as the photo changes. On the Ink 10, there’s a wave-like pattern that starts in one corner, and ripples across the screen. It’s more intentional, and doesn’t make it look like the frame is shorting out.

One thing that Aura does well is make it easy to add photos to its devices. For starters, you can sync your iCloud or Google Photos albums in the Aura app. And, to help narrow things down, the Aura app can filter photos by person, so that you can more easily find photos of particular individuals; unfortunately, there’s no pet filter. If you want to skip the app entirely, you can also either email or text photos to the display. Handy!

As someone who tests smart home devices for a living, I suspect my house, which has smart displays everywhere, is a bit different than most. So while I appreciate traditional digital photo frames — the Alexa Photo Frame is one of my favorites, for its innovative use of AI — it’s nice to have some tech that doesn’t look like tech.

Yes, there are some tradeoffs to an ePaper photo display like the Aura Ink 10. You’re not going to get colors that really fly off the screen, and you’re going to pay a premium over other photo frames. But, in a digital-everything world, I appreciate its subtleness.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales on tools to wind down by December 2, 2026.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

#3344. macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

In its blog post, Apple announced that apps will require “very explicit user action” to have Full Disk Access on your Mac. At the time of the announcement, Apple didn’t make it super clear what that would actually mean. Now, we have an idea of what’s to come.

Code sifter pdfu posted on X that Apple will be getting rid of a clever loophole that developers could use to make it easier for users to enable Full Disk Access. In current versions of macOS, if an app requests a file that would require Full Disk Access, the system denies the request and logs the app as an option in the Settings app for enabling Full Disk Access.

At that point, developers often prompt users to open that section of the Settings app and flip the toggle.

Starting as soon as macOS 27.3, apps that request files outside of the permission scope will no longer get logged, and as a result, won’t show up as an option for quickly toggling Full Disk Access, per leaker pdfu.

macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb

At the moment, developers can still request users to drag an app icon to the Settings panel to enable Full Disk Access, even once the feature flag for the aforementioned change is enabled. To me, it still doesn’t quite feel like you’ll need “very explicit user action” to enable Full Disk Access, but it’s possible this will change in the future. This is all still in development.

All in all, I’m not fully convinced that this solves the core problem. Developers are requesting Full Disk Access because they’d like to tap into things like iMessage, and there hasn’t been a better way of doing so. As long as that demand is there, users will likely still have to enable Full Disk Access and risk all sorts of other data, just so they can share their texts with an agent.

Granted, pdfu also mentions the idea of Private Folders, which could potentially allow users to grant scoped access to just the iMessage database folder. It’s unclear if that’ll be possible since there’s little detail on how Private Folders will work. If that’s the case, then hopefully Full Disk Access can stop being the default permission you have to provide for any personal data.

#3343. The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For

Editor’s note: This article contains major spoilers for the documentary “You Can See Everything.”

This is a joke offered by one of three people on a Zoom with Rolling Stone one October afternoon. Because like virtually everybody who’s been to the movies in the past month, and even many who haven’t, the subject these three are most keen to chat about is the brain-boggling, meme-launching, WTF-did-I-just-watch documentary You Can See Everything.

If you haven’t seen it yet, you undoubtedly know the elevator pitch: Nathan Fielder embeds himself in the home of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, right before Holmes reports to prison. You also know the major conversation-starter moments: The shower scene. The egg-whipping. The abundant close-ups of unblinking stares.

The one thing that makes this virtual coffee klatch a little different is that the folks ready to discuss the ins and outs of this cultural phenomenon include Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim. And if you’re among the many, many folks who’ve helped turn this gonzo experiment in nonfiction filmmaking into a blockbuster, you can likely guess who the third person in the chat might be. Hint: It’s not Holmes.

Rather, it’s the woman who’s played her not once, but now twice — Amanda Seyfried, the Dropout star whose presence in the documentary’s second half has been one of the best-kept moviegoing secrets in recent memory, and the aspect that sends it into a whole new stratosphere of mind-fuckery.

Seyfried joined her co-conspirators for an exclusive conversation — her first time on the record about the film, and the first time the three collaborators have discussed it since the premiere — to talk about how she was drawn into the project, that awkward on-camera phone call with Holmes, and how they’ve all been processing the experience. Making and releasing the film has been an emotional roller coaster for each of them (Oppenheim says it “made my brain and body feel on fire”), but Seyfried, for one, has enjoyed the ride.

“I have no regrets,” she says. “I’m having the time of my life right now!” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.Oppenheim: Well, where should we start?

Seyfried: My first question is: What am I doing here? What am I doing in this movie? How did I get here?

Fielder: That’s a great question, Amanda. How did you get here?

Oppenheim: I feel like there was a certain point in the process of making this where we wanted to expand the bubble [of people involved in the project]. But so many of the people we reached out to didn’t want to be on camera because Elizabeth had this toxic reputation.Fielder: This was two years after we had shot in that beach house with them. We were just like, “Where do we go next?” The Dropout kept coming up. Elizabeth’s parents really had very strong feelings about it, and they felt it was one of the main ways the general public knew about who Elizabeth Holmes was. So we thought it would be interesting to talk to you.

I got your phone number through Emma Stone. We had a 30-minute Zoom, and you were like, “Yeah, come over with cameras.” We wanted to show you what became the first half of the film, and then we would talk about it. That’s all you agreed to. Related Content ‘SNL’: Druski Impersonates ‘Crazy’ Elizabeth Holmes in Meta-Documentary Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ Haven't Seen Enough? The Books and Shows to Read and Watch After 'You Can See Everything' Watch Amanda Seyfried’s Joni Mitchell Cover Get Interrupted by Ghostface

The crazy thing to me [was that] you didn’t go through any talent reps or anyone. You just said, “Yeah, come over!” Why did you trust us like that?

Seyfried: I remember when [Emma] texted, and I was like, “Nathan Fielder? Ooh, I wonder if he wants to make something with me?”

My sister is a big fan [of yours, Nathan], and I know a lot of people are big fans of Nathan for You. I’d only seen The Curse. When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, “Oh, he just wants some advice. He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed.” After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed. It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening.

“It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings.”

Seyfried: I wasn’t nervous. There were just way more people than I expected coming into my apartment [laughs]. I had just gotten back from the Venice Film Festival, and I said this is the only time I can do it; I’m just never in the city. I didn’t know how long it was going to take. I thought, “Wait a minute, there’s cameras. I should probably put on some mascara …” There was no protection. There was no advocate for me. I just felt like I was totally game because I was so invested in what you were doing, and already had this strange level of trust in you guys.

Fielder: It’s not dissimilar to Elizabeth, I guess, who also just had a strange level of trust.

Seyfried: Not dissimilar … but not super similar, I would say.

Seyfried: I would say there was a lot of risk in the back of my head, and then when I told my agent and lawyer that I had already done it? Not the normal process [laughs]. But I go off and do my own thing sometimes, and nobody had any say or control over what I was doing with Nathan and Lance. My lawyer was like, “Well, now we have to retroactively set your deal in place because you need protection.” We weren’t even considering reenactments at that point.

Fielder: We should clarify that because, yeah, all you’d agreed to was just coming in, and we’d show you the stuff and talk.

Seyfried: I wasn’t even a subject at that point.Oppenheim: I think you said that you’d never play this person again. When we started showing you that stuff — there was a moment in the conversation where you started imitating her on camera, and you gave Nathan this look. What brought you back into that?Seyfried: Muscle memory. I think the reason I was able to capture my version of Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout was not her Nightline interview, or 60 Minutes, or whatever footage I’d seen. It was the 10 hours of deposition tapes, where she was present and completely consistent. That’s the thing that my brain is locked into. So even though it had been a bunch of years, I see her again in the footage … and I can’t help but tilt my head a little bit. It’s muscle memory when you play a character as intensely as I did for as long as I did. I do think there’s something almost uncontrollable. When I was talking to you, it was already coming out of me in some way.

“It wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies.”

Fielder: You started doing it, but you never actually said you would play her again. It’s so interesting, because the process of making this was to try to give as much information as we could to the audience on how we interpreted these moments that were happening in the house and with her. Anything that didn’t happen on camera, we took notes of. But we were talking about the oddness of these early meetings, and we always assumed that, well, obviously these things can’t be part of the film. But then we were sort of like, “Wait, would the idea of doing a re-creation work?” At first we didn’t even consider it because we thought it was a little lame, maybe, to do these types of things. But the way you engaged with it when we shot at your apartment, it felt to us like there was something in you. It was like you wanted to revisit it.

Oppenheim: It felt like you had unfinished business — like it was pouring out of you. You were unresolved or something.

Fielder: Did you have something unresolved?

Seyfried: Don’t we all? [Laughs.] I mean, now that people have seen the movie, isn’t everybody kind of feeling that? That’s the thing about how powerful this whole project is, the nuance of it and its capacity to be all things. You can’t resolve any of it. You can learn about how you feel and you can learn about your perspective on things, but …

It’s not that I was unresolved; it’s that I had more information now because of [your] footage. Anybody who’s watched this documentary knows that the first 90 [minutes] or so, there’s a lot of information there. So the idea that I could go on this journey with you guys, however you needed me, in whatever capacity, was very interesting to me.

Fielder: We started having conversations about: “OK, would you portray her again?” All I said was that we’d want you to re-create some initial conversations that happened off-camera. But then we also said, because this is a documentary, we didn’t want to discuss these scenes or show you scripts in advance. We just want you to show up, and we’ll talk about the scenes on camera. Anything that comes up in those conversations will potentially be part of it. People should know that you had no creative control over this project. Anything that was filmed—

Fielder: You had no approval over anything. You were just engaging with these scenes for the first time. Were you nervous at any point during this?

Seyfried: Yes! I mean, there was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything was scary, but I still had that drive that was more in the front seat — which was the literal front seat with you in the car. I was just like, “Let’s go, buddy! I want to put my hand in the fire!”

Fielder: We just had planned to do those first few re-creations, the meeting and the one at the house. Nothing beyond that. And then you were getting drawn in, and it seemed like you had to go to Billy. You’re now in this process, and it’s not like we can drive this thing forward because so much is based on your comfort level. What made you want to keep going beyond those re-creations?

Seyfried: I don’t know. I don’t know. It’s the same as whatever was driving you guys this whole time.Fielder: Why did you want to meet Billy?

Seyfried: I just … [pauses]. It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me. I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.

You wanted that, too, but it had to come from me because I don’t think you would have put me in that position. I did feel protected by you guys pretty early on. I felt like I trusted you. Even though I kept jokingly saying, “You’re not going to ruin my life, right?”

Fielder: And what was my answer? I forget.

Seyfried: “I’m not trying to. But maybe.” [Laughs.] Just kidding.

Fielder: That sounds like what I would say, actually.

Oppenheim: It was such a gigantic leap of faith. I don’t know if you know how amazing and also how insane it was that you were willing to put yourself out there in this way.

Seyfried: But I want people to know that it wasn’t like I jumped into the deep end. It was a process. “What are you doing on this date?” “I don’t know. I’m busy on this date, but I’m around on this date?” “OK, let’s meet here.” So it was just a step-by-step process. It wasn’t like a script, and we were going to shoot it. I wasn’t committing to shooting a movie. I was committing to each event or moment, and those are little leaps of faith that ended up feeling bigger.

Oppenheim: If you’re saying you’re a “Billy detective,” what did you feel after you met him? Did your feelings change at all?

Seyfried: Nothing changed. It only got worse. That’s very clear in the doc, I think.

Fielder: Did you feel like, “Oh, he’s different?” Or were you like, “He’s the same guy I saw in that footage?”

Seyfried: I had to put on a different hat [when I met him]. I was filtered. I wouldn’t necessarily call it acting, but … I was thinking about how I wanted to protect myself, but I also wanted to give the guy a chance to be as he is. I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children — with their children. I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of shit about him up until that point.

Because look, I do not like him. But I’m coming into this man’s house. I just wanted to be a presence, the way that you guys are so good at being present in these situations. But you also knew him. The whole crew knew him, and he knew them. Billy doesn’t know me at all. He just assumes many things about me, which is normal.

So I’m just trying to engage with him, and it’s fine. It’s going fine. And then [Elizabeth] calls, and that was just … what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least. Everything I’m feeling, you can see. I don’t even have to describe it to you.

“The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy.”

Fielder: I want people to know that everything that’s outside of the scripted reenactments, like that phone call, that’s all coming from you — we’re not saying, “Well, you have to say this or that” in any of these things. This is all just happening in real time.

Seyfried: We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. And I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls, and … Someone asked me if that was real, if that was really her on the phone. And I’m like, “It’s a documentary. Who else would it be?”

Oppenheim: Every time I watch the movie, it feels like your performance in the reenactments evolves, from that first one to the final one.

Seyfried: From insecurity to … um, security. [Laughs.]

Oppenheim: Did anything change over the course of it? Was it something in the way you prepared, or did experiencing all the stuff you did with us impact anything?

Seyfried: I think it had to do with intensity. I mean, that last scene in the prison is all from Nathan’s memory. [To Nathan] You did an amazing job trying to remember everything.

Fielder: The second I got out [of the visiting room], I recorded everything I could remember into my phone.

Seyfried: You did your due diligence with that. I think the stakes were so high at that point for all of us because it had just happened. The reenactments I was doing from the beginning … [they] were things that had happened when you were with them years prior. I was still insecure about it, and I was like, “I don’t know if I can still do the voice.” Also, the audience will have just seen her for 90 minutes — how are they gonna just suspend disbelief? It was very much like, “How am I going to do this? I don’t know if I can capture her anymore.”And then by the end, I had been doing it enough, and I really had a good time in the pizza house doing the A24 meeting [where we show Billy negotiating for movie profits]. I really got my stride, and then the stakes were so high because you had literally just gone to the prison. For most of the filming, we were like, “When are you gonna go? When can you go?”

Fielder: We were really focused on trying to get cameras in there because it was really frustrating to have these things that kept happening off-camera that were so relevant to our understanding. We were hopeful for a time that we could get cameras in there, but … I mean, you see it a little bit in the movie where I wasn’t excited about doing a re-creation of that final visit. Also, there was a rumor online that I had visited her before. That is bad information. I had never visited her in prison before that one [time] in the film. So, just to clarify that.

Anyway, I was nervous about re-creating that because the earlier re-creations were more about describing what happened in the house and in those early meetings. This one was: I’m asking her questions, and the way she responds and the expression on her face is what would be telling [the audience] about it. I was really skeptical that those things could be captured in a re-creation without it feeling goofy, or just, like, so detached from reality. It was the best we could do given all the constraints on access to her.

But then — and I don’t know if I ever told you this, Amanda — but it wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies. Because when anything was slightly off in what you were doing, we would talk about it. It was really like, “This is not how it was.”Seyfried: You were so specific.

Fielder: But when you got it, it was like, “Wow. This is it. This is what I experienced.” I never thought that would be possible in a re-creation. Really, it’s a testament to your performance. You came in with choices that you were making as a performer, which is great. But sometimes it would be off from what I had witnessed, and so we’d adjust until we got it right, and then it was incredible when you hit it. Even the way you responded to the questions when it was, like, almost nonanswers and certain things, it’s exactly how she answered.

Seyfried: Do you remember when we were in the barn and you were telling me I was doing it wrong? I remember that at one point I’m like, “How was it done, Nathan??”

Oppenheim: There’s an amazing expression on your face where it’s like, “Come on, man, which way is it?”

The performance you’re doing here — even though you’ve done the character before, it feels different than anything else you’ve ever done. I remember being behind the monitor for the final reenactment, and I did feel like I was seeing her. It was startling.

Seyfried: How did you edit together, like, 700 hours of footage? There could have been 1,000 versions of this movie.

“I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls!”

Oppenheim: This happened when we were shooting, but especially when we were in the edit room with Adam Locke-Norton — who’s edited a lot of Nathan’s stuff — we would gravitate toward the moments that we most disagreed on.

Fielder: “Disagreed on” in terms of what we were witnessing.Oppenheim: Right, the moments that provided the most cognitive dissonance. Our experience watching them would be so different from one another’s, and that felt like a powder keg or something.

Fielder: People are not, you know, normally this difficult for us to make sense of.Seyfried: Well, normally people answer a question. She doesn’t answer questions.

Oppenheim: She’s like a human optical illusion or something.Seyfried: A David Blaine trick.Oppenheim: [Laughs.] Yeah! A couple weeks ago, I asked Adam, “Do you feel that if someone saw all 700 hours, they would come away with a different conclusion — or different conclusions — than just watching the three-hour film?” And he said, “Actually, I don’t think so.” I just thought that was so telling that it’s like, wow, it’s not always the more you know about someone, the more you see someone. There had already been so much [coverage of] her case. The documentary, the book, the podcast …

Oppenheim: We wanted to do something that was forward-looking and not just regurgitating stuff that was already in the public record or had been extensively reported on.

Fielder: So, Amanda, when you arrived on the re-creation sets, it seemed like you were curious about what objects were in the real locations versus choices our set decorators or production design team made. Why was that something that interested you?

Seyfried: I think I was just grasping at anything that could ground me back into this world because it had been so long, and I think I was also experiencing some kind of weird, like, meta-vortex because I had just seen Elizabeth Holmes in this house, and the house is so specific …

Oppenheim: Like you’d somehow walked into the documentary.Seyfried: Yes! That’s it! It’s like if they still had the set of Family Matters up, and I walked onto the set. You become a part of what you’ve experienced in a way that you don’t get to do very often. Nobody had been [in Holmes and Evans’ beach house] for two years or whatever. And suddenly it’s like I’ve time-traveled two years into the past.

Fielder: It felt like you were stepping into our memories, in a way, and we wanted to capture that feeling of memory in the edit. Like [the audience was] transitioning from the first half [of the film] into these re-creations.

Seyfried: The way you shot it, who’s in it, the questions you asked, the way you lived inside this process — people cannot stop talking about it for a reason. So it was that much more intense for me when I walked in, because it was like she had just been there. The first moment — well, besides Billy in the shower — the first moment that stuck out to me when I was watching the footage in my apartment was him grabbing the eggs. You were like, “Feel free to stop whenever you want to ask me a question.” And when the egg moment happened, I immediately hit the space bar [to stop the video], and I was like, “What the fuck?” And you were like—Fielder: “Yeah! I know!”Seyfried: So, like, these moments, like, this experience that I had watching it — I’m now in that same space. It’s just crazy. It’s great for an actor. But it’s just weird for me.

Oppenheim: The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy.

Seyfried: Same!Oppenheim: What was going on in your head?

Seyfried: I was honestly trying to connect with him. We were all sitting there eating really good Chinese food, and, obviously, there were questions we wanted to ask. But for me, since I’m not an interviewer or an investigator, I’m not so good at asking questions and getting the timing right. And Nathan, you had a rapport with him. I was still creating this rapport. Plus, I’m in this man’s house with his kids. Did I say that earlier?

Oppenheim: You did. But I’m curious. Like when the conversation started to turn … I’m just behind the camera thinking, “What is going on?”

Seyfried: There was no reason for him to get that aggressive. [Pauses.] That’s the word I’m going to use, as it’s more diplomatic. If my jaw wasn’t obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged. I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, “Oh, I don’t think so, buddy.” I was in the frame of mind where I’m like, “OK, this guy is disrespectful, and I’m here in his home, I’m gonna argue this because I actually have a pretty solid stance on things. I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s “building monuments of love” to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her. And not only am I protective of myself, I’m just trying to set the record straight in a way where I’m trying to defend myself, too, while maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn’t kick us out, you know?

Oppenheim: I don’t have any memory of you saying, like, “Can we cut that out?” or anything like that.

Seyfried: I’m a people pleaser [laughs]. I think a lot of my friends who knew that I was doing this secret project were like, “Are you sure you’re OK? Are you sure you want to keep doing this?” And I was like, “Yeah, it feels like sure … maybe … I don’t know?” There was never a point at which I was just going to be like, “You know what? Let’s not do this.” I did get close to being like, “No reenactments. That just seems weird. That just seems like going back to the well, and it might be dry.” But the truth is, we all kept this idea alive.

I joined you both way later on. But I also feel like each of us has brought something very specific to this project. And when you needed me, I came because of how invested you were, and how I felt like we were all on the same page at a point. We were like a band. We were like a team. It felt like part of the team. And when I felt part of the team, it made me want to go even further. It’s not necessarily about being safe, but about doing something different. And it’s not just about doing something different, but doing something that confuses you and excites you and terrifies you. That’s the shit that we have to remind each other to commit to in order to create something so wild.

Oppenheim: Every time I watch it, I feel so overwhelmed by it all. I not only feel like I’ve been taken back in time to the place where it all happened, but I feel overwhelmed by some moment that I find really funny, or some moments I find extremely sad. To me, it was important to have that range. The more we could express the emotional experience we had with them in making the film, the more I thought the film would be successful at communicating something honest.

Fielder: Amanda, would you ever do something like this again, or do you regret it?

Seyfried: What are you talking about? I don’t regret it at all. I’m having the time of my life right now! I mean, I’m not going to do this again. But neither are you!

Soundbars are expensive. That's just the fact of the matter. You can easily drop a grand on the best soundbar system, and I've even tested $3,000+ models. Unfortunately, cheap soundbars can sound flat, narrow, or tinny, and I've only ever recommended a few sub-$400 models.

However, Samsung has changed the game with this deal. The Samsung Q900F is currently just $697 at Best Buy, down from $,1497 — a huge saving of $800. The Q900F is a 2025 model, but its sound is still excellent. It has a 7.1.2 channel setup, which means there are seven speakers in the central soundbar, a separate subwoofer, and two up-firing speakers for genuine Dolby Atmos immersion. This soundbar is also compatible with the lesser-spotted DTS: X, another surround sound technology found on some DVDs and Blu-rays.

At 53% off, I presume Best Buy is trying to shift leftover Samsung stock to make room for 2026's new releases (the QS90H and the Q990H, both of which I've tested and adored), so I don't see this sticking around for long. I'd grab it before it's too late.

The Samsung Q900F is a 2025 pre-flagship model. Samsung's "Q" line refers to its premium devices and includes the flagship Q990F and the pre-flagship Q900F (this model). The Q900F has a wireless subwoofer and built-in up-firing speakers for a 7.1.2 channel configuration. In short: genuine Dolby Atmos for room-filling, movie-theater sound.

As a soundbar + subwoofer combination, the Samsung Q900F requires a decent amount of space in your living room. It's 49 inches long, so I'd recommend a TV at least 55 inches or bigger — otherwise the soundbar will dwarf your TV, and it'll look strange.

The subwoofer itself will either need to go behind or next to your sofa — you can move it around to find the optimal placement. I have my Denon subwoofer next to the sofa, but it sometimes loses connection, forcing me to shuffle it around. I've never experienced a subwoofer disconnecting like that on a Samsung soundbar, but it's still worth noting.

The Q900F has 4K pass-through at 120Hz, which makes it ideal for gamers if your TV only has one HDMI 2.1 port. This means you can plug your console into the soundbar for 4K playback with no juddering or stuttering. Other flagships, like the JBL Bar 1300X MK2, still lack this.

Now onto the most important thing: sound quality. How does the Q900F actually sound? While I haven't personally tested it, I've tested 10 Samsung soundbars, namely the 2026 flagship Q990H, Q600F, Q600H, QS750F, QS90H... the list goes on. And what do they all have in common?

They sound excellent. Samsung soundbars all sound incredible. Dialogue is clear, especially thanks to the dialogue mode (which this model has), and bass is always confident and controlled thanks to the industry-leading subwoofer. Some features, like SpaceFit Sound Pro on pre-2026 models, are restricted to post-2021 Samsung TVs; again, not a dealbreaker but worth noting.

#3339. Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds

Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent.

Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously …

Rossmann is a repair technician who specializes in component-level logic board repairs and data recovery. He later became a key figure in advocating for right-to-repair legislation, which Apple initially opposed and later backed.

In a recent video, he claimed that some Apple store staff were signing up customers to trials of paid services subscriptions without their informed consent. Targets set by Apple are said to have encouraged the practice.

Customers accepting the offer of a personalized shopping experience could be shown the free trials of Apple services available to them based on their recent purchases. For example, buying an iPhone currently entitles you to a free three-month subscription to Apple TV. However, these trials automatically start debiting your payment method if you don’t cancel them before they end.

Staff were instructed to show these offers to customers and were allegedly set a 40% sign-up target, which Apple tracked as a performance metric. Crucially, the offers are shown on the employee’s device rather than on the customer’s phone. A store member told Rossman that some staff were hitting the Accept button without properly obtaining consent from customers in order to hit their target.

When I asked whether they’d seen a specialist press Agree with their own eyes, they answered “Yes, I saw some specialists press on behalf of the customer. So, they are hitting agree. They are signing the customer up to something without actually having the customer click okay, hit okay, or provide express consent.”

The store member also claimed that staff were describing the offer as a gift, which further disguised the fact that it would turn into a paid recurring subscription unless canceled.

At the time of writing, Apple has not responded directly to the accusations, but in a follow-up video yesterday Rossman cites a staff member describing the company’s response.

He says a memo was read out in the morning meeting stating that only customers could press the Accept button, and internal systems indicate Apple is no longer grading staff on the signup metric.

We have reached out to Apple for comment and will update with any response.

#3337. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3336. Comedian Lucy Beaumont Fears Being Blacklisted By TV Industry After Blowing Whistle On David Walliams

Comedian Lucy Beaumont has said she has risked her television career by speaking out about David Walliams because the industry doesn’t tolerate troublemakers.

In an interview with Sky News (watch below), the Taskmaster star and Hullraisers writer revealed that she was one of the “whistleblowers” on Walliams, who has been accused of using his fame and power to prey on teenage girls. Walliams, known for Little Britain and Doctor Who, strongly denies wrongdoing.

Beaumont told The Cathy Newman Show that a young person working on a TV show approached her with concerns that Walliams allegedly hosted teenagers in his dressing room. Beaumont said she contacted one of the young girls. Related Stories News David Walliams Being Cut From New Movie 'Fing!' Following Allegations; Comcast-Owned Sky Exits UK Distribution Of Film News 'Britain's Got Talent' Producer Urges "Anyone Who Feels They Have Been Subject Of Wrongdoing" To Come Forward Following David Walliams Allegations

“She was in a really bad way,” Beaumont said. “I was really worried she was going to take her own life because of it. She had put stuff online, and there was evidence that she was in a dressing room. I offered to pay legal fees to try and get her some protection — and I’m not saying necessarily that what she said was true — but I wanted to help her because it was a world that she was really out of her depth with.” Watch on Deadline

Beaumont continued: “I believe she had signed an NDA [non-disclosure agreement] to say — and this is the issue with some of these NDAs — the NDA wasn’t just about she couldn’t talk to the media. She added: “There’s no proper duty of care. There’s no social services that you deal with, and it’s partly because the industry is very well-managed.”

Turning to her decision to speak out, Beaumont said she doesn’t think she will work in television again because people “lose work” for challenging high-profile individuals and are painted as a “trouble causer.” She added that people are “very replaceable” in the business and there are “lots of other people who can do your job.” Beaumont joked that she would become a Pilates teacher.

ITV News and The Guardian published their investigation into Walliams on Tuesday, detailing how he allegedly used his position on shows like Little Britain and Britain’s Got Talent to meet teenagers and pursue sexual contact with them. “I am not a sexual predator… I have not broken the law,” Walliams told ITV News. “I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

He continued: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with… I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

#3335. Teens and parents can expect Instagram notifications about AI age estimation

Meta says it’s expanding its AI age estimation globally to automatically extend Instagram account protections to millions more teenagers. It says parents in the US can also expect to receive notifications later this month …

Instagram has a number of protections for the accounts of teenagers, but it’s very common for teens to lie about their age in order to circumvent them. Back in May, the company said it would be using AI-powered age estimation to address the problem.

The company said it would use the tool to block users aged below 13, and to ensure that those in the 13 to 17 range had limited accounts. Teen accounts have age-appropriate feeds, limitations on who can interact with them, and default time management tools – though things didn’t get off to the best of starts when a 12-year-old kid fooled it by using an eyebrow pencil to draw a fake moustache.

Meta today says that it is rolling out the (hopefully now eyebrow pencil-proof) tech globally.

We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.

The company goes on to say that parents in the US will receive a notification sometime this month, with a link to a video and an article about the system.

This month, parents in the United States will begin to see an in-feed video on Instagram explaining our approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article, written by Larry Magid, internet safety advocate and President and CEO of ConnectSafely, detailing our multi-layered age assurance approach, which includes keeping children under 13 off our platforms, providing age appropriate experiences for teens, and informing parents about ways they can partner with us to ensure their teens provide the correct age online.

If you don’t want to wait, you can read the article here.

Meta says the same protections will be rolled out to Threads and Facebook, although I would have thought being on Facebook in the first place is proof that it’s been a while since you were a teenager …

#3333. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3332. Jonathan Ross Explains Backstory Behind “Tasteless” David Walliams Joke

British TV presenter Jonathan Ross has landed himself in some hot water over the past week for his past association with both David Walliams and Russell Brand.

The Guardian and ITV News’ report into allegations against Walliams including from teenagers referenced a joke Ross made at the 2004 British Comedy Awards. “The comedy awards is 15 years old – 15 years old! And like most 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams,” Ross joked at the time.

Ross addressed the joke and the broader allegations this morning, saying in a statement he is “as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation.” Related Stories News Comedian Lucy Beaumont Fears Being Blacklisted By TV Industry After Blowing Whistle On David Walliams News David Walliams Being Cut From New Movie 'Fing!' Following Allegations; Comcast-Owned Sky Exits UK Distribution Of Film

Ross said the “tasteless joke that I would not dream of making today about anyone” was submitted to him by the Comedy Awards writing team at the time. Watch on Deadline

“I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect,” said Ross. “Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him. I also like to think that I would have acted upon that knowledge.”

Ross’ association with Walliams and Brand has been scrutinized in recent days.

Along with the Comedy Awards joke, The Guardian published an image of Ross with Walliams at a charity quiz. In the photo, Ross is sat at a table while Walliams has his arm around an 18-year-old who accused Walliams of “pleading with me to share a bed with him” and “putting his head in my lap and making me stroke his head.” There is no suggestion that Ross was aware of any of the behavior Walliams has been accused of.

Ross’ past association with Brand, who was jailed earlier this week for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault, has also come up in recent days. The pair created scandal in 2008 for prank calling Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs and making lewd comments about his granddaughter, who had previously been in a relationship with Brand.

After trying to have the articles blocked via the courts, the Walliams allegations dominated the news agenda yesterday and have called into question a culture that previously allowed men like Walliams and Brand to flourish. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said “the allegations are the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power in an industry where we have known for so long that the power imbalances are huge.”

Walliams has been dropped by his agent and his shows including Little Britain have been removed from BBC iPlayer. He is accused of using his celebrity to prey on women as young as 15, making contact with them through work, including on Britain’s Got Talent, to pursue them for sexual purposes.

Deadline has contacted Walliams’ legal representatives for comment. In a statement to ITV News, Walliams denied all allegations against him. When trying to prevent publication of the articles, Walliams’ lawyers revealed that he had made two attempts to take his life because of the allegations.

“I am not a sexual predator… I have not broken the law,” Walliams said. “I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”

He continued: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with… I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”

#3331. Apple pushing faster on agentic Siri would carry three big risks

Yesterday saw two reports about Apple software development. The first said that the company was aiming to give Siri more agentic capabilities “as soon as next year,” while the second said that CEO John Ternus is pushing Craig Federighi to speed up software development.

If accurate, it seems near-certain the two reports are connected. But if Ternus really is pushing for an acceleration in Siri’s ability to act as an AI agent, that comes with three potentially huge risks …

Both reports were by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, though he didn’t directly connect them. On the Siri side, his newsletter contrasted the agentic abilities of some competitor models, suggesting that Apple ultimately wants to achieve the same things.

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year.

The report about Ternus pushing Federighi for faster software development mentions “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” of which agentic capabilities would be the obvious candidate.

But agentic capabilities are among the most dangerous forms of AI given the multitude of things that could go very, very wrong.

The most obvious is simply failing to carry out the task. Depending on the importance of it, the consequences could range from annoyance through to significant harm.

Technology has long failed to live up to one of its biggest promises: relieving us of mundane work in order to devote our time to more fulfilling things. For example, obtaining tickets to a popular gig or other event, which currently involves scheduling time in order to repeatedly refresh a page, perhaps wait through a queuing system, and finally carry out the transaction. It would be great to be able to hand this off to an AI.

But even on something relatively unimportant like this, if we delegated the task and the AI failed to obtain the tickets, especially if this was due to a silly error, this could prove enormously frustrating. If the task were more important, the results could obviously be far worse.

Potentially even worse is achieving the task but doing so in inappropriate ways. We’ve already seen high-profile examples of this, like the Hugging Face hack caused by an AI model seeking so hard to carry out instructions that it used underhand methods to bypass crucial safeguards in the process.

Over two thousand real secrets, including passwords, API tokens, SSH root logins, and even admin-level cloud keys, were found leaking on GitHub after developers clicked “Yes, and don’t ask again” in Claude Code […] When a developer grants Claude Code permission to proceed with “Yes, and don’t ask again,” it saves the exact command, including secrets, to a file, .claude/settings.local.json, inside the project folder. This file should never be exposed publicly [but] Apiiro, an application security company, found 104,185 public copies of such files on GitHub across 103,617 repositories.

This was just a few days after Anthropic started encouraging Claude users to connect their bank and finance card accounts to the AI chatbot. (My own answer is “Hell, no.”)

When we delegate a task to an AI system that requires access to any of our personal data, and we’re not expected to check on it again until the task is complete, the potential for disaster here is enormous.

It’s worth prefixing this with a note that the reliability of the paired reports is far from certain. In particular, in a closed-door meeting between Ternus and Federighi, it’s hard to see how the content could have leaked unless one of the two men chose to do this. If Ternus leaked it, that suggests a very high level of frustration on his part. But leaving that aside …

I hope Ternus is pushing Federighi for improved software quality and not just new features...

We’re currently witnessing an AI arms race, with each company aiming to beat its competitors to next-generation capabilities, even while acknowledging a non-trivial possibility that the pace of development could put humanity’s future at risk.

In my view, the very last thing we need is Apple joining this race. I know it can be frustrating when Apple lags behind other companies in the introduction of some types of new tech, but this is one field in which I would be very happy to see Apple proceed very much more cautiously than others.

What’s your view on this? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

Not every Marvel hero will make it out of Doomsday alive

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Doomsday clock is ticking away. In just over a month, "Avengers: Doomsday” will land in theaters. The arrival of Robert Downey Jr.’s Victor von Doom promises to shake up the Marvel Cinematic Universe in a big way. This could mean waving goodbye to some beloved MCU heroes, because it’s hard to see every single Avenger surviving Doomsday.

“Avengers: Infinity War” saw the Marvel roster ruthlessly culled in a snap of Thanos’ fingers. While most of the heroes were un-blipped in the epic follow-up “Avengers: Endgame,” some deaths have proved rather more permanent, like Black Widow and, of course, Tony Stark, aka Iron Man.

I’m expecting “Doomsday” to have a similarly sizable impact on the MCU, maybe even a bigger one as Marvel looks to get back on track following its wilderness years post “Endgame.” Speculation about who will live and who will die is reaching a fever pitch, so I’m looking at the odds (courtesy of Polymarket) and making a few personal predictions.

Based on Polymarket’s current data (as of Nov. 10), Loki (Tom Hiddleston) is most likely to kick the bucket in “Doomsday,” with his brother, the God of Thunder himself, in second place. If both these predictions came true, Doomsday would be particularly brutal on the Thor family.

Spider-Man comes in third — an interesting prediction considering Spidey isn’t actually confirmed to appear (but is rumored). Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie), who’s taken up the mantle as Captain America, and Ant-Man (Paul Rudd) round out the top five, and the death of either character would hit longtime viewers hard, as Mackie and Rudd have been MCU staples for years.

At the foot of the list is Doctor Doom himself, though only with 9% odds, which feels appropriate. Surely Marvel will want to take Doom into 2027’s “Avengers: Secret Wars.” Frankly, all this Doomsday build-up leading to a titular villain who’s defeated after a single movie would be quite an anticlimax. I reckon Doom, like Thanos before him, is a multi-movie foe.

Diving into my personal predictions, I’ll guess first that Loki is safe. The trickster god was choked out in the opening scene of “Infinity War”; his death was used to display the overwhelming threat that Thanos posed. Multiverse shenanigans saw his return in his own Disney+ series, but killing off Loki a second time probably won’t have the same effect. I reckon Loki will survive.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Over the summer, Marvel teased that Ryan Reynolds’ Deadpool and Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine will return after teaming up in “Deadpool & Wolverine” for “Doomsday,” and I could totally see them getting on the wrong side of Dr. Doctor and meeting a grisly fate. Plus, both have healing factors, so Marvel could always rely on that to revive them later down the line if desired.

I expect the Fantastic Four to be safe, alongside Black Panther (Letitia Wright). But the Thunderbolts, rechristened The New Avengers, might take casualties. I think Florence Pugh’s Yelena will make it to the credits alive, but David Harbour’s Red Guardian might not. Ghost (Hannah John-Kamen) also looks in a precarious position, but, sorry to be blunt, I’m not sure killing off Ghost would even register with most viewers; the character is forgettable.

Based on the trailers, “Doomsday” is building around some of the MCU's original stars, namely Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans and Chris Hemsworth. As mentioned, I think Downey Jr.’s grand return will last beyond one Avengers movie, but the fate of Evans’ Steve Rogers and Hemsworth’s Thor is definitely up in the air. Thor especially has been a linchpin of the MCU since Phase One, so if Hemsworth is ready to hang up his hammer, Thor snuffing it in a showdown with Doom would probably leave fans in floods of tears.

“Avengers: Doomsday” is assembling one of the most stacked casts in Hollywood blockbuster history, and with so many returning characters from across the MCU (and beyond—Fox’s “X-Men” universe is also represented), it feels like at least some characters won’t make it. The clock is ticking, and come December 18, we’ll finally find out which Marvel heroes live or die.

Related Stories Documentary Riz Ahmed Boards Elham Ehsas' Short Film 'Forgotten Spaceman' About Afghanistan's First Astronaut Documentary IDFA Announces Competition Lineups, Adds 'Musk' And Elizabeth Holmes Documentary 'You Can See Everything'

The documentary contrasts ancient traditions in Kazanlak, Bulgaria’s “Valley of Roses,” with the town’s major industry – the Arsenal weapons factory. That defense contractor, founded in the 19th century, “provides work for thousands of people manufacturing weapons and ammunition,” according to a synopsis. “Through the lives of four residents, Tejedor examines the place this industry occupies in the town’s economy and identity, and the questions it raises for those whose lives depend on it.” Watch on Deadline

“The Big Boom! brings us face to face with a contradiction at the heart of today’s Europe – a town making the weapons of war while struggling with its own loyalties and beliefs,” commented Lightdox CEO Anna Berthollet. “Gabriel Tejedor finds a way into this reality that feels both clear-eyed and deeply human. As someone of Bulgarian origin myself, I find his sensitive portrayal of Kazanlak and its people particularly meaningful. He reveals the layers of history, identity and geopolitical influence that shape the region without reducing them to a political argument. We’re delighted to bring this timely film to audiences worldwide.”

The Big Boom! is the fifth feature directed by Tejedor, the filmmaker and journalist “whose work explores utopias and the relationship between individuals and authority across the former Soviet Union and its satellite states.”

“I have never been interested in war or weapons. But the invasion of Ukraine shattered my convictions,” Tejedor said in a statement. “Ever since, one question has haunted me: what does it mean to be a pacifist today? I do not judge the workers at Arsenal, nor the local population. The Big Boom! does not seek to lecture, but to confront the grey zones of a continent trapped in its own paradoxes.”

The film is a production of Mira Film Basel GmbH, co-produced by RTS Radio Télévision Suisse, SRG SSR, with the support of Swiss and regional film funds and cultural institutions.

Susanna Guggenberger produced The Big Boom! Cinematography is by Thomas Szczepanski; Christine Hoffet edited the film. The score is composed by Petar Dundakov.
